steps.overview: This step explains how one web request travels from a browser to a server and back: DNS, TCP or UDP, TLS, HTTP versions, status codes and connection reuse. It also teaches the latency numbers and quick estimates (QPS, storage, bandwidth) that every design interview and architect exam depends on. Questions about Route 53, load balancers (Layer 4 vs Layer 7), CDNs and timeouts on SAA-C03, GCP PCA and AZ-305 all assume this foundation.
objectives: Trace a URL request from DNS resolution to the rendered page, naming each round trip.
Compare TCP and UDP, and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and pick the right one for a workload.
Interpret common HTTP status codes, especially 3xx, 4xx and 5xx errors returned by load balancers.
Use approximate latency numbers to explain why caches, CDNs and same-region placement matter.
Produce a back-of-the-envelope estimate of QPS, daily storage and bandwidth for a given user base.

concepts.explanation: A client (browser, mobile app) sends a request and a server returns a response. The server keeps no memory of earlier requests unless you add state such as cookies, sessions or a database. Stateless servers are easy to scale horizontally behind a load balancer, which is why exams prefer them.

The browser checks its own cache, then the OS cache, then asks a recursive resolver. On a miss, the resolver asks a root server, then the TLD server (.com, .in), then the domain's authoritative name server, which returns the record (A, AAAA, CNAME). Each answer is cached for its TTL, so a low TTL allows fast failover but creates more DNS queries.

TCP is connection-oriented. It uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), and gives ordered, reliable delivery with retransmission and congestion control. UDP has no handshake and no delivery guarantee, so it has lower overhead. UDP suits DNS queries, video calls, gaming and QUIC. On AWS, a Network Load Balancer handles TCP and UDP at Layer 4.

TLS is negotiated after the TCP connection is open. The two sides agree on a cipher, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive session keys. TLS 1.2 needs about 2 round trips. TLS 1.3 needs 1, and supports 0-RTT resumption for returning clients. Terminating TLS at a load balancer or CDN removes this work from the backend servers.

HTTP/1.1 is text-based and uses persistent connections by default, but each connection carries one request at a time, so a slow response blocks the ones behind it (head-of-line blocking). HTTP/2 uses binary framing, multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK, but packet loss in TCP still stalls every stream. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. It has TLS 1.3 built in and independent streams, and it supports connection migration when the client's network changes.

Reusing one TCP+TLS connection for many requests avoids repeating the handshakes, which saves one or more round trips on every request. Servers and load balancers close connections that stay idle too long. The AWS ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds. If the backend's keep-alive timeout is shorter than the load balancer's, the backend may close a connection the balancer is still using, which causes intermittent 502 errors.

2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a client error and 5xx a server error. Know these pairs: 301 (permanent) vs 302 (temporary) redirect, 304 Not Modified (cache still valid), 401 (not authenticated) vs 403 (authenticated but not allowed), 404, 429 Too Many Requests (rate limited). On the server side: 500 is a generic error, 502 means the upstream sent a bad response, 503 means no capacity or no healthy target, and 504 means the upstream timed out.

concepts.term: Latency numbers every engineer should know
concepts.explanation: These are orders of magnitude, not exact figures. L1 cache is about 1 ns, main memory about 100 ns, an SSD random read about 100 µs, and a round trip inside one data centre about 0.5 ms. An HDD seek takes about 10 ms, and a cross-continent round trip about 100–150 ms. The lesson: memory is roughly 1,000× faster than SSD, and the network across continents is the slowest part. That is why we cache in memory (Redis) and serve content from the edge (CDN).

State your assumptions, then multiply step by step. Average QPS = daily requests ÷ 86,400 (round this to 10^5). Peak QPS = average × 2–3. Daily storage = writes per day × object size × number of replicas. Bandwidth = daily bytes served ÷ 86,400, converted to Gbps. Interviewers grade your reasoning and orders of magnitude, not exact digits.

keyFacts: A day has 86,400 seconds; use about 10^5 for quick maths. 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 requests/second on average.
Peak traffic is usually taken as 2–3× the average; say which multiplier you used.

Before the first byte arrives, a new HTTPS connection costs: DNS lookup (on a cache miss) + 1 RTT for the TCP handshake + 1 RTT for TLS 1.3 (2 RTT for TLS 1.2). HTTP/3 combines the transport and TLS handshakes into 1 RTT.
HTTP/2 removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking but not TCP-level blocking; HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) removes both.

Layer 7 (AWS ALB, GCP external HTTP(S) LB, Azure Application Gateway) routes on HTTP path and host. Layer 4 (AWS NLB, Azure Load Balancer) forwards TCP/UDP and is used when you need UDP, static IPs or very high throughput.

DNS TTL controls the trade-off between how fast a failover takes effect and how many queries reach the DNS servers. Route 53 alias records can point the zone apex (example.com) to AWS resources such as ALB and CloudFront.
A 502 or 504 from a load balancer points to the backend (bad response or timeout); a 503 usually means no healthy targets; a 429 means you are being rate limited.
Storage units: 1 KB = 10^3 bytes, 1 MB = 10^6, 1 GB = 10^9, 1 TB = 10^12. Bytes/second × 8 = bits/second (network links are measured in bits).

example.caption: Worked estimate: photo-sharing app with 10 million daily active users (state assumptions first)
example.code:
ASSUMPTIONS
  DAU = 10,000,000
  Uploads: 20% of users post 1 photo/day  -> 2,000,000 photos/day
  Stored size per photo (original + thumbnails) ~ 2 MB
  Views: each user sees 50 photos/day     -> 500,000,000 views/day
  Average served image (resized for mobile) ~ 200 KB
  Peak factor = 3x, replication factor = 3

WRITE QPS
  2,000,000 / 86,400 ~ 23/s average -> ~70/s at peak
READ QPS
  500,000,000 / 86,400 ~ 5,800/s average -> ~17,000/s at peak
  Read:write ratio ~ 250:1  => read-heavy; use cache + CDN

STORAGE
  2,000,000 x 2 MB = 4 TB/day raw
  x3 replicas      = 12 TB/day (object stores like S3 handle
                     redundancy for you, so count 4 TB billed)
  Per year: 4 TB x 365 ~ 1.5 PB raw

EGRESS BANDWIDTH
  500,000,000 x 200 KB = 100 TB/day
  100e12 B / 86,400 s ~ 1.16 GB/s ~ 9.3 Gbps average, ~28 Gbps peak
  Ingress: 4 TB/day ~ 46 MB/s ~ 0.4 Gbps

DESIGN TAKEAWAYS
  Store images in object storage (S3), serve via CDN (CloudFront).
  Keep metadata in a database; cache hot feeds in Redis.

pitfalls: Starting to calculate without stating assumptions (DAU, actions per user, object size, peak factor). Interviewers want to see these first.
Mixing up bits and bytes: network links are measured in Gbps, storage in GB. Forgetting the ×8 conversion makes your answer 8 times wrong.
Saying HTTP/2 fixes all head-of-line blocking. It fixes it only at the HTTP layer; TCP packet loss still stalls every stream until HTTP/3 (QUIC).
Choosing an Application Load Balancer for UDP traffic (gaming, VoIP, DNS). Exams expect a Network Load Balancer (Layer 4) here.
Confusing 401 with 403, and 502 with 504. 401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but forbidden. 502 is a bad upstream response; 504 is an upstream timeout.
Leaving a high DNS TTL on records you may need to fail over. Clients keep using the old IP until the TTL expires.

workflow.title: What happens when you type https://example.com and press Enter

steps.label: Parse URL, check caches
steps.detail: The browser reads the scheme, host and path, then checks its HSTS list and its DNS cache and the OS cache for the host's IP.

steps.label: Resolve DNS
steps.detail: On a cache miss, the recursive resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative servers and returns an A/AAAA record, which is cached for its TTL.

steps.label: Open TCP or QUIC
steps.detail: The browser does a TCP three-way handshake (1 RTT), or a QUIC handshake over UDP for HTTP/3, to the IP of the CDN edge or load balancer.

steps.label: Negotiate TLS
steps.detail: Client and server agree on TLS 1.3 keys, the certificate is validated against a trusted CA, and ALPN selects h2 or h3.

steps.label: Send HTTP request
steps.detail: The browser sends GET / with headers and cookies; the CDN or load balancer routes it to a healthy backend, which may read from a cache or database.

steps.label: Receive response and status
steps.detail: The server returns a status code (200, 301, 304, 5xx), headers such as Cache-Control, and the HTML body over the kept-alive connection.

steps.label: Render the page
steps.detail: The browser parses HTML, fetches CSS, JS and images over the same multiplexed connection, builds the DOM and CSSOM, then lays out and paints.

project.summary: A dependency-free Python lab that traces one web request phase by phase (DNS, TCP, TLS with ALPN, HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, status codes) and estimates daily storage, peak QPS and bandwidth for a photo-sharing app with 10 million daily users. server.py and trace_url.py show the request path, latency_numbers.py shows why round trips cost time, and estimate.py with config/photo_app.json does the hands-on estimation task.

files.code:
# request-path-lab (Step 1: Foundations)

Pure Python 3.10+ standard library. No installs.

## Files
- `config/photo_app.json` : assumptions for the estimate (change them and re-run).
- `estimate.py` : back-of-the-envelope QPS, storage per day and bandwidth.
- `latency_numbers.py` : latency numbers and handshake cost per protocol.
- `server.py` : tiny HTTP/1.1 server with keep-alive and real status codes.
- `trace_url.py` : times DNS -> TCP -> TLS -> first byte, then reuses the connection.

## Hands-on result (default config)
| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Uploads per day | 2,000,000 |
| Write QPS avg / peak (x3) | ~23 / ~69 |
| Read QPS avg / peak (x3) | ~11,574 / ~34,722 |
| New storage per day (1 copy) | ~4.6 TB |
| Storage per day (3 replicas) | ~13.8 TB |
| 5-year storage (3 replicas) | ~25 PB |
| Image egress avg / peak | ~18.5 Gbps / ~55.6 Gbps |

What this tells an interviewer: the system is read-heavy (~500:1),
so put images on object storage behind a CDN and cache feeds.
Writes are small in QPS but large in bytes.

## Try the request path
1. `PORT=8080 python3 server.py`
2. `python3 trace_url.py http://localhost:8080/` : no TLS step on plain HTTP.
   The server log shows the same client port for both requests = keep-alive.
3. `python3 trace_url.py http://localhost:8080/old` : 301 with a Location header.
   Also try `/limited` (429) and `/down` (503) and `/missing` (404).
4. `python3 trace_url.py https://example.com/` : shows TLS version and the
   ALPN protocol the server would pick (h2 means HTTP/2 is supported).

## Checkpoint script (say it in under 3 minutes)
1. Browser parses URL, checks HSTS and its caches.
2. DNS: browser/OS cache -> recursive resolver -> root -> TLD -> authoritative.
3. TCP 3-way handshake (1 RTT). For HTTP/3 this is QUIC over UDP instead.
4. TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT; QUIC merges transport + TLS into 1 RTT).
   ALPN picks h2 or http/1.1. Certificate is checked against the hostname.
5. HTTP request; server (often via CDN / load balancer) returns a status code.
6. Connection is kept alive and reused for CSS, JS, images.
7. Browser builds DOM + CSSOM, runs JS, lays out and paints the page.

## Notes
- Timings vary by network; run a few times and compare.
- trace_url.py speaks HTTP/1.1 only. HTTP/2 needs a framing library;
  here we only detect support through ALPN.

{
  "_comment": "Assumptions for a photo-sharing app. Decimal units: 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.",
  "daily_active_users": 10000000,
  "uploads_per_user_per_day": 0.2,
  "photo_views_per_user_per_day": 100,
  "peak_to_average_ratio": 3,
  "original_photo_bytes": 2000000,
  "thumbnail_bytes_total": 300000,
  "metadata_bytes": 1000,
  "served_image_bytes": 200000,
  "replication_factor": 3,
  "retention_years": 5
}

"""Back-of-the-envelope estimate: QPS, storage per day, bandwidth."""
import json
import sys

SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400  # round to ~100,000 when doing it in your head


def human_bytes(n: float) -> str:
    for unit in ["B", "KB", "MB", "GB", "TB", "PB"]:
        if n < 1000:
            return f"{n:,.1f} {unit}"
        n /= 1000  # decimal units, as cloud billing uses
    return f"{n:,.1f} EB"


def main(path: str = "config/photo_app.json") -> None:
    with open(path) as f:
        c = json.load(f)

    dau = c["daily_active_users"]
    peak = c["peak_to_average_ratio"]

    # 1. Requests per day -> average QPS -> peak QPS
    uploads_day = dau * c["uploads_per_user_per_day"]
    views_day = dau * c["photo_views_per_user_per_day"]
    write_qps = uploads_day / SECONDS_PER_DAY
    read_qps = views_day / SECONDS_PER_DAY

    # 2. Storage: original + thumbnails + metadata row, then replicas
    per_upload = (c["original_photo_bytes"] + c["thumbnail_bytes_total"]
                  + c["metadata_bytes"])
    storage_day = uploads_day * per_upload
    storage_day_repl = storage_day * c["replication_factor"]
    storage_total = storage_day_repl * 365 * c["retention_years"]

    # 3. Bandwidth: bytes served per day -> bits per second
    egress_day = views_day * c["served_image_bytes"]
    egress_gbps = egress_day * 8 / SECONDS_PER_DAY / 1e9
    ingress_gbps = storage_day * 8 / SECONDS_PER_DAY / 1e9

    print(f"Uploads/day          : {uploads_day:,.0f}")
    print(f"Write QPS avg / peak : {write_qps:,.1f} / {write_qps * peak:,.0f}")
    print(f"Read QPS  avg / peak : {read_qps:,.0f} / {read_qps * peak:,.0f}")
    print(f"Read:write ratio     : {read_qps / write_qps:,.0f}:1")
    print(f"Storage/day (1 copy) : {human_bytes(storage_day)}")
    print(f"Storage/day (x{c['replication_factor']})    : {human_bytes(storage_day_repl)}")
    print(f"Storage {c['retention_years']} years      : {human_bytes(storage_total)}")
    print(f"Ingress avg          : {ingress_gbps:,.2f} Gbps")
    print(f"Egress avg / peak    : {egress_gbps:,.1f} / {egress_gbps * peak:,.1f} Gbps")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(*sys.argv[1:])  # optional: path to another config file

"""Approximate latency numbers (order of magnitude matters, not exact values)."""

LATENCY_NS = [
    ("L1 cache reference", 0.5),
    ("Branch mispredict", 5),
    ("L2 cache reference", 7),
    ("Mutex lock/unlock", 25),
    ("Main memory reference", 100),
    ("Send 1 KB over 1 Gbps network", 10_000),
    ("Random 4 KB read from SSD", 150_000),
    ("Read 1 MB sequentially from memory", 250_000),
    ("Round trip within same datacenter", 500_000),
    ("Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD", 1_000_000),
    ("HDD disk seek", 10_000_000),
    ("Read 1 MB sequentially from HDD", 20_000_000),
    ("Packet round trip across continents", 150_000_000),
]

# Round trips needed before the first HTTP request byte can be sent
# (new connection, no session resumption, DNS already cached).
HANDSHAKE_RTTS = {
    "HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.2": 1 + 2,
    "HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.3": 1 + 1,
    "HTTP/3 over QUIC (TLS 1.3 built in)": 1,
    "HTTP/3 QUIC 0-RTT resumption": 0,
    "Reused keep-alive connection": 0,
}


def pretty(ns: float) -> str:
    if ns < 1_000:
        return f"{ns:g} ns"
    if ns < 1_000_000:
        return f"{ns / 1_000:g} us"
    return f"{ns / 1_000_000:g} ms"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for name, ns in LATENCY_NS:
        print(f"{name:<40} {pretty(ns):>10}")

    rtt_ms = 150  # try 2 for same region, 150+ for cross-continent users
    print(f"\nSetup cost before first request at RTT = {rtt_ms} ms")
    for proto, rtts in HANDSHAKE_RTTS.items():
        print(f"{proto:<40} {rtts} RTT = {rtts * rtt_ms} ms")
    # Lesson: memory >> SSD >> network. Cut round trips: keep-alive,
    # TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, and a CDN edge close to the user.

"""Tiny HTTP/1.1 server: keep-alive plus common status codes."""
import os
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

PORT = int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8080"))

# path -> (status, extra headers, body)
ROUTES = {
    "/": (200, {}, "hello from request-path-lab\n"),
    "/old": (301, {"Location": "/"}, "moved permanently\n"),
    "/limited": (429, {"Retry-After": "30"}, "too many requests\n"),
    "/down": (503, {"Retry-After": "60"}, "service unavailable\n"),
}


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    # HTTP/1.1 makes connections persistent by default (keep-alive).
    protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"

    def do_GET(self):
        status, headers, body = ROUTES.get(
            self.path, (404, {}, "not found\n"))
        data = body.encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        # Content-Length lets the client know where this response ends,
        # so the same TCP connection can carry the next request.
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.send_header("Keep-Alive", "timeout=5")
        for name, value in headers.items():
            self.send_header(name, value)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        # Same client port on consecutive lines = connection was reused.
        ip, port = self.client_address[:2]
        print(f"{ip}:{port} {fmt % args}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    Handler.timeout = 5  # close idle keep-alive connections after 5 s
    print(f"Listening on http://localhost:{PORT}")
    ThreadingHTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", PORT), Handler).serve_forever()

"""Trace one URL: DNS -> TCP -> TLS -> HTTP/1.1, then reuse the connection."""
import http.client
import socket
import ssl
import sys
import time
from urllib.parse import urlsplit


def ms(t0: float) -> str:
    return f"{(time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000:.1f} ms"


def probe_alpn(host: str, addr: tuple) -> str:
    # Offer h2 like a browser does; we only read the answer, then close.
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    ctx.set_alpn_protocols(["h2", "http/1.1"])
    with socket.create_connection(addr, timeout=5) as raw:
        with ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=host) as tls:
            return tls.selected_alpn_protocol() or "none"


def trace(url: str) -> None:
    u = urlsplit(url)
    https = u.scheme == "https"
    host, port = u.hostname, u.port or (443 if https else 80)
    path = u.path or "/"

    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # 1. DNS (OS resolver + caches)
    info = socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, type=socket.SOCK_STREAM)[0]
    addr = info[4][:2]
    print(f"1. DNS   {host} -> {addr[0]}  {ms(t0)}")

    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # 2. TCP three-way handshake = 1 RTT
    sock = socket.create_connection(addr, timeout=5)
    print(f"2. TCP   connected to {addr[0]}:{port}  {ms(t0)}")

    if https:  # 3. TLS handshake; certificate checked against host name
        ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
        ctx.set_alpn_protocols(["http/1.1"])  # we speak HTTP/1.1 below
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        sock = ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=host)
        print(f"3. TLS   {sock.version()} {sock.cipher()[0]}  {ms(t0)}")
        print(f"   ALPN if h2 offered: {probe_alpn(host, addr)}")
    else:
        print("3. TLS   skipped (plain http)")

    conn = http.client.HTTPConnection(host, port)
    conn.sock = sock  # reuse our timed socket instead of opening a new one
    for i in (1, 2):  # 4. Two requests on ONE connection = keep-alive
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        conn.request("GET", path, headers={"Connection": "keep-alive"})
        resp = conn.getresponse()
        body = resp.read()
        print(f"4.{i} HTTP {resp.status} {resp.reason}, {len(body)} bytes, "
              f"{ms(t0)} (no new handshake)")
        if resp.getheader("Location"):
            print(f"   redirect -> {resp.getheader('Location')}")
        if resp.will_close:  # server said Connection: close
            print("   server closed the connection; no reuse")
            break
    conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    trace(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "http://localhost:8080/")

objective.question: A service receives 1 million requests per day, spread evenly. Which is the closest average request rate?
options: About 12 requests per second
About 1,200 requests per second
About 120 requests per second
About 1.2 requests per second
objective.explanation: 1,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 11.6, so about 12 requests per second. The other options are off by one or more powers of ten.

objective.question: A browser opens a brand-new HTTPS connection over TCP with TLS 1.3. The DNS answer is already cached. How many network round trips must finish before the browser can send its first HTTP request?
options: 1 round trip
3 round trips
2 round trips
0 round trips
objective.explanation: The TCP handshake takes 1 RTT and the TLS 1.3 handshake takes 1 more, so 2 RTT in total. TLS 1.2 would make it 3 RTT. QUIC (HTTP/3) would make it 1 RTT.

objective.question: A mobile app runs on networks with frequent packet loss. It already uses HTTP/2, but one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection. Which change removes this stall?
options: Enable HPACK header compression
Raise the TCP receive window size
Move to HTTP/3, which runs over QUIC on UDP
Go back to HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive
objective.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, so a lost TCP segment blocks every stream (TCP-level head-of-line blocking). QUIC delivers each stream independently, which removes this. Header compression and window tuning do not change TCP's in-order delivery.

objective.question: A company is moving a multiplayer game server to AWS. The game uses UDP. Partners must allow-list fixed IP addresses, and traffic reaches millions of packets per second. Which load balancer fits best?
options: Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Amazon CloudFront with an origin group
Network Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
objective.explanation: NLB works at Layer 4, supports UDP, can have a static Elastic IP per Availability Zone, and handles very high throughput. ALB is Layer 7 and supports only HTTP/HTTPS. CloudFront is a CDN, not a UDP load balancer for game servers.

objective.question: Users see HTTP 504 errors from an Application Load Balancer during heavy report generation. Other pages work. What is the most likely cause?
options: The backend target did not respond before the load balancer's timeout
The TLS certificate on the listener has expired
No targets are registered in the target group
The client is being rate limited
objective.explanation: A 504 Gateway Timeout means the load balancer waited for the backend and got no response in time. This fits slow report requests. Rate limiting returns 429, no healthy targets usually gives 503, and an expired certificate breaks the TLS handshake before any HTTP status is returned.

objective.question: After a bad deployment, every request to a load-balanced web app returns HTTP 503. What should you check first?
options: Whether the DNS TTL is too high
Whether clients have reached their API rate limit
Whether HTTP/2 is enabled on the listener
Whether the health checks are failing so that no targets are healthy
objective.explanation: A 503 from a load balancer usually means it has no healthy targets to send traffic to. A bad deployment that fails health checks causes exactly this. DNS TTL, rate limits (429) and HTTP/2 settings would not cause 503s on every request.

objective.question: A team uses DNS-based failover between two regions. They want failover to take effect within about a minute. What is the trade-off of setting a low TTL such as 60 seconds?
options: TCP connections are reset every 60 seconds
TLS sessions cannot be resumed
More DNS queries reach the authoritative servers, which raises query volume and cost
Resolvers cache records for longer, so failover gets slower
objective.explanation: A low TTL makes resolvers re-query often, so changes spread quickly but query volume rises. A high TTL does the opposite. TTL has no effect on TCP resets or TLS session resumption.

objective.question: You want the zone apex example.com to point to an Application Load Balancer, using Amazon Route 53. Which record should you create?
options: An A record with the ALB's current IP addresses
A Route 53 alias record pointing to the ALB
An MX record pointing to the ALB
A CNAME record at the apex pointing to the ALB DNS name
objective.explanation: DNS rules do not allow a CNAME at the zone apex. ALB IP addresses change, so a fixed A record will break. A Route 53 alias record can point the apex to AWS resources such as ALB and CloudFront.

objective.question: A video service sends 100 MB per second of data to users. What network link capacity does this need, before headroom?
options: 800 Mbps
12.5 Mbps
8 Gbps
100 Mbps
objective.explanation: Network links are measured in bits, so 100 MB/s × 8 = 800 megabits per second. 12.5 Mbps is the result of dividing by 8 instead of multiplying.

objective.question: Users of an app upload 5 million photos per day. The average stored size is 200 KB. Using decimal units and ignoring replication, how much new storage is needed per day?
options: About 10 TB
About 1 PB
About 1 TB
About 100 GB
objective.explanation: 5 × 10^6 × 2 × 10^5 bytes = 10^12 bytes = 1 TB per day. The other options come from slipping one or more powers of ten.

objective.question: Which list is ordered correctly from fastest to slowest, using the commonly quoted latency numbers?
options: SSD random read, main memory reference, packet round trip between continents, HDD disk seek
Main memory reference, HDD disk seek, SSD random read, packet round trip between continents
Packet round trip between continents, HDD disk seek, SSD random read, main memory reference
Main memory reference, SSD random read, HDD disk seek, packet round trip between continents
objective.explanation: Typical orders of magnitude are: memory about 100 ns, SSD random read tens to hundreds of microseconds, disk seek about 10 ms, and a round trip between continents about 150 ms. The other lists break this order.

objective.question: A web page loads 40 small assets from the same origin over HTTPS with HTTP/1.1. Why does enabling keep-alive (persistent connections) make the page load faster?
options: It reuses open TCP and TLS connections, so each request avoids new handshake round trips
It sends all 40 requests in parallel over one connection with full multiplexing
It makes the browser skip DNS lookups
It compresses HTTP headers
objective.explanation: Keep-alive keeps the TCP and TLS connection open for later requests, so you avoid repeated handshake RTTs. Header compression and true multiplexing are HTTP/2 features. DNS caching is a separate mechanism.

objective.question: A company moves its REST API from api-old.example.com to api.example.com. Some third-party clients still send POST requests to the old host. The team wants a permanent redirect that clients must follow with the same method and body. Which response should the old host return?
options: 302 Found
307 Temporary Redirect
308 Permanent Redirect
301 Moved Permanently
objective.explanation: 308 is permanent and requires the client to repeat the same method and body. Many clients turn a POST into a GET after a 301 or 302. 307 keeps the method too, but it is temporary, so clients and caches will not treat the move as permanent.

objective.question: A team enables TLS 1.3 0-RTT (early data) on its edge proxy to cut latency for returning users. A security review flags a risk. Which requests should the proxy accept as early data?
options: All requests, because TLS 1.3 early data has the same replay protection as normal data
No requests carrying cookies, because early data is sent in plaintext
Only POST requests, because they carry a body that is encrypted
Only idempotent requests such as GET, because early data can be replayed by an attacker
objective.explanation: 0-RTT data is encrypted, but it has no protection against replay. Limit it to safe, idempotent requests such as GET. A replayed POST could repeat an action, for example a payment. Early data is not plaintext, so the cookie option is wrong.

objective.question: Users of a ride-hailing app often move from home Wi-Fi to mobile data in the middle of a session. Each switch forces a new TCP and TLS handshake, and in-flight requests fail. Which protocol feature addresses this directly?
options: QUIC connection IDs in HTTP/3, which let a connection survive a change of client IP address
TCP keep-alive probes with a shorter interval
TLS session tickets with a longer lifetime
HTTP/2 multiplexing over a single TCP connection
objective.explanation: A TCP connection is identified by its IP and port 4-tuple, so it breaks when the client IP changes. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID, which allows migration to the new network path. Session tickets only shorten the next handshake. Keep-alive and multiplexing do not survive an IP change.

objective.question: An engineer creates a new record for new.example.com. Ten minutes later some users still get 'host not found'. Before creating the record, the engineer ran the query below. What explains the delay?

code.code:
$ dig new.example.com A
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN
;; AUTHORITY SECTION:
example.com. 3600 IN SOA ns1.example.com. admin.example.com. (
    2026010101 7200 900 1209600 3600 )

options: Resolvers cached the NXDOMAIN answer, and can keep it for up to 3600 seconds based on the SOA record
The SOA refresh value of 7200 seconds blocks updates on the authoritative server
The registrar takes 24–48 hours to publish any new record
The new record's TTL has not expired yet
objective.explanation: This is negative caching. Resolvers cache an NXDOMAIN for the lower of the SOA record's TTL and its minimum field, here 3600 seconds. The new record's own TTL does not matter until that negative entry expires. Refresh controls secondary-server sync, not resolver caches.

objective.question: What does this NGINX reverse-proxy configuration achieve?
options: It keeps up to 32 idle persistent connections per worker to the upstreams, so NGINX avoids a new TCP handshake per request
It upgrades all upstream traffic to HTTP/2
It closes client connections after 32 requests
It limits each client to 32 concurrent requests
objective.explanation: `keepalive 32` keeps a pool of idle upstream connections in each worker process. For reuse to work, NGINX must speak HTTP/1.1 and clear the Connection header; by default it sends HTTP/1.0 with 'Connection: close'. The setting does not limit clients or change the protocol to HTTP/2.

objective.question: A news app has 100 million daily active users. Each user makes about 10 read requests per day. Assume peak traffic is 3 times the average. What is the approximate peak read QPS?
options: About 35,000
About 350,000
About 11,500
About 3,500
objective.explanation: 100M × 10 = 1 billion requests per day. Divide by about 86,400 seconds to get roughly 11,500 average QPS. Multiply by 3 for the peak, which gives about 35,000. The 11,500 option is the average, not the peak.

objective.question: A company runs a dynamic HTTPS API on an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1. Users in India and Australia report slow first requests, mostly caused by TCP and TLS handshakes over long round trips. Responses cannot be cached. Which solution reduces this latency with the least change?
options: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer to remove Layer 7 processing
Increase the ALB idle timeout so connections stay open longer
Lower the Route 53 TTL for the API record to 60 seconds
Put Amazon CloudFront in front of the ALB with caching disabled for the API, so TLS ends at nearby edge locations and the edge reuses connections to the origin
objective.explanation: CloudFront ends TCP and TLS close to the user. It then sends requests over persistent connections on the AWS backbone, which helps even when nothing is cached. DNS TTL does not affect handshake time. An NLB still needs handshakes over the long path. The idle timeout only helps connections that are already open.

subjective.question: Walk me through what happens when you type https://www.example.com into a browser and press Enter, up to the rendered page.
subjective.answer: The browser parses the URL and checks its own cache, the OS cache and then a recursive resolver for the IP address. On a cache miss, the resolver asks a root server, then the .com TLD server, then the authoritative server, and caches the answer for its TTL. The browser then opens a TCP connection with a three-way handshake, which costs 1 RTT. Next comes the TLS 1.3 handshake, 1 more RTT, where the server proves its identity with a certificate and both sides agree on keys. With HTTP/3, QUIC merges these two steps into 1 RTT. The browser sends a GET request. It usually first reaches a CDN or load balancer, which forwards it to an app server, which may call caches and databases. The response comes back with a status code such as 200. The browser parses the HTML, builds the DOM and CSSOM, fetches CSS, JS and images over the same reused connections, runs scripts, then does layout and paint.
keyPoints: DNS resolution chain and caching with TTL
TCP handshake 1 RTT plus TLS 1.3 1 RTT, or 1 RTT total with QUIC
HTTP request passes through CDN or load balancer to backend
Status code and response headers
Browser parsing, sub-resource fetches over reused connections, render

subjective.question: Compare TCP and UDP. Give one real use case where each is the better choice.
subjective.answer: TCP is connection-oriented. It needs a handshake, delivers bytes reliably and in order, retransmits lost segments, and has flow and congestion control. That makes it right for web pages, APIs, database connections and file transfer, where every byte must arrive correctly. The cost is handshake latency and head-of-line blocking: one lost segment holds up all data behind it. UDP has no connection setup and no built-in reliability or ordering. It just sends datagrams. That suits live voice and video, online games and DNS queries, where a late packet is useless and speed matters more. Many modern protocols build reliability on top of UDP only where needed. QUIC, which carries HTTP/3, is the main example: it adds per-stream reliability and encryption over UDP, so it avoids TCP's head-of-line blocking. On the cloud, UDP workloads need a Layer 4 load balancer such as AWS NLB or Azure Load Balancer.
keyPoints: TCP: reliable, ordered, handshake, congestion control
UDP: connectionless, no delivery guarantee, low overhead
TCP use case: APIs, databases; UDP use case: VoIP, gaming, DNS
QUIC builds reliability on top of UDP
UDP needs a Layer 4 load balancer

subjective.question: Explain the TLS handshake. Why is TLS 1.3 faster than TLS 1.2?
subjective.answer: TLS does three jobs. It authenticates the server with a certificate, agrees on shared session keys, and then encrypts the traffic. In TLS 1.2, the client sends ClientHello and the server replies with ServerHello, its certificate and key-exchange parameters. The client then sends its key-exchange message and Finished, and the server sends its Finished. That takes 2 round trips before application data can flow. TLS 1.3 cut the number of options, keeping only forward-secret key exchanges such as ECDHE. Because of this, the client can send its key share in the very first message. The server replies with its key share, certificate and Finished in one flight, so the handshake needs only 1 RTT. TLS 1.3 also supports session resumption and optional 0-RTT early data, although 0-RTT carries replay risk. On a 100 ms RTT link, saving one round trip saves 100 ms on every new connection. In practice, TLS usually terminates at the load balancer or CDN, which is the reason to place those close to users.
keyPoints: Goals: authentication, key agreement, encryption
TLS 1.2 handshake costs 2 RTT
TLS 1.3 sends the key share in the first flight, so 1 RTT
Resumption and 0-RTT, with replay caveat
TLS termination at the load balancer or CDN

subjective.question: How do HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ? When would you push for HTTP/3?
subjective.answer: HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol. It has persistent connections, but a connection handles one request at a time. Browsers open about six connections per host to get parallelism, and a slow response blocks the ones behind it on that connection. HTTP/2 is binary. It multiplexes many streams over a single TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK. This removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking and makes hacks like domain sharding unnecessary. However, everything still rides on one TCP connection, so one lost packet stalls all streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which uses UDP. Streams are independent, so a loss affects only its own stream. The transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are combined into 1 RTT, and connection migration lets a phone switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data without reconnecting. I would push for HTTP/3 when many users are on mobile or lossy networks with high RTT, which is common in India. CDNs and cloud HTTP load balancers increasingly support it, with a fallback to HTTP/2.
keyPoints: HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection, multiple connections
HTTP/2: binary, multiplexing, HPACK, but TCP head-of-line blocking remains
HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP, independent streams, 1-RTT setup
Connection migration helps mobile users
Choose HTTP/3 for lossy, high-latency mobile users

subjective.question: What are keep-alive and connection pooling, and why do they matter between services as well as for browsers?
subjective.answer: Keep-alive means the TCP connection, and the TLS session on top of it, stays open after a response so that later requests reuse it. HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default. Without this, every request would pay a fresh TCP handshake and TLS handshake, which is 2 RTT before any data moves, plus CPU for the key exchange. Connection pooling is the server-side version of the same idea. An app server keeps a pool of open connections to a database, a cache or another service and hands them out to requests. Between services this matters a lot. A microservice making thousands of calls per second could otherwise exhaust ephemeral ports, pile up sockets in TIME_WAIT, and spend CPU on handshakes. The trade-offs are that idle connections use memory and file descriptors, and that idle timeouts must line up across layers. For example, a backend's keep-alive timeout should be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout, or you can see intermittent 502 errors.
keyPoints: Reuse avoids repeated TCP and TLS handshake RTTs
Connection pools for databases and downstream services
Prevents port exhaustion and TIME_WAIT build-up
Idle connections cost memory and file descriptors
Align idle timeouts between load balancer and backend

subjective.question: Estimate the daily storage and peak QPS for a photo-sharing app with 10 million daily active users. State your assumptions.
subjective.answer: Assumptions: 10% of users upload one photo a day, which gives 1 million uploads per day. The average stored size is 2 MB, covering the original plus resized versions. Each user views 50 photos a day. Storage: 10^6 × 2 × 10^6 bytes = 2 × 10^12 bytes, so 2 TB per day. With 3× replication that is about 6 TB of raw capacity per day, roughly 2 PB a year, which points to object storage such as S3 with lifecycle tiering. Metadata at about 1 KB per photo is only about 1 GB a day. Write QPS: 10^6 divided by about 10^5 seconds gives about 10 per second on average. With a 3× peak multiplier, that is about 30 per second. Read QPS: 500 million views a day divided by 10^5 gives about 5,000 per second on average, or 15,000 per second at 3× peak. The system is read-heavy, with a read-to-write ratio of about 500:1. So images should be served from a CDN and metadata from a cache, while writes stay modest.
keyPoints: Clear, stated assumptions for upload rate, size and views
Storage of about 2 TB/day, plus replication and yearly growth
Use about 10^5 seconds per day for quick maths
Peak multiplier stated explicitly (3×)
Read-heavy ratio drives CDN and cache decisions

subjective.question: For the same photo app, estimate the outbound bandwidth and say what it means for the architecture.
subjective.answer: Assume 500 million photo views per day. Feeds show compressed, resized images, so assume about 200 KB per view, not the 2 MB original. Daily egress is 5 × 10^8 × 2 × 10^5 bytes = 10^14 bytes, which is 100 TB per day. Spread over 86,400 seconds, that is about 1.2 GB per second on average. Multiplying by 8 to convert to bits gives about 9 to 10 Gbps. With a 3× peak multiplier, that is close to 30 Gbps. Ingress from uploads is far smaller: 2 TB a day is about 23 MB/s, or under 200 Mbps. What this means: serving 30 Gbps from origin servers would be expensive and slow for far-away users. So a CDN such as CloudFront, Cloud CDN or Azure Front Door should absorb most reads, with high cache hit rates on popular images. Serving the right image size per device, and modern formats like WebP or AVIF, directly cut this number. Egress cost usually becomes a major line item in the budget.
keyPoints: Use served size, not original size, for read bandwidth
Convert bytes to bits by multiplying by 8
Average about 10 Gbps, peak about 30 Gbps at 3×
Ingress is much smaller than egress
CDN, right-sized images and egress cost

subjective.question: Explain how DNS resolution works and how TTL affects failover design.
subjective.answer: The client's stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP, a public service or the cloud VPC. If the answer is not cached, the resolver asks a root server, which points it to the TLD servers, for example .com. The TLD server points to the domain's authoritative name servers, such as Route 53, Cloud DNS or Azure DNS, and those return the record. Every layer caches the answer for the record's TTL. DNS queries mostly use UDP port 53 and fall back to TCP for large responses. TTL is a trade-off. A low TTL, such as 60 seconds, means a change or health-check-based failover reaches users quickly, but it creates more queries and slightly more lookup latency. A high TTL, such as hours, reduces load but leaves users on a dead endpoint for longer. Some resolvers and clients also cache for longer than the TTL. For that reason, critical failover often uses anycast or a global load balancer rather than relying only on DNS.
keyPoints: Stub, recursive, root, TLD, authoritative chain
Caching at every layer for the TTL
UDP port 53, TCP fallback for large responses
Low TTL means fast failover but more queries; high TTL the reverse
Some clients ignore TTL, so consider anycast or a global load balancer

subjective.question: When would you choose a Layer 4 load balancer over a Layer 7 one? Name the options on AWS, GCP and Azure.
subjective.answer: A Layer 7 load balancer understands HTTP. It can route by host and path, for example sending /api to one service and /images to another. It can terminate TLS, rewrite headers, use cookies for stickiness and integrate with a WAF. Examples are AWS Application Load Balancer, the GCP external Application Load Balancer (HTTP(S)) and Azure Application Gateway. A Layer 4 load balancer only sees IP addresses, ports and TCP or UDP. It forwards connections without reading their content. I would choose Layer 4 when the protocol is not HTTP, for example game traffic over UDP, MQTT or a database protocol. I would also choose it when clients need static IP addresses to allow-list, or when I need very high throughput with extremely low added latency. Examples are AWS Network Load Balancer and Azure Load Balancer, and GCP offers network load balancers as well. The trade-off is that Layer 4 loses content-based routing and HTTP-aware health checks, so that logic must live elsewhere.
keyPoints: Layer 7: host and path routing, TLS termination, WAF
Layer 4: TCP/UDP forwarding without reading content
Choose Layer 4 for UDP, static IPs or very high throughput
Correct product names per cloud
Trade-off: loss of content-aware routing

subjective.question: Your API returns a mix of 429, 502, 503 and 504 errors behind a load balancer. How do you read each one, and what do you check?
subjective.answer: A 429 Too Many Requests means a rate limiter is throttling the caller. It could be an API gateway, a WAF rule or the app itself. I check the limits and the client's retry behaviour, and I add backoff with jitter or raise the quota. A 502 Bad Gateway means the load balancer got an invalid response from the backend, or the connection was closed. Common causes are crashing processes, wrong ports, or the backend's keep-alive timeout being shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout. A 503 Service Unavailable from a load balancer usually means there are no healthy targets. That happens when health checks fail after a deploy, when the target group is empty, or when the service is overloaded and shedding load. A 504 Gateway Timeout means the backend did not answer in time. I look for slow database queries, calls to downstream services, or the load balancer timeout being lower than real request times. In all cases I compare load balancer metrics against target metrics and logs to see which layer is failing.
keyPoints: 429 means rate limiting; fix with backoff and quotas
502 means a bad backend response or closed connection
503 means no healthy targets or overload
504 means a backend timeout
Compare load balancer metrics against target logs

subjective.question: Why should engineers know rough latency numbers? Give examples of how they change design decisions.
subjective.answer: Rough numbers tell you where time goes before you write any code. A main memory read is about 100 ns. An SSD random read is tens to hundreds of microseconds. A round trip within one data centre is about 0.5 ms. A disk seek is about 10 ms. A round trip between continents is about 150 ms. These differ by orders of magnitude, and that drives choices. Caching hot data in memory, for example in Redis, beats hitting a disk-backed database on every request. A page that makes 10 sequential calls across regions takes at least 1.5 seconds, so you either parallelise the calls or keep chatty services in one region. For users in India served from a US region, each new HTTPS connection costs several 200 ms-plus round trips. That argues for a CDN or a nearby region such as Mumbai, plus connection reuse and HTTP/3. Compressing data before sending it over the network is usually worth the CPU it costs. The exact values change with hardware, but the ratios between them stay useful.
keyPoints: Know the orders of magnitude: memory, SSD, DC round trip, disk, cross-continent
Memory caches versus disk-backed reads
Sequential remote calls add up; parallelise or co-locate
Place data close to users with a CDN or nearby region
Exact numbers change, but the ratios hold

subjective.question: Explain the client–server model. Why do we prefer stateless application servers when scaling?
subjective.answer: In the client–server model, clients such as browsers or mobile apps send requests, and servers own the resources and business logic and send back responses. Clients never talk to the database directly. That gives one place for security, validation and change. To scale from one server to many, we put a load balancer in front and add identical app servers. This is called horizontal scaling. It works cleanly only if the servers are stateless, meaning no user session or uploaded file lives only in one server's memory or on its local disk. Then any server can handle any request. The load balancer does not need sticky sessions, failed instances can be replaced, and autoscaling can add or remove servers freely. State is moved to shared stores: sessions go to Redis or a database, or into signed tokens such as JWTs, and files go to object storage. Sticky sessions are a workaround, but they cause uneven load and lose sessions when a server dies.
keyPoints: Clients request, servers own logic and data
Horizontal scaling behind a load balancer
Stateless servers mean any instance can serve any request
Move state to Redis, a database, tokens or object storage
Downsides of sticky sessions

subjective.question: A service calls an internal API about 2,000 times per second. Under load it logs 'cannot assign requested address' errors and p99 latency spikes. You run the command below on the caller. What is happening, and how do you fix it?

code.code:
$ ss -s
Total: 61234
TCP:   60890 (estab 112, closed 60511, orphaned 0, timewait 60498)

subjective.answer: About 60,000 sockets are in TIME_WAIT, but only 112 are established. This means the caller opens a new TCP connection for each request and then closes it. The side that closes first keeps the socket in TIME_WAIT for a while. That ties up the ephemeral port for that destination IP and port. At 2,000 new connections per second, the port range runs out, and connect() fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Each new connection also pays a handshake, and a TLS handshake if used, which causes the latency spikes. The real fix is connection reuse. Use an HTTP client with a keep-alive connection pool, sized for the concurrency. Check that neither side sends 'Connection: close'. Make sure the server's idle timeout is longer than the client's, so the server does not close pooled connections first. Short-term relief is possible: widen the ephemeral port range, or enable tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing connections. These only hide the design problem.
keyPoints: TIME_WAIT count far above established count means no connection reuse
Ephemeral port exhaustion causes the 'cannot assign requested address' error
Fix with keep-alive connection pooling in the HTTP client
Align idle timeouts so the client closes idle connections before the server does
Port range or tcp_tw_reuse tuning is a stop-gap, not the fix

subjective.question: Estimate the storage and write QPS for a chat app with 50 million daily active users. Each user sends 40 messages a day, averaging 100 bytes. Messages are kept for 5 years. State your assumptions.
subjective.answer: First, the message count: 50M users × 40 messages = 2 billion messages per day. Write QPS: 2 × 10^9 ÷ ~86,400 seconds is about 23,000 average. If peak is about 3 times the average, plan for roughly 70,000 writes per second. Raw storage: 2B × 100 bytes = 200 GB per day. Metadata such as IDs, timestamps and indexes could double that, so call it about 400 GB per day. Over 5 years: 400 GB × 365 × 5 is about 730 TB. With 3 replicas, that is about 2.2 PB. Conclusions: one database node cannot handle 70k writes per second or petabytes of data. We need a horizontally partitioned store, for example a wide-column database sharded by conversation ID. We should also tier old messages to cheaper storage. I would say out loud that I round 86,400 to 100,000 for quick maths, and that media attachments are out of scope here.
keyPoints: Show the steps clearly: daily volume, then per second, then peak factor
Add overhead for metadata and indexes, and multiply by replication
Round numbers sensibly and say so out loud
Turn the numbers into design decisions such as sharding and tiering
State what is out of scope, for example media files

subjective.question: One load balancer serves shop.example.com and api.example.com on the same IP address, each with its own certificate. A few old clients get certificate name mismatch errors, while modern browsers work. Explain the cause and your options.
subjective.answer: With several certificates on one IP, the server must know which hostname the client wants before it sends a certificate. The client sends this in the TLS ClientHello using the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension. Very old clients, such as some legacy Android versions, old Java runtimes and embedded devices, do not send SNI. The load balancer then returns its default certificate, and the name does not match. On AWS, the ALB and NLB TLS listeners pick a certificate using SNI, and fall back to the listener's default certificate. Options: first, use one certificate that covers both names, either a SAN certificate or a wildcard such as *.example.com, and make it the default. Second, give legacy clients their own endpoint with that name as the default certificate. Third, upgrade or retire those clients. I would check this with `openssl s_client -connect host:443` with and without `-servername`. I would also check that the certificate chain is complete, because missing intermediate certificates cause similar errors on some clients.
keyPoints: SNI carries the hostname in the ClientHello so the server can choose a certificate
Clients without SNI receive the default certificate
Fix with a SAN or wildcard default certificate, or a separate endpoint
Test with openssl s_client with and without -servername
Also check for an incomplete intermediate certificate chain

subjective.question: Explain what these response headers do. Describe what the browser does on a repeat visit after 10 minutes and after 2 hours.

code.code:
HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/javascript
cache-control: public, max-age=3600
etag: "a1b2c3"
last-modified: Mon, 05 Jan 2026 10:00:00 GMT

subjective.answer: `cache-control: public, max-age=3600` lets browsers and shared caches such as CDNs store the file. It stays fresh for one hour. The ETag is a version identifier for the content. Last-Modified is a date-based fallback. After 10 minutes the copy is still fresh, so the browser uses it from cache. No network request is made, and DevTools shows it as 'from memory/disk cache'. After 2 hours the copy is stale, so the browser revalidates it. It sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match: "a1b2c3"`, and possibly `If-Modified-Since`. If the file has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body. That costs only a round trip, and the browser marks its copy fresh again. If the file has changed, the server returns 200 with the new body and a new ETag. For fingerprinted file names such as app.3f9a.js, I would set a long max-age with `immutable` instead, so revalidation is never needed.
keyPoints: max-age sets how long the copy stays fresh; public allows shared caches
A fresh copy is served with no network request
A stale copy is revalidated with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since
304 means no body is sent and the cached copy is reused
Fingerprinted assets can use a long max-age with immutable

subjective.question: Why can a single new TCP connection not use a fast, long-distance link at full speed straight away? Explain how this affects the design of large downloads and CDNs.
subjective.answer: TCP does not know the path's capacity at the start, so it uses slow start. It begins with a small congestion window, typically about 10 segments (around 14 KB), and roughly doubles it each round trip. Throughput is limited to about window ÷ RTT. So on a 200 ms path, the first round trips move only tens of KB, and full speed may take many round trips. To fill a link, the window must reach the bandwidth-delay product. For 1 Gbps × 200 ms, that is about 25 MB in flight, which also needs large enough socket buffers. Packet loss cuts the window and slows things down again. Design impact: reuse warm connections with keep-alive instead of opening new ones. Put CDN edges near users so the RTT is short and the window grows quickly. CDNs also keep warm, long-lived connections to the origin. For very large transfers, parallel ranged downloads, such as S3 multipart download, or better congestion control such as BBR, help use the bandwidth.
keyPoints: Slow start begins with a small window that grows each round trip
Throughput is about window ÷ RTT; long RTT means slow ramp-up
The bandwidth-delay product sets how much data must be in flight
Warm, reused connections and nearby edges reduce the impact
Parallel ranged transfers and BBR help with large files

subjective.question: A user says your website works on office Wi-Fi but fails on mobile data with 'site can't be reached'. The servers are healthy. How do you troubleshoot this from the DNS and network side?
subjective.answer: Different networks mean different resolvers and often different IP stacks, so I would compare them. First, I would resolve the name the way each network does. For example, `dig www.example.com A` and `dig www.example.com AAAA` against the carrier's resolver, and also against 8.8.8.8 and the authoritative server using `dig @ns1...`. A common cause is a broken AAAA record. Mobile networks are often IPv6-first, so phones connect over IPv6 to an address that is not listening, or is blocked by a security group. Wi-Fi may be IPv4-only, so it works there. Second, check for a stale cached answer after a recent IP change. The resolver may still serve the old IP until its TTL runs out, or a negative answer may be cached. Third, check carrier DNS filtering, or a split-horizon setup where the office resolves to a private IP. Then test the TCP and TLS path from that network with `curl -v`. Fixes: correct or remove the AAAA record, open IPv6 on the load balancer and security groups, and wait for the TTL to expire.
keyPoints: Compare answers from the carrier resolver, a public resolver and the authoritative server
Check both A and AAAA records; IPv6-only paths often break
Consider stale or negative caching after a recent change
Look for split-horizon DNS or carrier filtering
Confirm with curl -v from the failing network

subjective.question: A product team in Bengaluru wants first page load under 300 ms for Indian users. All servers are in us-east-1. Use rough latency numbers to show whether this is possible, and propose a design.
subjective.answer: The round trip between India and the US East Coast is about 200–250 ms, because light in fibre covers roughly 200 km per millisecond and real routes are long. A cold HTTPS request needs DNS, a TCP handshake, a TLS 1.3 handshake and then the request itself. That is about 3 round trips even with DNS cached, so 600–750 ms before any server time. HTML that loads CSS and API calls adds more round trips. So the 300 ms target is impossible from us-east-1, whatever the hardware. The design must bring the conversation closer to users. Put a CDN such as CloudFront in front, so TCP and TLS end at a Mumbai or Chennai edge with an RTT of about 10–30 ms. Cache static assets and cacheable HTML at the edge. For dynamic APIs, the edge reuses warm connections to the origin, which removes handshakes from the long path. For truly low latency, deploy the application and a read replica in ap-south-1 (Mumbai). Also cut round trips with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, preconnect hints and inlined critical CSS.
keyPoints: An India–US round trip is about 200+ ms; a cold HTTPS request needs about 3 round trips
Physics makes the target impossible from a single US region
Edge termination and caching remove long-path handshakes
A regional deployment in ap-south-1 serves dynamic data close to users
Reduce round trips with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and preconnect hints

steps.overview: This step teaches you to scale the web and app tier by adding identical, stateless servers behind a load balancer, instead of buying ever-bigger machines. You will learn how L4 and L7 load balancers route traffic, where session state must go so any server can handle any request, and how CDNs take load off your origin. These ideas come up constantly in SAA-C03 high-availability questions, in GCP and Azure architect case studies, and in almost every system design interview.
objectives: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling and choose the right one for a given workload and failure requirement
Select an L4 or L7 load balancer and a routing algorithm (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing) for a scenario
Move session state out of web servers into a shared store such as Redis/ElastiCache or DynamoDB, or into signed tokens
Design a multi-AZ web tier with an Auto Scaling group and health checks that survives one availability zone failing
Explain when a CDN can cache static and dynamic content, and how TTLs and cache keys affect hit ratio

concepts.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine with more CPU and RAM. It is simple but has a hardware ceiling, usually needs a restart, and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more identical machines behind a load balancer. It gives near-linear capacity and fault tolerance, but only works cleanly if servers are stateless.

A stateless server keeps no client-specific data between requests in its own memory or disk. Any instance can serve any request, so you can add, remove or replace instances freely. State still exists, but it lives in a shared store (cache, database, object storage) or in the client (a signed token).

An L4 load balancer routes by IP address, port and protocol (TCP/UDP) without reading the request content; it is very fast and can preserve client IPs. An L7 load balancer understands HTTP/HTTPS, so it can route by path, host header, headers or query strings, terminate TLS and set cookies. On AWS, Network Load Balancer is L4 and Application Load Balancer is L7; on GCP and Azure the equivalents are the network/passthrough vs application load balancers, and Azure Load Balancer (L4) vs Application Gateway (L7).

Round robin sends each new request to the next server in turn; it is fair only when requests cost about the same. Least connections (on AWS ALB: least outstanding requests) sends the request to the server with the fewest active requests, which handles uneven or long-running requests better. Weighted variants let bigger servers take more traffic.

Servers and keys are placed on a hash ring, and each key goes to the next server clockwise. When a server is added or removed, only about 1/N of keys move, unlike simple modulo hashing where most keys remap. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out uneven load. It is used when a key should keep hitting the same node, for example cache shards, not for general stateless web traffic.

The load balancer pins a user to one server, usually with a cookie, so in-memory session data stays usable. This hurts scaling: load becomes uneven, new instances get little traffic, scale-in or a crash logs users out, and one AZ failure loses all sessions held there. The replacement is externalised state: a shared session store or stateless signed tokens such as JWTs.

Session data is written to a fast shared store keyed by session ID, usually Redis (Amazon ElastiCache, Memorystore, Azure Cache for Redis) or a key-value database like DynamoDB with TTL. Every web server reads the same data, so any instance can serve the user. Make the store itself highly available, for example Redis with replicas across AZs, or it becomes the new single point of failure.

Instances run in an Auto Scaling group spread across at least two (ideally three) availability zones behind a regional load balancer. Health checks remove failed instances, and Auto Scaling replaces them. You must keep enough spare capacity in the remaining AZs to carry peak load when one AZ goes down.

A CDN such as Amazon CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door or Cloudflare caches content at edge locations close to users. Static assets (images, JS, CSS, often stored in S3) cache with long TTLs and versioned file names. Dynamic content can still benefit: short TTLs (even a few seconds) for popular pages, careful cache keys, and TLS termination plus persistent connections to the origin.

The cache key decides which requests share a cached object; adding unnecessary headers, cookies or query strings to it fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio. The TTL decides how long an object stays at the edge before revalidation. Use origin Cache-Control headers to control TTL, and invalidation or versioned URLs to push changes.

keyFacts: Horizontal scaling needs stateless servers; vertical scaling is a quick fix but keeps a single point of failure and a hardware ceiling.
AWS ALB = Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS, path and host routing, WebSockets, gRPC); NLB = Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS, static IP per AZ, ultra-low latency); Gateway Load Balancer is for third-party network appliances.
ALB routing algorithms: round robin (default), least outstanding requests, and weighted random. NLB uses flow hashing.
Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB and off by default for NLB.
ALB sticky sessions use either a load-balancer cookie (AWSALB, duration-based) or an application cookie; the exam answer for scalable sessions is usually ElastiCache or DynamoDB instead.
ALB deregistration delay (connection draining) defaults to 300 seconds, letting in-flight requests finish before an instance is removed.
Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when one of N nodes changes; modulo hashing remaps most keys.
Survive one AZ loss: with N AZs, each AZ must hold peak/(N-1) capacity. Three AZs need 1.5x peak in total; two AZs need 2x peak.
CloudFront default TTL is 24 hours unless the origin sends Cache-Control headers or you change the cache policy; use versioned file names rather than frequent invalidations.
Use Origin Access Control (OAC) so the S3 bucket behind CloudFront is private and only reachable through the CDN.

example.caption: Worked estimate: a web tier that survives losing one AZ (AWS)
example.code:
Requirement: peak = 6,000 req/s, one instance handles 1,000 req/s
Need at peak: 6 healthy instances, even with one AZ down

Option A - 2 AZs:
  If one AZ fails, the other must carry 6 instances
  Per AZ = 6 -> total = 12 instances (2.0x peak)

Option B - 3 AZs:
  If one AZ fails, the other two must carry 6
  Per AZ = 6 / 2 = 3 -> total = 9 instances (1.5x peak)
  -> 3 AZs is cheaper and still survives one AZ loss

Design:
  Route 53 -> CloudFront (static from private S3 via OAC,
                          dynamic with short TTL)
  -> ALB (subnets in AZ-a, AZ-b, AZ-c, cross-zone on)
  -> Auto Scaling group: min 9, desired 9, max 18,
     ELB health checks, target tracking on CPU or
     requests per target
  -> No sticky sessions; sessions in ElastiCache for Redis
     (primary + replicas in other AZs, Multi-AZ failover)
  -> Database: RDS/Aurora Multi-AZ (covered in later steps)

AZ-b fails:
  ALB health checks mark AZ-b targets unhealthy
  Traffic shifts to AZ-a and AZ-c (3 + 3 = 6 = peak)
  Users stay logged in: sessions are in Redis, not on servers
  ASG launches replacements in healthy AZs

pitfalls: Choosing sticky sessions to 'fix' logouts after scaling out. It hides the real problem; the scalable answer is a shared session store or signed tokens.
Sizing the Auto Scaling group for normal load only. If you lose one AZ out of two, you lose half your capacity at the worst moment unless you pre-provision for it.
Picking NLB when the question needs path-based or host-based routing, or picking ALB when the question needs a static IP, UDP or extreme throughput at low latency.
Moving sessions to a single Redis node in one AZ. You have just moved the single point of failure; use replicas across AZs with automatic failover.
Putting cookies, Authorization headers or all query strings in the CDN cache key by default, which kills the hit ratio, or caching personalised pages publicly and leaking user data.
Using consistent hashing for a general stateless web tier. It creates hot spots and affinity you do not need; round robin or least connections is the usual right choice there.

workflow.title: How a request flows through a scalable, AZ-resilient web tier

steps.label: DNS resolves to the CDN
steps.detail: Route 53 or another DNS returns the CDN edge address closest to the user.

steps.label: Edge serves cached content
steps.detail: The CDN returns static assets and short-TTL dynamic pages from cache, and forwards misses to the origin.

steps.label: Load balancer picks a target
steps.detail: The regional ALB routes by path or host and uses round robin or least outstanding requests across healthy targets in all AZs.

steps.label: Stateless instance handles request
steps.detail: Any instance in the Auto Scaling group can serve the user because it holds no local session data.

steps.label: Session read from shared store
steps.detail: The instance loads the session by ID from Redis or DynamoDB, or validates a signed token.

steps.label: Health checks remove failures
steps.detail: If an instance or a whole AZ fails, health checks stop traffic to it and connection draining finishes in-flight requests.

steps.label: Auto Scaling restores capacity
steps.detail: The group launches replacement instances in healthy AZs and scales out on CPU or request-count targets.

project.title: multi-az-web-tier
project.summary: A stateless Node.js cart API whose session data lives in Redis, not in server memory. Two replicas sit behind an nginx L7 load balancer (least connections) with an edge-style cache, so you can kill one instance and keep your cart. It also includes Terraform that builds the same web tier on AWS to survive one Availability Zone going down: an ALB and Auto Scaling group across AZs, Multi-AZ ElastiCache for sessions, and CloudFront in front. app/server.js shows the stateless service and the external session store. nginx/nginx.conf shows L7 balancing, failover and the cache key. docker-compose.yml runs the local lab. infra/main.tf builds the multi-AZ ALB and Auto Scaling group. infra/session_cdn.tf adds the Multi-AZ session store and the CDN.

curl -s -c jar -b jar 'http://localhost:8080/api/cart/add?item=book'
curl -s -c jar -b jar 'http://localhost:8080/api/cart/add?item=pen'
docker compose stop app1
curl -s -c jar -b jar 'http://localhost:8080/api/cart/add?item=pen'
