objective.explanation: With consistent hashing, only the keys that fall into the new server's ranges move, which is about 1/(N+1) of all keys. Virtual nodes spread those ranges around the ring, so the moved keys come evenly from all servers instead of only its neighbours. Plain hash mod N would remap most keys.

objective.question: A multi-tenant SaaS app stores data in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL with partition key /tenantId. A few large tenants are close to the 20 GB logical partition limit and cause hot partitions. Queries usually filter by tenantId and often also by userId. Which change fits BEST?
options: Keep /tenantId and raise the container's provisioned RU/s until throttling stops
Use hierarchical partition keys such as /tenantId then /userId, so large tenants span several physical partitions and tenant-scoped queries still stay targeted
Change the partition key to /id so that every document goes to its own logical partition
Switch the account to Strong consistency so writes spread across replicas
objective.explanation: Hierarchical partition keys (subpartitioning) let one tenant's data go beyond a single logical partition, while queries on tenantId, or on tenantId plus userId, are still routed only to the relevant partitions. More RU/s does not lift the per-logical-partition limits, /id turns tenant queries into cross-partition fan-outs, and the consistency level has nothing to do with data distribution.

objective.question: Review this DynamoDB UpdateItem request used by a profile-edit API. What behaviour does it implement?
options: Optimistic concurrency control: the update succeeds only if version is still 7; otherwise it fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException and the client must re-read and retry
An idempotent upsert that always overwrites bio and sets version to 8
A multi-item ACID transaction across the Profiles table and its indexes
Pessimistic locking: the item stays locked until the client sends version 8
objective.explanation: The ConditionExpression checks the version the client read earlier. If another writer changed it first, the write is rejected, which prevents lost updates without holding locks. It is not a lock, it does not always overwrite, and a single-item conditional write is not a TransactWriteItems call.

subjective.question: Which database would you choose for a social feed, a financial ledger and a session store? Justify each choice.
subjective.answer: For a ledger I choose a relational ACID database such as Aurora PostgreSQL, Spanner or Azure SQL. Money needs atomic multi-row transfers, constraints and Serializable isolation or careful row locking. A lost update means real financial loss. I prefer double-entry, append-only rows over in-place balance updates. For a session store I use in-memory key-value such as ElastiCache for Redis, or DynamoDB with TTL. Access is always by session ID, reads need sub-millisecond latency, data expires on its own, and losing a session only means the user logs in again. For a feed I use wide-column or key-value storage such as Cassandra or DynamoDB, with Redis as a cache. Feeds are write-heavy with fan-out on write, they are read by user_id sorted by time, and they tolerate eventual consistency. For celebrity accounts I would use a hybrid of fan-out on write and fan-out on read.
keyPoints: Ledger: relational ACID, Serializable or locking, append-only entries
Session store: in-memory key-value with TTL, access only by session ID
Feed: wide-column or key-value plus cache, fan-out, eventual consistency is acceptable
Match the consistency requirement to the business cost of being wrong

subjective.question: Design the schema and shard key for a chat app's messages table that supports 1:1 and group chats at large scale.
subjective.answer: The access pattern drives the design. The main query is 'latest N messages in a conversation, then page backwards'. Schema: conversation_id (partition or shard key), message_id (clustering or sort key, time-ordered, such as a Snowflake ID or ULID), sender_id, body, type, created_at and edited or deleted flags. Sharding by conversation_id keeps each chat on one shard, so a read is a single-partition range query. Sharding by user_id would duplicate group messages, and sharding by time creates one hot shard. A time-ordered ID avoids timestamp collisions and gives stable pagination. For very large or very busy groups, I add a time bucket to the key, for example conversation_id#month, so partitions do not grow without limit or turn hot. A separate table keyed by user_id lists each user's conversations with last-message metadata for the inbox. Cassandra or DynamoDB fit well because the workload is write-heavy and follows an LSM-friendly pattern.
keyPoints: Partition key conversation_id, sort key time-ordered message_id
Single-partition range read for the latest messages and pagination
Time bucketing to cap partition size and avoid hot partitions
Separate per-user inbox table; LSM-based wide-column or key-value store

subjective.question: Compare the four NoSQL families with relational databases, and give one good use case for each.
subjective.answer: Relational databases store normalised tables with joins, constraints and ACID transactions. They suit orders, billing and anything with complex queries. Document stores such as MongoDB and Firestore keep nested JSON documents. They suit product catalogues or user profiles, where data is read as one unit and the schema changes often. Key-value stores such as Redis and DynamoDB give very fast lookups by key and suit sessions, caches and carts. Wide-column stores such as Cassandra and Bigtable organise data by partition key and sorted clustering columns. They suit write-heavy time-series data, feeds and messages. Graph databases such as Neo4j and Neptune store nodes and edges and suit friend-of-friend queries, recommendations and fraud rings. The trade-off is that NoSQL usually gives up joins and flexible queries in exchange for horizontal scale and predictable latency. You must model your tables around known access patterns.
keyPoints: Relational: joins, constraints, ACID
Document: nested aggregates, flexible schema
Key-value: lookup by key; wide-column: partition plus sorted columns
Graph: relationship traversal; NoSQL means modelling around access patterns

subjective.question: Explain how B-trees and LSM trees work, and when you would pick each.
subjective.answer: A B-tree keeps sorted keys in fixed-size pages arranged as a shallow balanced tree. Lookups take a few page reads, and range scans are efficient. Writes update pages in place and are protected by a write-ahead log, so they cause random I/O. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and most relational databases use B-trees. An LSM tree writes first to a log and an in-memory memtable, then flushes it as an immutable sorted SSTable. Background compaction merges SSTables. Writes are sequential and very fast. A read may have to check the memtable and several SSTables, so bloom filters are used to skip files. Compaction also consumes I/O and causes write amplification. Cassandra, RocksDB, Bigtable and the storage behind many NoSQL systems use this design. I pick an LSM tree for write-heavy ingestion such as logs, metrics and chat. I pick a B-tree for read-heavy OLTP with many range queries and predictable read latency.
keyPoints: B-tree: in-place page updates, strong reads and range scans
LSM: memtable, SSTables, compaction; sequential and fast writes
LSM read cost reduced with bloom filters; compaction adds write amplification
Write-heavy workload: LSM; read-heavy with range queries: B-tree

subjective.question: In leader–follower replication, what is replication lag and how do you give users read-your-writes consistency?
subjective.answer: All writes go to the leader, which streams changes to followers. With asynchronous replication, followers can be seconds behind. A user who updates their profile and then reads from a follower may see the old value. That delay is replication lag. Fixes include: reading data the user can edit, such as their own profile, from the leader; routing a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write; or tracking the write's log position and reading only from a replica that has caught up to it. Synchronous replication removes lag for one follower, but the leader then has to wait, which hurts write latency and availability. Many systems use semi-synchronous replication, with one synchronous follower and the rest asynchronous. On AWS, read replicas are asynchronous and are used for scaling reads. Multi-AZ is for failover. Aurora replicas share one storage volume, so lag is usually low.
keyPoints: Asynchronous followers can return stale data
Read your own data from the leader, or route to the leader for a time window after a write
Track replication position; semi-synchronous replication as a compromise
Read replicas for scaling vs Multi-AZ for high availability

subjective.question: When would you use multi-leader replication, and how do you handle write conflicts?
subjective.answer: Multi-leader replication lets each region, or an offline client, accept writes locally and sync them later. This gives low write latency for global users and keeps writes working when a region is cut off. Examples include multi-region databases and collaborative or offline apps. The cost is conflicts: two leaders change the same record at the same time. Strategies are: avoid conflicts by routing each record's writes to one home leader; last-write-wins using timestamps, which is simple but silently loses data and depends on clocks; merge with CRDTs, such as counters and sets, that converge automatically; or keep all versions, for example with version vectors, and let the application or the user resolve them. I would not use multi-leader for a ledger or for inventory decrements unless I can make every write commutative. For those, a single leader or a globally consistent database like Spanner is safer.
keyPoints: Use case: multi-region low-latency writes and offline clients
Conflicts are inevitable under concurrent writes
Resolution: avoid via a home leader, LWW, CRDTs, version vectors
Not suitable for strongly consistent data such as money

subjective.question: Explain leaderless replication and quorums. What do sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and read repair do?
subjective.answer: In leaderless systems such as Dynamo-style stores and Cassandra, the client or a coordinator sends each write to all N replicas and waits for W acknowledgements. Reads query replicas and wait for R responses. If W + R > N, the read and write sets overlap, so at least one response holds the latest value. A common setup is N=3, W=2, R=2, which tolerates one node being down. Read repair means that when a read sees a stale replica, it writes the newer value back to it. Anti-entropy runs in the background to compare replicas. A sloppy quorum accepts writes on nodes outside the key's normal replica set during a failure. This keeps writes available, but the W + R > N guarantee no longer holds. Hinted handoff later delivers those writes to the correct nodes. Quorums still do not give linearizability under every race, for example concurrent writes or failed partial writes, so conflict handling is still needed.
keyPoints: W + R > N gives overlapping replica sets; N=3, W=2, R=2
Read repair and anti-entropy fix stale replicas
Sloppy quorum plus hinted handoff trade consistency for availability
Quorum is not full linearizability

subjective.question: Compare range, hash and directory-based sharding.
subjective.answer: Range sharding gives each shard a contiguous key range, such as A–F or dates in January. Range scans are efficient and easy to reason about. However, sequential keys such as timestamps send all new writes to one shard, and uneven data creates hot shards. Hash sharding applies a hash to the key and spreads data evenly, which suits point lookups by ID. Range queries then have to scatter across every shard. With mod N, adding nodes remaps most keys, so consistent hashing or fixed virtual partitions are used instead. Directory sharding keeps a lookup service that maps each key or tenant to a shard. It is the most flexible: you can move one big tenant to its own shard. The cost is an extra lookup, and the directory must be highly available and cached. In practice I use hash for user or entity data, range or composite keys for time-series data, and a directory for multi-tenant SaaS.
keyPoints: Range: efficient scans, risk of hotspots with sequential keys
Hash: even spread, scattered range queries, consistent hashing
Directory: flexible placement, extra lookup and a single point to protect
Choose based on query pattern and tenant skew

subjective.question: What causes hot partitions, and how do you reshard a live system safely?
subjective.answer: Hot partitions come from low-cardinality or skewed keys, such as status or country, and from sequential keys like timestamps. They also come from celebrity keys, such as a viral post or a large tenant. In DynamoDB, one partition supports about 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU, so one hot key gets throttled even when the table has spare capacity. Fixes: choose high-cardinality keys with even access; add write sharding with suffixes and aggregate on read; put a cache in front of hot reads; or isolate big tenants. For resharding, pre-split into many logical partitions and move whole partitions between nodes, rather than rehashing every key. A safe live migration uses dual writes or change data capture to the new layout, a backfill of historical data, verification and a gradual cut-over of reads, followed by retiring the old shards. Managed services such as DynamoDB, Bigtable and Spanner split partitions automatically, but they cannot fix a single key that is hot.
keyPoints: Causes: skewed, low-cardinality, sequential or celebrity keys
Per-partition limits throttle hot keys
Fixes: key suffixing, caching, tenant isolation
Reshard with logical partitions, dual writes or CDC, backfill, gradual cut-over

subjective.question: Walk through the SQL isolation levels and the anomalies each one allows.
subjective.answer: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, which means seeing uncommitted data. Read Committed blocks dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads: the same row can change between two reads in one transaction. It also allows lost updates if the code does read-modify-write without locks. Repeatable Read, or snapshot isolation, gives each transaction a consistent snapshot, so repeated reads match. Write skew is still possible, and phantoms depend on the engine: InnoDB uses gap locks, while PostgreSQL's snapshot avoids most phantoms. Serializable makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, which prevents write skew and phantoms. The cost is locking or aborts, so the application must retry. PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed and MySQL InnoDB to Repeatable Read. For money I use Serializable, or Read Committed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and atomic updates such as UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - x WHERE balance >= x.
keyPoints: Dirty read, non-repeatable read, lost update, write skew, phantom
Snapshot isolation still allows write skew
Serializable costs aborts and retries
Defaults: PostgreSQL Read Committed, InnoDB Repeatable Read

subjective.question: Explain ACID versus BASE with an example of where each fits.
subjective.answer: ACID stands for Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints and invariants hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and Durability (committed data survives a crash). It suits bank transfers, orders and inventory, where a partial or stale result is a bug. BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state and Eventually consistent. The system stays up and replicas converge over time, which suits likes, feeds, view counts and product reviews, where a short delay is fine. These are design choices, not fixed product labels. DynamoDB is eventually consistent by default, but it offers strongly consistent reads at twice the RCU and TransactWriteItems for ACID across items. Cosmos DB lets you tune consistency from Strong down to Eventual. Spanner provides ACID at global scale. In an interview I choose per use case, often within one system.
keyPoints: ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
BASE: available, soft state, eventual consistency
Examples: payments use ACID; likes and feeds use BASE
Modern databases let you tune this per operation

subjective.question: How do you read a query plan and decide which indexes to add? What do indexes cost?
subjective.answer: I run EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, to see the real plan. I check whether the planner uses a sequential scan or an index scan, and I compare estimated rows with actual rows. A large gap means stale statistics, which I fix with ANALYZE. I also look for expensive sort, hash join and nested-loop steps. Then I design indexes around the query. In a composite index, equality columns go first, then range or sort columns. The leftmost-prefix rule matters: an index on (a, b) helps queries filtering on a, but not queries filtering only on b. A covering index, using INCLUDE or all selected columns, allows index-only scans. Indexes on low-selectivity columns are rarely used. The costs: every index slows inserts and updates, uses disk and memory, and adds write amplification. On DynamoDB, each GSI also consumes its own write capacity. I index the queries that run often, then measure the effect again.
keyPoints: EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE; compare estimated vs actual rows
Composite index order: equality columns, then range or sort; leftmost prefix
Covering indexes allow index-only scans
Indexes cost write speed, storage and GSI capacity

subjective.question: A multi-tenant B2B SaaS runs on one PostgreSQL instance that is close to its vertical limit. You must shard it. How do you choose the shard key, and how do you handle cross-shard queries and very large tenants?
subjective.answer: I would shard by tenant_id, because almost every query is scoped to one tenant. That keeps joins, foreign keys and transactions inside one shard. I would use a directory, a tenant-to-shard lookup table, rather than hash mod N. A directory lets me place, move and isolate individual tenants without remapping everyone. Reports that span tenants, such as internal admin analytics, should not hit the OLTP shards. I would stream changes through CDC into a warehouse like BigQuery, Redshift or Synapse. For the few whale tenants, I give each one a dedicated shard. If one tenant outgrows even that, I sub-shard it by a second key such as tenant_id plus account_id. To cut over, I copy the data, dual-write or replay the CDC stream, verify row counts and checksums, then switch the directory entry. Citus-style distributed Postgres follows the same model, using tenant_id as the distribution column.
keyPoints: tenant_id keeps most queries, joins and transactions on a single shard
A directory or lookup table gives flexible placement and per-tenant moves
Cross-tenant analytics go to a warehouse through CDC, not scatter-gather on OLTP
Whale tenants get dedicated shards or sub-sharding
Safe migration: backfill, replay changes, verify, then flip the mapping

subjective.question: A query that used to take 20 ms now takes 4 seconds. Interpret this EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and explain what you would do.

code.code:
Nested Loop  (cost=0.85..120.4 rows=12 width=64)
             (actual time=0.05..4012.7 rows=1840211 loops=1)
  -> Index Scan using idx_orders_status on orders o
       (rows=10) (actual rows=1520033 loops=1)
       Index Cond: (status = 'PENDING')
  -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
       (rows=1) (actual rows=1 loops=1520033)
Planning Time: 0.3 ms
Execution Time: 4015.2 ms

subjective.answer: The key signal is the gap between estimated and actual rows. The planner expected about 10 PENDING orders but found 1.5 million. Because of that, it chose a nested loop that probes customers_pkey 1.5 million times. A hash join would be much better at that row count. The cause is usually stale or too-coarse statistics, for example after a bulk load or a backlog that suddenly made PENDING common. First I would run ANALYZE orders. If the column is skewed, I would raise its statistics target so the most-common-values list captures it. Then I would check that the plan switches to a hash join. I would also question the query itself. If it only needs a page of results, adding LIMIT and a composite index on (status, created_at) helps. A partial index on PENDING rows is another option. Finally, I would make sure autovacuum and autoanalyze keep up with the table's churn.
keyPoints: Compare estimated rows with actual rows to spot bad cardinality estimates
A nested loop with a huge loops count signals the wrong join strategy
Fix the statistics first: ANALYZE and a higher statistics target for skewed columns
Reconsider the query shape: LIMIT, composite or partial indexes
Make sure autoanalyze keeps up with data changes

subjective.question: An order service and a payment service each own their own database. Placing an order must reserve stock and charge the card. Compare two-phase commit with the saga pattern, and explain how the transactional outbox helps.
subjective.answer: Two-phase commit uses a coordinator. It asks every participant to prepare, then tells all of them to commit. This gives atomicity, but participants hold locks while waiting for the coordinator. A coordinator failure can block them, and many modern services and managed NoSQL stores do not support XA anyway. A saga breaks the work into local transactions: reserve stock, charge the card, confirm the order. Each step has a compensating action, such as releasing stock or refunding. If one step fails, the earlier steps are undone. Sagas can be orchestrated by a workflow engine like Step Functions, or choreographed through events. The trade-off is that sagas give no isolation, so other users can see intermediate states. I handle that with pending statuses and idempotent steps. The outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem. The service writes its business row and an event row in the same local transaction. A relay or CDC then publishes the event, so the database and the message stream never disagree.
keyPoints: 2PC: atomic but blocking, lock-heavy, and depends on the coordinator
Saga: local transactions plus compensating actions, eventually consistent
Sagas lack isolation, so use pending states and idempotency
Orchestration versus choreography
Outbox: the event is written in the same transaction as the data and published through CDC or a relay

subjective.question: Your primary database fails and a follower is promoted. Replication was asynchronous. What can go wrong during failover, and how do you design to limit the damage?
subjective.answer: With asynchronous replication, writes acknowledged by the old leader but not yet shipped are lost when a follower is promoted. If those writes were tied to external effects, such as IDs already handed out or emails already sent, you can get duplicates or inconsistency. The second risk is split brain. The old leader comes back, or was never really dead, and keeps accepting writes alongside the new leader. To prevent this, I use fencing. The old leader's writes are rejected through a fencing token or epoch, its network access is revoked, or it is shut down (STONITH). Failure detection needs sensible timeouts, because too short a timeout causes needless failovers under load. To reduce data loss, I use semi-synchronous replication or synchronous standbys. Managed options do this for you: RDS Multi-AZ replicates synchronously to the standby, and Aurora uses quorum writes in shared storage. Clients should reconnect through a DNS endpoint or proxy and retry idempotent operations.
keyPoints: Async replication means acknowledged writes can be lost (RPO greater than 0)
Split brain with two leaders, prevented by fencing tokens or STONITH
Timeout tuning trades false failovers against detection speed
Synchronous or semi-synchronous replicas, or managed Multi-AZ, reduce data loss
Clients use endpoints or proxies and idempotent retries

subjective.question: Model an e-commerce order system in a single DynamoDB table. Access patterns: get a customer's profile, list a customer's orders newest first, get an order with its line items, and find orders by status for operations staff. Explain the trade-offs compared with a normalised relational schema.
subjective.answer: I start from the access patterns, not the entities. Customer profile: PK=CUST#id, SK=PROFILE. Orders: PK=CUST#id, SK=ORDER#timestamp#orderId. One Query on the customer's PK, with ScanIndexForward=false and begins_with ORDER#, lists orders newest first. Line items go under their own item collection: PK=ORDER#orderId, SK=ITEM#n, plus an SK=META summary item, so one Query returns the order and its lines. For status lookups, I add a GSI with GSI1PK=STATUS#status and GSI1SK=created_at. If one status like PENDING gets very hot, I add a shard suffix to the GSI key. The trade-offs against relational are real. Every query is a single-partition, predictable low-latency read at any scale. But I duplicate data, such as the order summary in two places, so updates must be coordinated, often with TransactWriteItems. New ad hoc queries need new indexes or an export to analytics. In a normalised SQL schema, new queries are easy to add, but joins get expensive at very high scale.
keyPoints: Design keys from access patterns; overload PK and SK with prefixes
Item collections give one-query fetches (customer's orders, order plus line items)
A GSI covers the status lookup; write-shard hot status values
Denormalisation means duplicated data and coordinated or transactional updates
Inflexible for ad hoc queries, unlike SQL joins

subjective.question: This transfer code runs under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED isolation. Identify the concurrency bugs, and give at least two ways to fix them.

code.code:
def transfer(conn, src, dst, amount):
    with conn.transaction():
        bal = conn.execute(
            "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=%s", (src,)
        ).fetchone()[0]
        if bal < amount:
            raise InsufficientFunds()
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance=%s WHERE id=%s",
                     (bal - amount, src))
        dst_bal = conn.execute(
            "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=%s", (dst,)
        ).fetchone()[0]
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance=%s WHERE id=%s",
                     (dst_bal + amount, dst))

subjective.answer: This is a read-modify-write with no lock, so it suffers lost updates. Two concurrent transfers from the same account can both read a balance of 100. Both pass the check, and both write 100 minus their amount. One debit vanishes, and the account can effectively go negative. The same happens on the destination credit. Fix one: use atomic conditional updates, for example UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = %s AND balance >= %s, then check that the row count is 1. The credit becomes balance = balance + %s. Fix two: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on both rows before computing. Lock them in a consistent order, such as lowest id first, so two opposite transfers cannot deadlock. Fix three: run the transaction at SERIALIZABLE (or REPEATABLE READ, which in PostgreSQL aborts on concurrent update) and retry on serialization failures. For a real ledger, I would also use append-only entries and an idempotency key per transfer.
keyPoints: The bug: lost update from an unlocked read-modify-write under READ COMMITTED
Atomic UPDATE with a balance check in the WHERE clause
SELECT FOR UPDATE with consistent lock ordering to avoid deadlocks
Higher isolation plus a retry loop on serialization failures
Ledger best practice: append-only entries and idempotency keys

subjective.question: In a sharded database, the primary key is user_id but you also need to look up users by email and by phone. Compare local (document-partitioned) and global (term-partitioned) secondary indexes, and say which you would use here.
subjective.answer: A local secondary index lives on each shard and indexes only that shard's rows. Writes stay cheap and consistent, because the index updates in the same local transaction. But a lookup by email has to scatter-gather to every shard, and tail latency grows with the shard count. A global secondary index is partitioned by the indexed value itself, so email X lives on the shard that owns hash(X). A lookup touches one shard, but every write may update an index on a different node. That usually happens asynchronously, which makes the index eventually consistent, as with DynamoDB GSIs. Synchronous updates would need a distributed transaction. For email and phone login lookups, which are high-volume point reads, I would use a global index, or an explicit lookup table keyed by email that maps to user_id. Uniqueness of email must be enforced at that global layer, for example with a conditional put on the email key. Local indexes suit queries that already include the shard key, such as a user's orders filtered by status.
keyPoints: Local index: cheap consistent writes, but scatter-gather reads across all shards
Global index: single-shard reads, but cross-node and often asynchronous writes
Eventual consistency of global indexes (for example DynamoDB GSIs)
Point lookups like email or phone suit a global index or a lookup table
Enforce uniqueness at the global key, for example with a conditional write

steps.overview: This step explains how data stays correct when it lives on many machines that can fail or lose contact. You will learn CAP and PACELC, the main consistency models, quorums and Raft, and how idempotency keys make retries safe. Exam questions on SAA-C03, GCP PCA and AZ-305 often hinge on these trade-offs: DynamoDB read modes, SQS FIFO deduplication, Cosmos DB consistency levels, and multi-region writes.
objectives: Explain CAP and PACELC in plain words and classify common databases by their trade-offs.
Choose between strong, eventual, causal and read-your-writes consistency for a given business requirement.
Calculate quorum settings (R + W > N) and state how many node failures a Raft cluster tolerates.
Implement an idempotency key on a payment API so a retried request never charges a customer twice.
Compare distributed ID schemes (auto-increment, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, Snowflake) for ordering, index locality and coordination cost.

concepts.explanation: A network partition (P) will happen in any real distributed system. During a partition, a system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write or gets an error) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response). So the real choice is CP or AP, and it applies only while the partition lasts.

PACELC extends CAP. If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. For example, DynamoDB and Cassandra with default settings are PA/EL, while a single-leader SQL database with synchronous replicas leans PC/EC. It explains why strong consistency costs latency even when nothing is broken.

Strong (linearizable) consistency means that once a write is acknowledged, every later read returns it. Eventual consistency means replicas converge if writes stop, but a read may briefly return stale data. Use strong consistency for balances, inventory and locks. Use eventual consistency for likes, feeds and analytics, where it gives lower latency and higher availability.

Causal consistency means that if write B depends on write A (for example, a reply to a comment), every reader sees A before B. Read-your-writes is a session guarantee: a user always sees their own updates, even if other users see them later. Azure Cosmos DB offers five levels (Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual), and Session is the default.

With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. If R + W > N, the read set and the write set overlap, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. Cassandra exposes this as tunable consistency levels such as ONE, QUORUM and ALL, and LOCAL_QUORUM keeps quorums inside one data centre for latency.

Raft is a consensus algorithm in which one elected leader accepts writes and replicates them to followers in a log. An entry is committed once a majority stores it. If the leader fails, followers time out and hold an election, and terms (epoch numbers) stop an old leader from causing split-brain. etcd (the store behind Kubernetes), Consul and CockroachDB use Raft.

The client generates a unique key, usually a UUID, for each logical operation and sends it with every retry of that operation. The server stores the key with the request hash and the final response. A repeat request returns the stored response instead of running the operation again. This turns at-least-once delivery into an effectively-once outcome.

Over an unreliable network you cannot guarantee that a message is delivered exactly once. A lost acknowledgement forces a retry, and the receiver may then process the same message twice. What systems actually provide is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or deduplicated processing. Kafka's exactly-once semantics and SQS FIFO deduplication both work only within defined boundaries.

A Snowflake ID is a 64-bit ID: 1 unused sign bit, a 41-bit millisecond timestamp from a custom epoch, a 10-bit machine ID and a 12-bit sequence. Each node generates IDs without coordination, and the IDs are roughly time-sortable. The scheme depends on unique machine IDs and reasonably correct clocks.

UUIDv7 is a 128-bit UUID standardised in RFC 9562 (2024). It starts with a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits. Because new IDs are time-ordered, they append to B-tree indexes instead of scattering inserts like random UUIDv4, which improves database write performance. No machine-ID coordination is needed.

keyFacts: Quorum rule: R + W > N gives overlapping reads and writes. A common setting is N=3, W=2, R=2.
A Raft or Paxos cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures: 3 nodes tolerate 1, and 5 nodes tolerate 2. Use odd cluster sizes.
DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default. A strongly consistent read (ConsistentRead=true) uses twice the read capacity and is not supported on global secondary indexes.
Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT and DELETE operations since December 2020.
SQS standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. SQS FIFO queues give ordering within a message group and deduplicate messages within a 5-minute deduplication interval.
Snowflake layout is 1 + 41 + 10 + 12 bits, which allows 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node.
The default consistency level in Azure Cosmos DB is Session, which guarantees read-your-writes within a session.
HTTP GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by specification. POST is not, so payment POSTs need an idempotency key.

example.caption: Idempotent payment endpoint (FastAPI + PostgreSQL). Table: idem_keys(key text primary key, req_hash text, status text, response jsonb).
example.code:
import hashlib, json
import psycopg
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()
conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=pay")

@app.post("/payments")
def create_payment(body: dict, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    req_hash = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    with conn.transaction():
        cur = conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO idem_keys(key, req_hash, status) VALUES (%s, %s, 'IN_PROGRESS') "
            "ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING key", (idempotency_key, req_hash))
        if cur.fetchone() is None:  # key seen before
            h, status, resp = conn.execute(
                "SELECT req_hash, status, response FROM idem_keys WHERE key = %s",
                (idempotency_key,)).fetchone()
            if h != req_hash:
                raise HTTPException(422, "Key reused with a different request body")
            if status == "IN_PROGRESS":
                raise HTTPException(409, "Original request still processing; retry later")
            return resp  # replay stored result, no second charge
    # gateway_charge is a placeholder for your payment provider's client
    charge = gateway_charge(body["amount"], body["card_token"], idempotency_key)
    resp = {"payment_id": charge.id, "status": "succeeded"}
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("UPDATE idem_keys SET status = 'DONE', response = %s WHERE key = %s",
                     (json.dumps(resp), idempotency_key))
    return resp

pitfalls: Checking the key with a SELECT and then doing a separate INSERT creates a race. Two concurrent retries can both pass the check. Use a unique constraint, an atomic insert, or a conditional write such as a DynamoDB ConditionExpression attribute_not_exists.
Generating the idempotency key on the server per request is useless. The client must create the key once per logical operation and reuse it on every retry.
Not forwarding the key to the payment gateway is a trap. If your server crashes after the charge but before saving the result, only the gateway's own idempotency handling prevents a double charge.

Assuming SQS FIFO or Kafka exactly-once removes the need for idempotent consumers is wrong. Deduplication windows and transaction boundaries are limited, and side effects outside them can still repeat.
Confusing CAP consistency (linearizability) with ACID consistency (integrity constraints) is a common mistake. They are different ideas with the same name.
Choosing an even cluster size (such as 4 nodes) for Raft adds cost without adding fault tolerance. It still tolerates only 1 failure, the same as 3 nodes.

workflow.title: How a retried payment request is handled safely

steps.label: Client creates idempotency key
steps.detail: The client generates a UUID for this checkout attempt and sends it in the Idempotency-Key header on every retry.

steps.label: Server atomically reserves key
steps.detail: The server inserts the key, a request hash and status IN_PROGRESS under a unique constraint, so only one request can win.

steps.label: Duplicate returns stored outcome
steps.detail: If the key already exists, the server returns the saved response, returns 409 if still in progress, or returns 422 if the body differs.

steps.label: Charge with key forwarded
steps.detail: The winning request calls the payment gateway and passes the same key, so the provider also deduplicates.

steps.label: Persist result and mark DONE
steps.detail: The server stores the final response against the key in a transaction before replying to the client.

steps.label: Expire keys after retention window
steps.detail: A TTL (for example DynamoDB TTL or a scheduled cleanup) removes old keys once retries are no longer expected.

project.title: idempotent-payments-api
project.summary: A small Node.js payment API on PostgreSQL that is safe to retry: the same Idempotency-Key never creates a second charge, even when retries arrive at the same time. server.js holds the idempotency logic, schema.sql holds the unique-key guarantee, ids.js builds UUIDv7 and Snowflake IDs, retry-demo.js proves a customer is charged only once, and docker-compose.yml runs the database.
project.run:
docker compose up -d
npm install
npm start
npm run demo

files.code:
# Local PostgreSQL for the payments API.
# schema.sql runs automatically the first time the volume is created.
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: pay
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pay
      POSTGRES_DB: payments
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - ./db/schema.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/01-schema.sql:ro
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U pay -d payments"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  pgdata:

-- One row per Idempotency-Key. The PRIMARY KEY is the real safety net:
-- the database (one leader, strong consistency) allows only one claim per key.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS idempotency_keys (
  idem_key      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- detects the same key reused with a different body
  response_code INT,                    -- NULL until the first request finishes
  response_body JSONB,                  -- stored so retries get the exact same answer
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- The ledger of charges. Each charge links to exactly one idempotency key.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments (
  id           BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,      -- Snowflake ID: time-ordered 64-bit integer
  public_id    UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- UUIDv7: time-ordered, safe to show to clients
  idem_key     TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES idempotency_keys (idem_key),
  customer_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount_paise BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_paise > 0), -- money as integer paise, never float
  currency     CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS payments_customer_idx ON payments (customer_id);

-- In production, delete old keys with a scheduled job, e.g. after 24 hours:
-- DELETE FROM idempotency_keys WHERE created_at < now() - interval '24 hours';

# idempotent-payments-api

Week 6 hands-on: make a payment API safe to retry with an idempotency key.

## Run
1. `docker compose up -d` starts PostgreSQL 17 and loads `db/schema.sql`.
2. `npm install` then `npm start` runs the API on port 3000 (`PORT`, `DATABASE_URL`, `WORKER_ID` are optional env vars).
3. `npm run demo` sends 7 requests for one payment and checks the ledger holds 1 charge.

## Read the files in this order
- `db/schema.sql`: the PRIMARY KEY on `idem_key` lets only one request claim a key.
- `src/server.js`: claim key, charge, save response, all in ONE transaction. Retries replay the saved response.
- `src/ids.js`: UUIDv7 (public ID) and Snowflake (internal 64-bit ID). Both sort by time.
- `scripts/retry-demo.js`: concurrent and late retries, plus key misuse (422).

## Checkpoint: why a retry must never charge twice
A client cannot tell "the request was lost" from "the response was lost". After a timeout,
it must retry, and the first attempt may already have charged the card. So the server must
recognise the retry. The client sends the same `Idempotency-Key` on every attempt. The server
stores the key with the result. A second request with that key gets the stored result, not a new charge.

Why it holds under races: two requests with the same key both try `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`.
PostgreSQL makes the second one wait for the first transaction. If the first commits, the second
sees the conflict and replays. If the first fails and rolls back, the key is released and the retry can proceed.

## Exactly-once is a myth
Networks give at-most-once or at-least-once delivery. We pick at-least-once (retries) and add
idempotent processing. The result is exactly-once *effect*, not exactly-once delivery.

## Links to the theory
- CAP / PACELC: a payment ledger chooses consistency (C) over availability during a partition,
  and accepts extra latency (PC/EC) for strong reads. One Postgres leader gives that here.
- Read-your-writes: the replay query reads from the same primary, never a lagging replica.
- Scaling out: keep keys on the primary or a strongly consistent store. A replicated store
  uses a leader elected by consensus (for example Raft) or quorums where R + W > N.

## Real-world notes
- If you call an external payment gateway, pass the same idempotency key to it too, where it supports one.
- Expire keys after a fixed window (for example 24 hours) and document that window for clients.
- Store money as integer paise, never as floating point.

objective.question: A key-value store replicates each item to N=3 nodes. The team wants every read to see the latest acknowledged write without reading all replicas. Which read (R) and write (W) quorum setting achieves this?
objective.explanation: The overlap rule is R + W > N, and 2 + 2 = 4 is greater than 3, so every read set overlaps every write set. The other options sum to 2 or 3, which is not greater than N, so a read can miss the latest write.

objective.question: Your team runs a Raft-based configuration store on 5 nodes. How many node failures can the cluster tolerate while still electing a leader and committing writes?
objective.explanation: A cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures, so 5 nodes tolerate 2 and still keep a majority of 3. Losing 3 or more nodes leaves no majority, so no leader can be elected and no writes can be committed.

objective.question: An order service on Amazon DynamoDB looks up orders by customer email through a global secondary index (GSI). After a write, the support dashboard must always show the latest order status. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Query the base table by its primary key with ConsistentRead=true after resolving the order ID
Enable DynamoDB Streams on the GSI to make it strongly consistent
Double the read capacity on the GSI so reads become strongly consistent
Set ConsistentRead=true on the GSI query
objective.explanation: Strongly consistent reads are not supported on global secondary indexes, so the strong read must go to the base table with ConsistentRead=true, which uses twice the read capacity. Streams and extra capacity do not change the GSI's consistency model.

objective.question: A batch job overwrites an existing object in Amazon S3 with a PUT and then immediately starts a job that reads the same key. What will the read return?
options: A 404 error until replication finishes
The new version only if S3 Versioning is enabled
The new version, because S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE
Possibly the old version for a few seconds because overwrites are eventually consistent
objective.explanation: Since December 2020, Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT and DELETE operations, including overwrites. The old eventual-consistency caveat for overwrites no longer applies, and versioning is not required.

objective.question: A payment platform publishes payment events to Amazon SQS. Events for the same customer must be processed in order, and accidental duplicate sends from the producer must be dropped. Which design fits best?
options: SQS standard queue with a visibility timeout of 12 hours
SQS FIFO queue with a single message group ID for all messages and no deduplication ID
SQS FIFO queue using customer ID as the message group ID and a deduplication ID per payment
SQS standard queue with long polling
objective.explanation: FIFO queues keep order within a message group and drop duplicates that arrive within the 5-minute deduplication interval. Grouping by customer ID gives per-customer order and still allows parallel work across customers. Standard queues give only at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering.

objective.question: A social app on Azure Cosmos DB must let each user see their own new comment immediately after posting it. Other users can see it a little later. The team wants the lowest latency and cost that meets this need. Which consistency level should they use?
options: Bounded staleness
Session
Eventual
Strong
objective.explanation: Session is the Cosmos DB default and guarantees read-your-writes within a session, which is exactly the requirement. Strong and Bounded staleness add latency and cost the app does not need. Eventual does not guarantee the user sees their own write.

objective.question: PACELC extends CAP. What does the 'ELC' part describe?
options: Else (no partition), choose between latency and consistency
During an election, choose between latency and correctness
Else, choose between leader election and consensus
During a partition, choose between latency and consistency
objective.explanation: PACELC says: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. The other options misread the letters.

objective.question: A network partition splits a CP (consistency-first) database cluster into a 2-node majority side and a 1-node minority side. What does the minority side typically do?
options: Refuses or blocks requests it cannot serve consistently, so it becomes unavailable
Promotes itself to leader to stay available
Serves stale reads and accepts writes, marking them as tentative
Accepts writes and merges them later with last-writer-wins
objective.explanation: A CP system gives up availability on the side that cannot reach a majority, so it rejects or blocks those requests. Accepting writes on both sides is AP behaviour. Self-promotion without a majority would risk split-brain.

objective.question: A Snowflake-style ID uses 1 sign bit, 41 timestamp bits (milliseconds), 10 machine bits and 12 sequence bits. What is the maximum number of IDs one node can generate in a single millisecond?
objective.explanation: The 12-bit sequence gives 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node. 1,024 is the number of machine IDs from the 10 machine bits, and 2^41 relates to the timestamp range.

objective.question: A team uses random UUIDv4 primary keys in a relational database and sees slow inserts and index bloat at high write rates. Why does switching to UUIDv7 usually help?
options: UUIDv7 begins with a Unix millisecond timestamp, so new keys are roughly ordered and inserts land near the end of the B-tree
UUIDv7 is generated by the database, which avoids network calls
UUIDv7 is guaranteed unique across all systems without any randomness
UUIDv7 is shorter than 128 bits, so indexes are smaller
objective.explanation: UUIDv7 puts a millisecond timestamp in its leading bits, so keys increase over time. This gives good B-tree locality and fewer page splits than random UUIDv4. It is still 128 bits, it still contains random bits, and it can be generated by the application.

objective.question: A client retries POST /payments with the same Idempotency-Key as an earlier successful request, but the amount in the body has changed from 500 to 5,000. What should a well-designed payment API do?
options: Reject the request with an error, because the key is being reused with different parameters
Charge 5,000 and refund 500 automatically
Return the stored response from the first request without any check
Process the new amount, because the body is different
objective.explanation: The server should store a fingerprint (hash) of the original request with the key and reject a reuse whose parameters differ, since that is a client bug, not a retry. Silently replaying or processing the new amount would hide the bug or risk a wrong charge.

objective.question: A consumer reads from an SQS standard queue and credits a wallet for each message. Product asks for 'exactly-once' processing. What is the realistic design?
options: Rely on SQS standard queues, which deliver each message exactly once
Accept at-least-once delivery and make the consumer idempotent, for example by recording processed message or transaction IDs in the same transaction as the credit
Delete the message before processing so it can never be redelivered
Switch to UDP, which delivers each packet exactly once
objective.explanation: Over unreliable networks you cannot guarantee exactly-once delivery. You get effectively-once results from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. Standard queues are at-least-once, and deleting before processing risks losing messages (at-most-once).

objective.question: A payment service records idempotency keys in Amazon DynamoDB. The command below runs twice with the same key, a few seconds apart. What happens on the second run?

code.code:
aws dynamodb put-item \
  --table-name Idempotency \
  --item '{"pk":{"S":"key-123"},"status":{"S":"IN_PROGRESS"}}' \
  --condition-expression "attribute_not_exists(pk)"

options: The second put fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException and the existing item is unchanged
DynamoDB merges both items and keeps two versions of key-123
The second put succeeds only if the table has DynamoDB Streams enabled
The second put overwrites the first item and returns success
objective.explanation: The condition attribute_not_exists(pk) only lets the write succeed when no item with that key exists, so the second call is rejected with ConditionalCheckFailedException. Without the condition, PutItem would silently overwrite. Streams have no effect on conditional writes, and DynamoDB does not keep multiple versions of an item.

objective.question: A Snowflake-style ID generator runs on each application server. After an NTP correction, one server's clock jumps back by 200 ms. What is the safest behaviour for the generator?
options: Refuse to issue IDs, or wait, until the clock passes the last timestamp it used, and raise an alert
Switch the machine ID bits to a random value for the next 200 ms
Reset the sequence counter to zero and continue normally
Keep generating IDs from the new clock value, because the sequence bits will keep them unique
objective.explanation: If the clock goes backwards, the node could reuse timestamp and sequence values it already issued, which creates duplicate IDs. Standard Snowflake implementations reject or wait until time moves past the last used timestamp. Resetting the sequence makes duplicates more likely, and random machine IDs can collide with other nodes.

objective.question: A web app on Amazon Aurora MySQL sends writes to the cluster (writer) endpoint and all reads to the reader endpoint. Users sometimes update their profile and then see the old values on the next page. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Add more Aurora Replicas to spread the read load
Convert the cluster to an Aurora Global Database
Route a user's reads to the writer endpoint for a short time after that user writes, and keep other reads on the reader endpoint
Enable Multi-AZ on the Aurora cluster
objective.explanation: Aurora Replicas are asynchronous and usually lag by milliseconds, so a read right after a write can be stale. Sending that user's reads to the writer for a short window gives read-your-writes consistency without moving all reads. More replicas or a Global Database do not remove replica lag, and Aurora's storage is already spread across AZs.

objective.question: A fintech company needs a globally distributed relational ledger on Google Cloud. It needs SQL, horizontal write scaling and strongly consistent reads and writes across regions. Which service fits?
options: Cloud Spanner with a multi-region configuration
Cloud SQL with cross-region read replicas
BigQuery with scheduled queries
Cloud Bigtable with multi-cluster routing
objective.explanation: Cloud Spanner is a horizontally scalable relational database that gives strong, externally consistent transactions across regions. Bigtable replication across clusters is eventually consistent. Cloud SQL cross-region replicas are asynchronous and the primary does not scale writes horizontally. BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not a transactional ledger.

objective.question: A scheduler uses a lock lease so that only one leader writes to shared storage. The leader has a long garbage-collection pause, its lease expires, and a new leader is elected. The old leader then resumes and writes. What prevents this stale write from corrupting data?
options: Using a fencing token: a number that grows with each new lease, which the storage checks and uses to reject writes with an older token
Having the old leader check its local clock before each write
Running the lock service on an odd number of nodes
Making the lease duration longer than any possible GC pause
objective.explanation: A paused process cannot know its lease expired, so checking its own clock just before writing is not safe. A fencing token lets the storage reject any write with a lower token than one it has already seen. No lease length can rule out every pause, and an odd cluster size protects the lock service's own quorum, not the storage.

objective.question: In a 5-node Raft cluster, node E was partitioned away and missed many committed entries. When it reconnects, it times out and starts an election with a higher term. Why can E not become leader?
options: Voters refuse to vote for a candidate whose log is less up-to-date than their own (by last log term, then last log index)
The current leader holds a lease that blocks any election for one hour
Other nodes ignore any message that carries a higher term
Raft always elects the node with the lowest node ID
objective.explanation: Raft's election restriction says a node votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date as its own. This makes sure a new leader holds all committed entries. A higher term is not ignored: it makes the current leader step down. But E cannot collect a majority of votes. Raft has no ID-based priority and no hour-long leases.

objective.question: A Kafka producer in a payments pipeline uses the settings below. What do they guarantee?

code.code:
enable.idempotence=true
acks=all
retries=2147483647
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5

options: The broker drops duplicates caused by this producer's own retries, per partition, using a producer ID and sequence numbers, and keeps order
Consumers will never see a message more than once, even after they crash
The broker drops any two messages that have the same message key
Each payment is written exactly once into the downstream database, end to end
objective.explanation: The idempotent producer gives each producer a producer ID and numbers its messages per partition. The broker can then drop duplicates from retries and keep order with up to 5 in-flight requests. It does not remove duplicates by business key. It also does not make consumer processing or database writes exactly-once; that needs transactions or idempotent consumers.

subjective.question: Explain the CAP theorem in plain words. Why is 'pick any two of three' a misleading summary?
subjective.answer: CAP says that when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. Consistency here means every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. Availability means every request to a working node gets a non-error response. The 'pick two' summary is misleading because partitions are not optional. Networks do fail, so every real distributed system must tolerate partitions. The real choice is only made during a partition. A CP system refuses some requests to stay correct. An AP system keeps answering but may return stale data or accept conflicting writes. When there is no partition, a system can be both consistent and available. Also, CAP's 'consistency' is linearizability, not the 'C' in ACID. In interviews I say: 'Partitions will happen. For this feature, do we prefer an error or stale data?'
keyPoints: The choice between C and A only applies during a partition
Partition tolerance is mandatory in real networks
CAP consistency means linearizability, not ACID consistency
Frame it as: an error or stale data, per feature

subjective.question: What does PACELC add to CAP? Classify two example systems.
subjective.answer: CAP only describes behaviour during a partition. PACELC adds the normal case. If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency. Else, choose Latency or Consistency. This matters because partitions are rare, but the latency cost of consistency is paid on every request. Synchronous replication to a quorum or to another region gives consistency but adds round trips. Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra with low consistency levels are usually PA/EL. They stay available in a partition and favour low latency normally, at the cost of stale reads. Systems like Google Spanner, or a relational database with synchronous replication, are PC/EC. They give up availability in a partition and accept higher write latency for strong consistency. Many systems are tunable per request. For example, DynamoDB lets you choose eventually or strongly consistent reads, so the classification depends on how you configure them.
keyPoints: PAC covers the partition case; ELC covers normal operation
Latency versus consistency is a cost paid on every request
Dynamo/Cassandra-style stores are typically PA/EL
Spanner or synchronously replicated databases are PC/EC
Many stores are tunable per request

subjective.question: Compare strong and eventual consistency. Give one feature that needs each and explain why.
subjective.answer: With strong consistency, once a write is acknowledged, every later read from any client sees it. The system behaves like a single copy. With eventual consistency, replicas converge if writes stop, but a read may return old data for a while. Strong consistency costs latency and availability because writes must coordinate with a majority or with the leader. An account balance or inventory check before a sale needs strong consistency. If two readers see a stale balance, you can overdraw money or oversell stock. A like counter, view count or news feed can be eventual. Showing 1,203 likes instead of 1,205 for a second harms no one, and you gain speed and availability. On AWS, DynamoDB reads are eventual by default, and you set ConsistentRead=true for the balance read, which uses twice the read capacity. Choose per feature, not per system.
keyPoints: Strong: every read after an acknowledged write sees it
Eventual: replicas converge, but stale reads are possible
Money and inventory need strong consistency; counters and feeds can be eventual
Strong consistency costs latency, availability and money (for example, double DynamoDB RCU)

subjective.question: Explain causal consistency and read-your-writes consistency with examples. How would you implement read-your-writes?
subjective.answer: Read-your-writes means a user always sees their own updates. If I change my profile photo and refresh, I must not see the old one, even if other users still do. Causal consistency is broader. If one operation could have influenced another, everyone sees them in that order. For example, if Asha posts a question and Ravi replies, no reader should see Ravi's reply without Asha's question. Unrelated writes can appear in any order. Both are weaker than strong consistency, so they are cheaper and still prevent the most confusing anomalies. To implement read-your-writes, I can route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write. I can use sticky sessions to one replica. Or I can have the client carry a session token or version number, so a replica serves the read only once it has caught up to that version. Azure Cosmos DB's default Session level does this with session tokens.
keyPoints: Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own updates
Causal: cause-and-effect ordering is preserved for all readers
Both are weaker and cheaper than strong consistency
Implementation options: read from leader after a write, sticky sessions, or session tokens/versions
Cosmos DB Session consistency is the default

subjective.question: Explain quorum reads and writes with N, R and W. What happens with N=3, W=2, R=2 when one node is down, and what are the limits of quorums?
subjective.answer: N is the number of replicas for each item. W is how many must acknowledge a write. R is how many we read from. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write, using versions to pick the newest. With N=3, W=2, R=2, one node can be down and both reads and writes still succeed, because two nodes remain. If two nodes are down, both fail. Tuning trades cost: W=3, R=1 gives fast reads but writes fail if any node is down, while W=1 favours write availability but loses overlap. Limits: concurrent writes still need conflict resolution. Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff can break the overlap guarantee. Failed partial writes can leave some replicas updated. So quorums give strong-ish reads, not full linearizability, without extra care.
keyPoints: R + W > N guarantees overlap between read and write sets
N=3, W=2, R=2 tolerates one node down for both reads and writes
Tuning R and W trades read cost, write cost and availability
Caveats: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and partial writes

subjective.question: Describe how Raft works at a high level: leader election and log replication.
subjective.answer: Raft keeps a replicated log consistent across a cluster, usually 3 or 5 nodes. Each node is a follower, a candidate or the leader. Time is split into numbered terms. Followers expect regular heartbeats from the leader. If a follower's randomised election timeout passes with no heartbeat, it becomes a candidate. It increases the term, votes for itself and asks the others for votes. A node grants at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. The candidate that wins a majority becomes leader. The randomised timeouts make split votes rare. All client writes go to the leader. The leader appends each write to its log and replicates it to followers. An entry is committed once a majority has stored it, and only then is it applied and acknowledged. Because any two majorities overlap, a new leader always holds every committed entry. etcd and Consul use Raft.
keyPoints: Roles are follower, candidate and leader; terms act as logical epochs
Randomised election timeouts; one vote per term; winning needs a majority
The vote check ensures the new leader has an up-to-date log
An entry is committed once stored on a majority; overlapping majorities keep it safe

subjective.question: Why do consensus clusters use odd sizes? Compare 3, 4 and 5 nodes.
subjective.answer: Consensus needs a majority to elect a leader and commit writes. A cluster of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures. With 3 nodes the majority is 2, so it tolerates 1 failure. With 4 nodes the majority is 3, so it still tolerates only 1 failure. You pay for an extra node, every write waits for one more acknowledgement, and you gain no extra fault tolerance. With 5 nodes the majority is 3, so it tolerates 2 failures. Even sizes also make an even network split worse. A 4-node cluster split 2–2 has no majority on either side, so the whole cluster stops. That is why we use 3 or 5, and rarely 7. Bigger clusters slow writes because more nodes must respond. For zone resilience, I place a 3-node cluster across three availability zones, so losing one zone still leaves a majority.
keyPoints: 2f+1 nodes tolerate f failures
4 nodes tolerate the same as 3 but cost more and write slower
A 2–2 split on an even cluster leaves no majority
Spread nodes across availability zones; bigger clusters add write latency

subjective.question: Hands-on task: design a POST /payments endpoint that is safe to retry using an idempotency key. Walk through the storage and flow.
subjective.answer: The client creates a unique key, for example a UUID, for each logical payment and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header. It reuses the same key on every retry. On the server, I keep an idempotency table with the key as a unique primary key, plus a hash of the request body, a status (in_progress, succeeded or failed), the stored response and an expiry time. When a request arrives, I try to insert the key with status in_progress. If the insert succeeds, I process the payment. I pass the same key to the payment provider so the provider also deduplicates. Then I save the response and mark the key succeeded. If the key already exists and has succeeded, I return the stored response without charging again. If it is still in progress, I return a conflict so the client retries later. If the body hash differs, I reject the request as key misuse. Keys expire after a retention window, for example 24 hours.
keyPoints: Client generates one key per logical payment and reuses it on retries
The unique constraint on the key is the atomic deduplication point
Store status, request hash and response; replay the response on repeats
Pass the key to the downstream payment provider
Handle in-progress requests, mismatched bodies and key expiry

subjective.question: Checkpoint: explain to a product manager why a retried payment request must never charge the customer twice, and how we guarantee it.
subjective.answer: Imagine the customer taps Pay. Our server charges the card, but the response is lost because the mobile network drops. The app sees a timeout. It cannot know whether the charge happened, so the safe move is to retry. Without protection, the retry looks like a brand-new payment and the customer is charged twice. That means refunds, support tickets, possible chargebacks and lost trust. Retries are normal and unavoidable, because timeouts, load balancer failovers and client libraries all retry. POST is not idempotent by the HTTP specification, unlike GET, PUT and DELETE. So we make it idempotent ourselves. The app sends the same idempotency key on every attempt for that one payment. The server records the key and its result the first time. Any repeat with that key returns the original result instead of charging again. So the customer can retry safely as often as needed.
keyPoints: A lost response makes the client unsure, so retrying is correct behaviour
Without deduplication, a retry becomes a second charge
POST is not idempotent by the HTTP specification; GET, PUT and DELETE are
The idempotency key maps every retry to one recorded outcome

subjective.question: Why is 'exactly-once delivery' called a myth? What do systems that claim exactly-once actually provide?
subjective.answer: Over a network, the sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement. If it does not retry, messages can be lost, which is at-most-once. If it retries, messages can be duplicated, which is at-least-once. No protocol removes this ambiguity, so exactly-once delivery is not guaranteed end to end. What we can build is exactly-once effect, often called effectively-once. We combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing. The consumer records a unique message or business ID in the same transaction as its side effect, or the operation is naturally idempotent, like setting a status instead of incrementing it. Features marketed as exactly-once work within a boundary. SQS FIFO deduplicates only within a 5-minute interval, and Kafka transactions cover reads and writes inside Kafka. Once you call an external system such as a card network, you need idempotency keys again.
keyPoints: A lost message and a lost acknowledgement look the same to the sender
The realistic choices are at-most-once or at-least-once delivery
Effectively-once = at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer
Vendor exactly-once guarantees hold only within a boundary, such as the SQS FIFO 5-minute window

subjective.question: Compare database auto-increment IDs, UUIDv4, Snowflake IDs and UUIDv7 for a large distributed system.
subjective.answer: Auto-increment IDs are small and ordered, but a single database hands them out. That becomes a bottleneck and is hard to use across shards. They also reveal business volume to anyone who sees them. UUIDv4 is 128-bit random and needs no coordination, but random keys scatter B-tree inserts and hurt index performance. Snowflake IDs are 64-bit: 1 sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 machine bits and 12 sequence bits. That allows 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node. They are compact and roughly time-sortable, but you must assign unique machine IDs and handle clock skew. If the clock moves backwards, the generator should wait or fail rather than risk duplicates. UUIDv7 is 128-bit with a leading Unix millisecond timestamp and random bits. It is time-ordered, needs no machine-ID coordination and is standardised in RFC 9562. I pick Snowflake when 64-bit size matters and UUIDv7 as the simple default.
keyPoints: Auto-increment: central bottleneck, hard to shard, leaks business volume
UUIDv4: coordination-free but random, which hurts index locality
Snowflake: 64-bit, 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node; needs machine IDs and clock-skew handling
UUIDv7: time-ordered 128-bit, no coordination, RFC 9562

subjective.question: Two identical payment requests with the same idempotency key reach two different API servers at the same millisecond. How do you prevent a double charge, and what failure cases remain?
subjective.answer: The check and the claim must be one atomic step. A read-then-insert sequence has a race: both servers read 'not found' and both charge. So I make an atomic insert the gate. I use the database's unique constraint on the key, or a conditional write such as a DynamoDB PutItem with attribute_not_exists on the key, or Redis SET NX. Only one server wins and moves the key to in_progress. The loser gets a conflict and returns 409, or waits and then returns the stored result. Remaining risks: the winner may crash after charging but before saving the response. To handle that, I pass the same key to the payment provider so the provider's retry is deduplicated, and I run a reconciliation job that resolves stuck in_progress records by checking the provider. The idempotency store must be strongly consistent. An eventually consistent read could miss the first claim.
keyPoints: Read-then-write has a race; use an atomic insert or conditional write
Options: unique constraint, DynamoDB attribute_not_exists, Redis SET NX
The loser returns a conflict or the stored result
Handle a crash after charging: provider-side idempotency plus reconciliation
The idempotency store must be strongly consistent

subjective.question: Review this payment handler. Explain how it can still charge a customer twice, even with only one server and no concurrent requests, and describe how you would fix it.

code.code:
def create_payment(key, req):
    row = db.get(key)
    if row:
        return row.response
    result = psp.charge(req.card, req.amount)
    db.insert(key, result)
    return result

subjective.answer: The gap is between psp.charge and db.insert. If the process crashes, times out or loses its database connection after the PSP charges the card but before the key is saved, the client retries. db.get finds nothing and the card is charged again. There is also a check-then-act race when two requests run at the same time. My fix has three parts. First, insert the key with status IN_PROGRESS under a unique constraint before calling the PSP, so only one caller proceeds. Second, pass our idempotency key (or a derived one) to the PSP, because most payment providers dedupe on it. A retried charge then returns the original result. Third, run a recovery job for records stuck in IN_PROGRESS. It asks the PSP for the real outcome and marks each record SUCCEEDED or FAILED. Only then do we save the response and return it on every later retry.
keyPoints: Crash between the external charge and saving the record leaves no trace, so a retry charges again
Reserve the key first (IN_PROGRESS) using a unique constraint or conditional write
Pass an idempotency key downstream to the payment provider
Reconcile stuck IN_PROGRESS records by asking the PSP for the real outcome

subjective.question: An order service writes a row to its database and then publishes an 'OrderPlaced' event to a message broker. Sometimes the event is missing, and sometimes it is sent for an order that was rolled back. Explain the root cause and a reliable design.
subjective.answer: This is the dual-write problem. The database and the broker are two separate systems with no shared transaction. If the service commits the row and then crashes before publishing, the event is lost. If it publishes first and then the commit fails, the event describes an order that does not exist. The standard fix is the transactional outbox. In the same local database transaction, the service writes the order row and an outbox row that holds the event. A separate relay then reads the outbox, either by polling or through change data capture such as DynamoDB Streams or Debezium, and publishes to the broker. It marks each row as sent. The relay can crash and publish twice, so delivery is at-least-once. Each event therefore carries a unique ID, and consumers dedupe on it or apply changes idempotently.
keyPoints: Two systems with no shared transaction cause lost or phantom events
Transactional outbox: business row and event row commit in one local transaction
A relay or CDC publishes from the outbox
Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent and dedupe by event ID

subjective.question: A Dynamo-style store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 with sloppy quorums and hinted handoff. Explain what these features do during a partial outage, and why they weaken the usual 'R + W > N means you read the latest write' guarantee.
subjective.answer: In a strict quorum, a write must reach W of the N 'home' replicas for that key. If two home replicas are down, the write fails. With a sloppy quorum, the coordinator accepts writes on any healthy nodes, even ones outside the key's home set, so writes stay available. Those stand-in nodes keep a 'hint'. When a home replica recovers, hinted handoff sends it the missed writes. The trade-off is consistency. The W nodes that acknowledged a write may not overlap with the R home nodes a later read contacts, so R + W > N no longer guarantees the read sees the latest write until handoff finishes. Systems add read repair and anti-entropy, often using Merkle trees, to converge. Conflicting versions are resolved with vector clocks or last-writer-wins. This is a deliberate choice of availability over consistency during partitions.
keyPoints: Sloppy quorum accepts writes on healthy non-home nodes to stay available
Hinted handoff delivers missed writes when home replicas return
Read and write sets may not overlap, so R + W > N no longer guarantees fresh reads
Convergence uses read repair, anti-entropy and conflict resolution

subjective.question: Two users edit the same shopping cart in an active-active, multi-region, eventually consistent database. Explain how concurrent writes can conflict and compare ways to resolve them. Would you use the same approach for an account balance?
subjective.answer: With active-active replication, both regions accept writes locally and replicate them asynchronously. If user A adds an item in Mumbai and user B removes one in Singapore at the same time, each region applies its own write first. When they sync, the database has two concurrent versions. Last-writer-wins by timestamp is simple, but it silently drops one update and depends on clocks. Vector clocks detect that the versions are concurrent and keep both as siblings, so the application can merge them, for example by taking the union of cart items. CRDTs, such as an observed-remove set, merge automatically and always converge. For a cart, a merge that sometimes brings back a removed item is acceptable. For an account balance it is not, because concurrent debits could overdraw the account. Balances need strong consistency: a single leader per account, or a consensus-backed store such as Spanner, with conditional or transactional updates.
keyPoints: Async multi-region writes create concurrent conflicting versions
Last-writer-wins loses updates and depends on clocks
Vector clocks detect concurrency; CRDTs merge automatically
Money needs strong consistency and a single source of truth, not merging

subjective.question: A team spreads a 3-node Raft cluster across Mumbai, Singapore and Frankfurt for disaster recovery. Write latency jumps sharply. Explain why using PACELC, and suggest placement options with their trade-offs.
