      # Latency SLO: 99% of requests under 300 ms. Alert when fewer than 99% are fast.
      - alert: LatencySLOBreach
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.3"}[30m]))
            / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[30m])) < 0.99
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: ticket }
        annotations:
          summary: "Fewer than 99% of requests finish within 300 ms"

      # Limiter failing open means no abuse protection. Ticket, do not page.
      - alert: RateLimiterFailingOpen
        expr: sum(rate(rate_limiter_errors_total[5m])) > 0
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: ticket }
        annotations:
          summary: "Redis unreachable; rate limiter is allowing all traffic"

      # Cause-based alert kept for diagnosis: a scrape target is down.
      - alert: ApiInstanceDown
        expr: up{job="api"} == 0
        for: 2m
        labels: { severity: ticket }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.instance }} is not responding to scrapes"

objective.question: A public REST API must reject a client that has exceeded its rate limit. Which response best follows common practice?
options: HTTP 403 Forbidden with an error message
HTTP 400 Bad Request with X-RateLimit-Remaining set to 0
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
HTTP 503 Service Unavailable with no headers
objective.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the status code for rate limiting, and Retry-After tells the client when it may try again. 503 suggests the server is unhealthy, 403 suggests a permission problem, and 400 suggests a malformed request.

objective.question: An API must allow short bursts of up to 50 requests while holding the long-term average at 10 requests per second. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Fixed window counter, because it resets every second
Token bucket with a refill rate of 10 per second and a capacity of 50
Sliding window log with a 1-second window
Leaky bucket, because it processes requests at a fixed output rate
objective.explanation: A token bucket refills at a steady rate and its capacity sets the burst size, so it allows bursts while holding the average rate. A leaky bucket smooths traffic out and does not allow bursts. A fixed window or a 1-second log enforces a per-window count and has no separate burst setting.

objective.question: A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00. What happens?
options: All 200 requests are accepted, so the client gets double the limit in about two seconds
The limiter switches to leaky bucket mode automatically
Only 100 requests in total are accepted across both minutes
The second batch is rejected because the limiter tracks the last 60 seconds
objective.explanation: Fixed windows reset at the boundary, so traffic around the edge can reach twice the limit. Sliding window log or sliding window counter algorithms fix this. Fixed windows do not look back 60 seconds, and limiters do not change algorithm by themselves.

objective.question: Your API runs on 40 stateless servers behind a load balancer. Each server keeps its own in-memory counter, and clients get far more than their limit. What is the most common fix?
options: Divide the limit by 40 and keep the counters local
Store counters in a shared, low-latency store such as Redis and update them atomically, for example with a Lua script
Write every request to a relational database and count rows
Use sticky sessions so each client always reaches one server
objective.explanation: A shared store with atomic increment or check-and-update gives one consistent count across all servers at low latency. Sticky sessions break when servers scale or fail, dividing the limit fails when load is uneven, and a relational database is too slow for checking every request.

objective.question: A company exposes a REST API through Amazon API Gateway. Free-tier customers should get 10 requests per second and 10,000 requests per month. Paid customers should get higher limits. What should a solutions architect use?
options: Usage plans with API keys, with a separate throttle (rate and burst) and quota for each tier
An Application Load Balancer with a target group for each tier
Lambda reserved concurrency for each customer
AWS WAF rate-based rules for each customer
objective.explanation: API Gateway usage plans link API keys to per-client throttling (rate and burst, applied as a token bucket) and to quotas per day, week or month. WAF rate-based rules block by IP and do not handle tiered monthly quotas. Lambda concurrency and ALB target groups do not meter individual API customers.

objective.question: After a database outage, thousands of clients retry at exactly 1, 2 and 4 seconds. Each wave of retries crashes the recovering database again. What is the best change?
options: Retry immediately with no delay
Add random jitter to the exponential backoff and cap the number of retries
Increase the retry count to 10
Remove timeouts so requests wait longer
objective.explanation: Jitter spreads retries over time, so clients do not arrive in synchronised waves (the thundering herd problem). A retry cap stops the retries from adding unlimited load. Immediate retries, more retries or no timeouts all make the overload worse.

objective.question: A mobile app calls POST /payments. The response times out, and the app is not sure whether the charge succeeded. How can the app retry safely?
options: Send a unique idempotency key with the request so the server returns the original result for duplicates
Retry with a shorter timeout
Never retry POST requests under any condition
Change the method to GET so it becomes idempotent
objective.explanation: An idempotency key lets the server spot a duplicate request and return the stored result instead of charging twice. GET must not change state, so it cannot be used for payments. Never retrying hurts reliability, and a shorter timeout does not stop duplicate charges.

objective.question: A circuit breaker for a failing downstream service has been open for 30 seconds. What does it normally do next?
options: Moves to closed and sends all traffic at once
Starts retrying every failed request that it rejected earlier
Moves to half-open and lets a few trial requests through; it closes if they succeed and opens again if they fail
Stays open until an operator resets it
objective.explanation: After a cool-down, the breaker goes half-open and probes with a small number of requests before it fully closes. Sending all traffic at once could overload a service that is still recovering. Manual reset is not the standard design, and breakers do not replay requests they rejected.

objective.question: One service calls both a slow recommendations API and a critical payments API from the same thread pool. When recommendations slows down, payments also fail. Which pattern isolates the two?
options: Leaky bucket rate limiting
Read replicas
Cache-aside
Bulkhead: give each dependency its own thread or connection pool
objective.explanation: Bulkheads split resources into separate pools, so one slow dependency cannot use up the threads another dependency needs. Caching, rate limiting and read replicas do not separate resource pools.

objective.question: A request passes through an API service at 99.9% availability, which calls a database at 99.9% availability in series. What is the approximate availability of the whole path?
objective.explanation: Availabilities in series multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, or about 99.8%. The path is less available than either part. Redundant copies in parallel, not serial calls, raise availability.

objective.question: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 30 days. In the last hour it has been burning the error budget at 14.4 times the allowed rate, and this is confirmed by a short 5-minute window. Following the Google SRE Workbook, what should happen?
options: Do nothing until the monthly budget is fully used
Alert only if CPU is also above 90%
Page the on-call engineer, because about 2% of the monthly budget has been used in one hour
Open a low-priority ticket for next week
objective.explanation: A burn rate of 14.4 over 1 hour uses about 2% of a 30-day budget (14.4 × 1 / 720 hours). The Workbook recommends a page for this. Tickets are for slower burns, waiting means the SLO will be missed, and CPU is a cause metric, not a user symptom.

objective.question: A web dashboard must show live order-status updates that the server pushes to browsers. Clients never send data back on this channel. You want the simplest option over standard HTTP with automatic reconnection. What should you choose?
options: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
gRPC bidirectional streaming from the browser
Short polling every 100 ms
WebSockets
objective.explanation: SSE is a one-way stream from server to client over plain HTTP. The browser EventSource API reconnects automatically. WebSockets are two-way and more complex than needed here, browsers cannot use native gRPC bidirectional streaming, and fast polling wastes resources.

objective.question: A developer wrote this rate-limit check for an API that runs on 20 servers sharing one Redis instance. Under load tests, clients regularly get more than LIMIT requests per minute. What is the main cause?

code.code:
def allow(client_id):
    key = f"rl:{client_id}:{int(time.time() // 60)}"
    count = r.get(key)
    if count is not None and int(count) >= LIMIT:
        return False
    r.incr(key)
    r.expire(key, 60)
    return True

options: The EXPIRE call resets the counter to zero on every request
The key uses the minute number, so each server computes a different key
Redis INCR is not atomic when called from more than one server
The GET and INCR are separate steps, so many servers can read the same count before any of them increments it
objective.explanation: This is a check-then-act race. Concurrent requests all read a count below LIMIT and then all increment it. INCR itself is atomic, and EXPIRE only sets a TTL; it does not reset the value. The fix is to INCR first and compare the returned value, or to run the whole check in a Lua script.

objective.question: A company is splitting a monolith into internal microservices on AWS. The services need low-latency calls, strongly typed contracts that are shared between Go and Java teams, and bidirectional streaming. Traffic between services goes through an Application Load Balancer. Which approach fits best?
options: REST with JSON and an OpenAPI specification, using long polling for streaming
Server-Sent Events between services, behind a Network Load Balancer
gRPC with Protocol Buffers, using ALB target groups configured for the gRPC protocol version
GraphQL over HTTP/1.1, with one schema shared by all services
objective.explanation: gRPC gives compact binary Protobuf messages, code-generated typed clients in many languages, and bidirectional streaming over HTTP/2. ALB supports gRPC as a target group protocol version. REST with long polling and SSE cannot do efficient bidirectional streaming, and GraphQL is mainly for flexible client-driven queries, not internal streaming RPC.

objective.question: An Azure API Management instance has this inbound policy. What is its effect?

code.code:
<inbound>
  <base />
  <rate-limit-by-key calls="100"
      renewal-period="60"
      counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />
</inbound>

options: It caps each subscription at 100 calls in total, and the cap never resets
It queues extra calls and sends them to the backend at 100 calls per minute
It limits each subscription to 100 calls per 60 seconds and returns HTTP 429 when a subscription exceeds that
It limits the whole API to 100 calls per minute across all callers
objective.explanation: rate-limit-by-key keeps a separate counter for each key, here the subscription ID, and renews it every renewal-period seconds. Calls over the limit get 429 Too Many Requests. It rejects extra calls rather than queuing them. Long-term caps such as monthly volume use quota-by-key instead.

objective.question: After a deploy, the Prometheus server's memory use grows quickly and queries time out. The only change was the metric definition shown below. The platform has 2 million active users. What is the best fix?

code.code:
REQUEST_LATENCY = Histogram(
    "http_request_duration_seconds",
    "Request latency",
    ["route", "status", "user_id"],
)

options: Increase the Prometheus scrape interval from 15 to 60 seconds
Remove the user_id label, keep low-cardinality labels such as route and status, and record user_id in logs or trace attributes
Use a counter instead of a histogram and keep the user_id label
Switch from a Histogram to a Summary so that percentiles are computed on the client
objective.explanation: Every unique label combination creates a new time series, and a histogram multiplies that by its buckets. A per-user label therefore causes a cardinality explosion. High-cardinality identifiers belong in logs and traces. Changing the metric type or the scrape interval does not fix the number of series.

objective.question: In a tracing tool, every request to the checkout service appears as two separate traces: one for the API gateway and checkout service, and another starting at the inventory service. Both services are instrumented with OpenTelemetry. What is the most likely cause?
options: The two services send logs to different log groups
The clocks on the two hosts are out of sync by a few milliseconds
The checkout service makes its outgoing HTTP call to inventory without propagating the trace context header, such as W3C traceparent
The trace sampling rate is set too low on the inventory service
objective.explanation: Spans join one trace only when the caller passes the trace ID and parent span ID downstream, usually in the traceparent header. If the HTTP client is not instrumented, or the header is dropped, the callee starts a new root trace. Clock skew distorts span timings but does not split a trace. Sampling decides whether a trace is kept, not how it is linked.

objective.question: A legacy payment processor accepts at most 5 requests per second and fails if requests arrive in bursts. Your service receives traffic in sudden spikes. You must smooth the outgoing calls to a steady rate, and it is acceptable for requests to wait briefly. Which approach fits best?
options: A fixed window counter of 5 requests per second
A leaky bucket: put requests in a bounded queue and drain it at a constant 5 per second
A circuit breaker that opens when the processor returns errors
A token bucket with a capacity of 500 and a refill rate of 5 per second
objective.explanation: A leaky bucket gives a constant output rate whatever the input pattern, so it smooths bursts into a steady flow. Its bounded queue rejects requests once it is full. A large token bucket deliberately allows bursts, and a fixed window can still let 5 requests arrive together at a window boundary. A circuit breaker reacts to failures; it does not shape traffic.

objective.question: A request passes through 4 service layers: gateway, API, order service and database client. Each layer makes up to 3 attempts, 1 try plus 2 retries, when the layer below fails. The database is down. In the worst case, how many database calls can one user request cause, and what is the best mitigation?
options: 81 calls; increase the timeout at every layer so that fewer retries are triggered
12 calls; add jitter so that the retries spread out over time
81 calls; retry at only one layer, usually the one closest to the failure, and use a retry budget plus a circuit breaker
12 calls; add exponential backoff at every layer
objective.explanation: Retries multiply across layers: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 attempts against the failing dependency. The fix is to retry at a single layer and cap retries with a retry budget, so they stay a small fraction of traffic, and with a circuit breaker. Backoff and jitter only spread the calls out over time; they do not reduce how many there are.

subjective.question: Compare REST, gRPC and GraphQL. When would you choose each one?
subjective.answer: REST models resources with HTTP verbs and usually JSON. It is simple, cacheable through HTTP and understood by every client, so I use it for public APIs. gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. It gives compact binary messages, strict contracts, generated client code and streaming. It suits internal service-to-service calls where latency and type safety matter, but browsers need a proxy such as gRPC-Web. GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs from one endpoint. This avoids over-fetching and stops a screen from making many round trips, which helps mobile and complex front ends. The costs are harder HTTP caching, the risk of expensive queries (so you need depth and cost limits), and N+1 resolver problems that need batching. A common setup is GraphQL or REST at the edge and gRPC between internal services.
keyPoints: REST: resources, HTTP caching, best for public APIs
gRPC: HTTP/2 plus Protobuf, low latency, streaming, internal use
GraphQL: client picks the fields, avoids over-fetching
GraphQL needs query cost limits and handles caching less well
Combine them: GraphQL or REST at the edge, gRPC inside

subjective.question: You are building a chat app and a news notification feed. Would you use WebSockets, SSE or long polling for each? Explain why.
subjective.answer: For chat I would use WebSockets. Chat needs low-latency messages in both directions on one long-lived connection, and WebSockets give a full-duplex channel after an HTTP upgrade. For the notification feed I would use SSE. Data only flows from server to client, SSE runs over normal HTTP, works well with existing infrastructure, and the browser reconnects automatically and can resume with Last-Event-ID. Long polling is the fallback when proxies or old clients block the other two. The client holds a request open until there is data, then reconnects at once. It works almost everywhere, but each message costs a new request and adds overhead. For both WebSockets and SSE you must plan for many open connections per server, load balancers that support long-lived connections, heartbeats, and a pub/sub layer such as Redis so that any server can deliver a message to any client.
keyPoints: WebSockets: full-duplex, right for chat
SSE: one-way over HTTP, auto-reconnect, right for feeds
Long polling: fallback that works widely but costs more
Plan connection limits, heartbeats and load balancer timeouts
Use pub/sub to deliver messages across servers

subjective.question: Design a rate limiter for a public API that runs on many servers.
subjective.answer: First I settle the requirements: limits per API key or user, plus per IP for anonymous traffic; for example 100 requests per minute with small bursts allowed. The check must add only a millisecond or two. I put the limiter in the API gateway or as middleware, so every server enforces it the same way. State lives in a shared Redis cluster, sharded by client key. I use a token bucket or sliding window counter, carried out in one Lua script so the read, update and decision happen atomically with no race conditions. Keys get a TTL so memory cleans itself up. Rejected calls get 429 with Retry-After, and responses include headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining. Rules are stored in config so tiers can change without a deploy. For very hot keys, servers can take small batches of tokens and count them locally. I also decide whether to fail open or fail closed if Redis is unavailable, and I monitor how many requests are rejected.
keyPoints: Limit per key or user, plus per IP for anonymous traffic; enforce at the gateway or middleware
Shared Redis store with atomic Lua script; sharded; TTL on keys
Token bucket or sliding window counter
429 with Retry-After and remaining-quota headers
Decide fail-open or fail-closed, plus local batching for hot keys

subjective.question: Explain the sliding window log and sliding window counter algorithms. What are the trade-offs?
subjective.answer: A sliding window log stores a timestamp for every request, often in a Redis sorted set. On each request you remove entries older than the window, count what is left, and allow the request if the count is under the limit. It is exact and has no boundary burst problem, but memory grows with the request rate, so it is costly at high volume. A sliding window counter keeps only two counters: the current fixed window and the previous one. It estimates the count as the current count plus the previous count multiplied by the share of the previous window that still overlaps the sliding window. For example, 30 seconds into a minute, the estimate is the current count plus half of the previous count. This uses tiny, constant memory and smooths out boundary bursts, but it is an approximation that assumes requests were spread evenly. Most production systems choose the counter version, or a token bucket.
keyPoints: Log: one timestamp per request, exact, memory-heavy
Counter: two windows combined by weighting, constant memory
Counter is approximate and assumes even spread
Both fix the fixed-window boundary burst
Counter or token bucket is the usual production choice

subjective.question: Your shared Redis store for rate limiting goes down. Should the limiter fail open or fail closed? Justify your answer.
subjective.answer: It depends on what the limiter protects. If its main job is fair use and quota billing for a public API, I usually fail open. I let requests through, maybe with a fallback local in-memory limit for each server, because rejecting all traffic would turn a Redis problem into a full outage for customers. If the limiter protects a fragile backend, or blocks abuse such as brute-force login attempts or expensive operations, I would fail closed or use a strict local limit, because letting traffic through unchecked could cause wider damage or a security incident. In both cases I keep the Redis call on a tight timeout, so a slow Redis does not add latency to every request. I put a circuit breaker around it, raise an alert, and run Redis with replication and automatic failover to make the situation rare.
keyPoints: Fail open protects availability for normal quota use
Fail closed for security or fragile-backend protection
Fallback local per-server limits
Tight timeout and circuit breaker on the Redis call
Replication and failover; alert on the failure

subjective.question: How do you set timeouts and retries correctly in a chain of microservices?
subjective.answer: Every network call needs a timeout. Without one, slow dependencies hold threads until the caller fails too. I base timeouts on the dependency's latency percentiles, for example a little above its p99, and I pass a deadline down the chain so inner calls never wait longer than the outer request has left. I retry only transient errors such as timeouts, 503 or connection resets, and never errors like 400. I retry only idempotent operations: GET, PUT and DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter, so clients do not retry in synchronised waves. I cap attempts and use a retry budget, for example retries may be at most about 10% of traffic. Retry at one layer only. If three layers each retry three times, one user request can become 27 calls to the bottom service, and this amplification causes retry storms.
keyPoints: Timeouts on every call, based on percentiles; pass deadlines down the chain
Retry only transient errors and idempotent operations
Exponential backoff with jitter
Cap attempts and use a retry budget
Avoid retrying at many layers (amplification)

subjective.question: What is a circuit breaker? Describe its states and how it improves reliability.
subjective.answer: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and stops calling it when it is clearly failing. In the closed state, calls pass through and the breaker tracks failures or slow calls over a rolling window. When the failure rate crosses a threshold, it trips to open. Calls then fail fast at once, or return a fallback such as cached data or a default response, without touching the dependency. After a cool-down it moves to half-open and lets a few trial requests through. If they succeed it closes; if they fail it opens again. This helps in two ways. Callers stop wasting threads and time waiting on a dead service, so failures do not cascade upward. The struggling service also gets room to recover instead of being hit by more traffic and retries. Libraries such as Resilience4j provide this pattern, and service meshes like Istio offer similar outlier detection.
keyPoints: Closed state tracks failures over a window
Open state fails fast or returns a fallback
Half-open state probes with a few trial requests
Prevents cascading failures and thread exhaustion
Gives the downstream service time to recover

subjective.question: Explain bulkheads and load shedding. How are they different, and when would you use each?
subjective.answer: A bulkhead isolates resources so that one failure stays contained. The name comes from the sealed compartments in a ship. In practice you give each dependency or tenant its own thread pool, connection pool or set of instances. If the recommendations service hangs, it can use up only its own pool, and payments keep working. Load shedding is about the service's own total capacity. When it is overloaded, it deliberately rejects some requests early and cheaply, for example with 503 or 429, so it can still serve the rest with good latency. Without shedding, queues grow, every request times out and throughput collapses. Good shedding is based on priority: drop background or low-value traffic first, and keep checkout and login. Signals for shedding include queue length, number of in-flight requests or latency. Use bulkheads to stop a failure spreading between parts; use load shedding to survive more traffic than you can handle.
keyPoints: Bulkhead: separate pools per dependency or tenant
Load shedding: reject early when overloaded
Shedding protects latency and stops throughput collapse
Shed low-priority traffic first
Signals: queue depth, in-flight requests, latency

subjective.question: Explain logs, metrics and traces. How would you use them together to debug a sudden latency spike?
subjective.answer: Metrics are numbers aggregated over time, such as request rate, error rate and latency histograms. They are cheap to store, good for dashboards and alerts, and tell you that something is wrong. Traces follow one request across services as a set of spans, so they show where the time went. Logs are detailed, timestamped records of events, and they tell you why it happened. For a latency spike, an SLO or p99 latency alert fires first, based on metrics. I break the metrics down by endpoint, region and version to find the scope, and check whether a deploy happened. Then I open sample traces of slow requests and see that, for example, a database span takes 800 ms. Finally I filter logs by the trace ID to find the exact error or slow query. The key is to put the same trace ID in logs, metrics exemplars and traces, using standards such as OpenTelemetry.
keyPoints: Metrics: aggregated, cheap, for alerting (that something is wrong)
Traces: one request across services (where the time went)
Logs: detailed events (why it happened)
Debug flow: metric alert, then split by dimension, then traces, then logs
Link all three with trace IDs; OpenTelemetry

subjective.question: Define SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget. Then set an SLO for a checkout API.
subjective.answer: An SLI is a measured indicator of service quality, usually good events divided by valid events, for example the share of requests that succeed. An SLO is the internal target for that SLI over a window. An SLA is a contract with customers, with penalties if it is missed, so it should be looser than the SLO. The error budget is 100% minus the SLO: the unreliability you are allowed. For checkout I would define two SLIs measured at the load balancer. Availability: non-5xx responses divided by valid requests. Latency: requests served under 500 ms divided by all requests. My SLOs: 99.9% availability and 99% of requests under 500 ms, over a rolling 30 days. A 99.9% target allows about 43.2 minutes of full downtime a month. If the budget is used up, we freeze risky releases and put the effort into reliability work. Leftover budget can be spent on faster releases.
keyPoints: SLI = good events / valid events
SLO is the internal target; SLA is the contract, looser than the SLO
Error budget = 100% − SLO; 99.9% ≈ 43.2 minutes per 30 days
Example: availability and latency SLIs for checkout
Budget policy: freeze releases when the budget is used up

subjective.question: Your service has a 99.9% SLO. What exactly would you alert on, and what would you not page for?
subjective.answer: I would page on SLO burn rate using multiwindow alerts, as suggested in the Google SRE Workbook. Burn rate is how fast the budget is being used compared with the allowed speed. Page if the burn rate is 14.4 or more over 1 hour, which uses 2% of the 30-day budget, confirmed by a 5-minute window. Also page if the burn rate is 6 or more over 6 hours, which uses 5%, confirmed by a 30-minute window. The short windows make the alert clear quickly once the problem is fixed. Slower burns, such as a burn rate of 1 over 3 days, open a ticket instead of waking someone. All of these are symptoms users feel: error rate and latency against the SLO. I would not page on causes such as high CPU, memory or a single pod restart. Those go on dashboards, guided by USE for resources and RED for services, and are used for debugging. Paging on causes creates noise and alert fatigue, and it still misses failures nobody predicted.
keyPoints: Burn rate = actual budget use / allowed use
Page at 14.4 over 1 hour (2%) and 6 over 6 hours (5%), with short confirmation windows
Open tickets for slow burns
Alert on symptoms (errors, latency), not causes (CPU)
Cause metrics go on dashboards; avoid alert fatigue

subjective.question: Why should latency be measured with percentiles rather than averages? How do the four golden signals, RED and USE fit in?
subjective.answer: Averages hide the tail. If 98% of requests take 50 ms and 2% take 5 seconds, the average is about 150 ms, which looks fine, yet 1 in 50 users waits 5 seconds. Pages that make many backend calls often hit that slow tail, so p95 and p99 match what users really feel. Percentiles should be calculated from histograms. You cannot average percentiles from different servers. The four golden signals from Google SRE are latency, traffic, errors and saturation, and they are the minimum for any user-facing system. RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) applies them to request-driven services: requests per second, failed requests, and latency distribution. USE (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) applies to resources such as CPU, disks, queues and connection pools. In practice, RED metrics feed the SLOs and alerts, while USE metrics help you find which resource is the bottleneck when RED shows a problem.
keyPoints: Averages hide tail latency; use p95 and p99
Calculate percentiles from histograms; never average percentiles
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
RED for services, USE for resources
RED drives alerts; USE helps find the cause

subjective.question: This GraphQL API is slow when clients ask for orders with their customers. Explain the problem, how you would fix it, and how you would protect the API from very expensive queries.
subjective.answer: This is the N+1 query problem. One query fetches 100 orders. Then the customer resolver runs once per order, so we make 100 more database calls, one for each customer. Latency and database load grow with the result size. The usual fix is a DataLoader. It collects all the customerIds requested in one tick of the event loop, sends one batched query such as WHERE id IN (...), and caches results for the rest of that request. A join done in the parent resolver also works. GraphQL lets the client shape the query, so one request can be very expensive. A simple request-per-second limit is not enough. I would limit query depth, compute a cost per query (for example, list fields multiplied by their page size) and rate limit on cost points per client. I would also require pagination arguments, and for public clients I would consider persisted queries, which allow only approved queries to run.
keyPoints: Identifies N+1: 1 parent query plus one query per child
DataLoader batching and per-request caching, or a join
Rate limit on query cost, not just on request count
Depth limits, mandatory pagination, persisted queries

subjective.question: Walk through what this Redis Lua script does. Why run it as a script, and what problems could still appear in production?

code.code:
local key = KEYS[1]
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local d = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1]) or capacity
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens = tokens - 1
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate) * 2)
return allowed

subjective.answer: It is a token bucket. It reads the stored token count and the last update time, adds tokens for the elapsed time at the configured rate, and caps the total at capacity. If at least one token is left, it takes one and allows the request. It then saves the new state and sets a TTL, so idle buckets expire. Redis runs a Lua script atomically, so the read, the refill and the write cannot interleave between many API servers. That removes the check-then-act race. Problems that remain: now comes from the app servers, so clock skew between them can grant extra tokens or take some away. Calling redis TIME inside the script avoids this. In Redis Cluster, each bucket uses one key, so it stays in one slot, but a very hot client can overload one shard. Every request also adds a network round trip, and you need a plan for when Redis is unavailable. Finally, return remaining tokens and a retry time so that you can set the rate-limit and Retry-After headers.
keyPoints: Recognises a token bucket with lazy refill
Lua gives atomicity across servers and removes race conditions
Clock skew from client-supplied time; use Redis TIME
TTL cleanup, hot keys and shard limits, Redis round-trip latency
Return Retry-After and remaining-quota headers

subjective.question: A company runs a live chat feature on 30 servers using WebSockets. Messages sometimes do not reach users connected to a different server, and after each deploy many users disconnect at once. How would you redesign this?
subjective.answer: WebSocket connections are stateful. A user is pinned to one server, so a message that arrives at server A cannot reach a user connected to server B unless the servers share state. I would add a pub/sub backbone such as Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka or NATS. Each server subscribes to the channels for its connected users, and any server can publish to them. A presence or connection registry maps each user to a gateway server. I would keep the WebSocket gateways thin and put the business logic in stateless services behind them. To handle deploys, I would drain connections gradually: stop sending new connections to a server, then close old ones in batches. Clients must reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter. Otherwise every client reconnects at once and causes a thundering herd. Clients should also resume from a last-seen message ID so that nothing is lost. I would set load balancer idle timeouts higher than the heartbeat interval and send ping/pong frames. Finally, I would monitor open connections per node and reconnect rates.
keyPoints: WebSocket connections are stateful; cross-server fan-out needs pub/sub
Connection registry, and thin gateway servers separate from logic
Graceful connection draining during deploys
Client reconnect with backoff, jitter and resume from last message ID
Heartbeats and load balancer idle timeouts

subjective.question: Your team has used up its error budget for the month, with 10 days left in the SLO window. Product managers still want to ship two features. What should an error budget policy say, and how would you handle this conversation?
subjective.answer: An error budget policy is a document agreed in advance by engineering, SRE and product. It says what happens when the budget is spent, so the decision is not argued again under pressure. A typical policy says: when the budget is exhausted, freeze non-critical feature releases until the service is back within its SLO. Security fixes and reliability work are still allowed. The postmortems behind the budget burn should produce action items, and those get priority. If a single incident used more than a set share of the budget, for example 20%, it needs a postmortem with tracked fixes. In the conversation, I would point to the agreed policy and show the data: which incidents or releases used the budget, and the burn rate now. I would offer options. For example, ship a feature behind a feature flag to a small canary group, or ship it after the reliability fixes land. If leadership overrides the freeze, that should be an explicit and documented decision. And if we keep missing an SLO that users do not complain about, the right move may be to revisit the SLO rather than fight over it.
keyPoints: The policy is agreed in advance by product and engineering
Freeze non-critical releases; allow security and reliability fixes
Postmortems and prioritised action items
Use data on burn sources; offer canary or feature-flag options
An override is explicit, or the SLO itself is revisited

subjective.question: This Resilience4j circuit breaker on a payments client keeps opening and closing many times a minute, even when the downstream service is mostly healthy. Explain what is wrong and how you would tune it.

code.code:
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payments:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 2
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 1
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 1s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 1

subjective.answer: The breaker judges health from far too little data. The sliding window holds only 2 calls, and minimumNumberOfCalls is 1. So a single failure gives a 50% or even 100% failure rate and trips the breaker. After only 1 second it moves to half-open and lets 1 trial call through. One lucky success closes it, and one unlucky failure opens it again. That is why it flaps. I would use a larger window, for example the last 50–100 calls, or a time-based window of 30–60 seconds. I would raise minimumNumberOfCalls to about 20 so that low traffic cannot trip it. I would increase waitDurationInOpenState to 15–30 seconds to give the dependency time to recover, and allow several half-open trial calls. I would also count slow calls with a slow-call threshold tied to the client timeout, and decide which exceptions count as failures: a 400 validation error should not open the breaker. Then I would expose the breaker state as a metric and alert on transitions.
keyPoints: The window and minimum call count are too small, so statistics are noisy
A short open duration and a single half-open probe cause flapping
Larger window, higher minimum calls, longer wait, more probe calls
Count only real dependency failures and slow calls
Monitor breaker state changes

subjective.question: A company produces 50,000 traces per second, and tracing costs are too high. Engineers say that when an incident happens, the traces they need are usually missing. Compare head-based and tail-based sampling and propose a strategy.
subjective.answer: Head-based sampling decides at the start of a request, for example to keep 1% of traces. The decision travels in the trace context, so all services keep or drop the same trace. It is cheap and simple. But it decides before it knows the outcome, so most rare errors and slow requests are thrown away. That explains the missing traces. Tail-based sampling buffers all spans of a trace in a collector, such as the OpenTelemetry Collector's tail sampling processor, until the trace completes. It then keeps traces by rule: all errors, everything above a latency threshold such as p99, and a small random share of normal traffic. It costs collector memory, and all spans of one trace must reach the same collector instance, so you need trace-ID-aware load balancing. I would combine the two: light head sampling to limit volume, tail rules that keep 100% of errors and slow traces, and a higher rate for critical routes such as checkout. I would also link metrics to example traces using exemplars, and put the trace ID in every log line.
keyPoints: Head sampling is cheap but blind to the outcome
Tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces after completion
Tail sampling needs collector buffering and trace-ID-aware routing
A hybrid policy with per-route rates
Exemplars and trace IDs in logs link the three signals

subjective.question: A team changed this Protobuf message used by a gRPC API that mobile apps call. Older app versions began showing wrong values. Explain why, and describe how to evolve gRPC and REST APIs without breaking clients.
subjective.answer: Protobuf identifies fields on the wire by their field number, not by their name. Version 2 reused number 2 for a string currency. Old clients still read field 2 as int64 amount_paise, so they misread the bytes or drop the field, and amounts break silently. The safe way to change it is to never reuse or retype a field number. Mark removed fields as reserved, by number and by name, so that nobody reuses them. Add new fields with new numbers. Treat new fields as optional: old clients ignore unknown fields, and new code must handle a missing value. For a breaking change, create a new package or service version, such as orders.v2, and run both until old clients are gone. Mobile apps stay installed for a long time, so that can take months. In REST, apply the same rules. Add fields and never rename or remove them, version breaking changes with a path such as /v2 or a header, announce deprecations with a timeline, and run contract tests in CI. For Protobuf, a tool such as buf breaking can catch these changes before deploy.
keyPoints: Protobuf uses field numbers on the wire; reusing a number corrupts data
Use reserved for removed fields; add new fields with new numbers
Only additive changes; clients must ignore unknown fields
Use versioned packages or URLs for breaking changes; run both versions
Breaking-change checks and contract tests in CI

steps.overview: This step applies everything so far to twelve classic system design problems, end to end. It covers URL shortener, pastebin, rate limiter, news feed, chat, notifications, video streaming, ride hailing, autocomplete, distributed cache, key-value store and web crawler. Interviews test these designs directly. The cloud architect exams (SAA-C03, Google PCA, AZ-305) test the same building blocks as scenario questions: caching, queues, sharding, CDNs and consistency choices.
objectives: Run a timed 45-minute design using a fixed structure: requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, deep dive and trade-offs.
Estimate QPS, storage and bandwidth from user numbers using back-of-envelope maths.
Choose and justify the core technique for each classic design, for example base62 IDs, token bucket, fan-out, WebSockets, geohash, trie or consistent hashing.
Map each design component to managed cloud services such as DynamoDB, ElastiCache, SQS, S3 and CloudFront.
State at least three explicit trade-offs per design, including consistency vs availability, latency vs cost, and write vs read amplification.

concepts.explanation: Short keys are usually base62 encodings (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) of a unique number. The number can come from a counter, a ticket server, or a Snowflake-style ID made of timestamp, machine ID and sequence. Hashing the long URL (MD5/SHA) and truncating it needs collision checks. Pastebin follows the same pattern, but stores the content in object storage (S3) and only metadata in the database.

Token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size and refills at a fixed rate. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate. Fixed window counters are simple but allow double bursts at window edges. Sliding window log and sliding window counter fix this, at a memory or accuracy cost. In distributed setups, counters usually live in Redis with atomic INCR/EXPIRE or Lua scripts. Rejected requests get HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

concepts.term: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read (news feed)
concepts.explanation: Fan-out on write (push) copies a new post ID into every follower's precomputed feed cache. Reads are fast, but writes are heavy for users with millions of followers. Fan-out on read (pull) builds the feed at request time, so writes are cheap and reads are slow. The standard answer is a hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities, merged at read time.

Chat clients keep a persistent WebSocket connection to stateful chat servers. A presence/session service maps each user to the server holding their connection. Messages are stored in a wide-column or key-value store such as Cassandra or DynamoDB, partitioned by conversation ID and sorted by a time-ordered message ID. Offline users receive push notifications. Delivery and read receipts are extra acknowledgement messages.

Producers publish events to a queue (Kafka, SQS). Workers per channel (push via APNs/FCM, SMS, email) consume and send them. Workers check user preferences and rate limits, deduplicate with an idempotency key, and retry with exponential backoff. Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue. Delivery is at-least-once, so deduplication matters.

An upload goes to object storage. A transcoding job, defined as a DAG of tasks, converts it into multiple resolutions and bitrates and splits it into small segments. Players use adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS or MPEG-DASH) to switch quality as bandwidth changes. Popular content is served from a CDN such as CloudFront. Metadata lives in a database, and view counts are aggregated asynchronously.

Drivers send location updates every few seconds. These go to an in-memory geo index, not the main database. Geohash turns latitude/longitude into prefix-comparable strings, so nearby searches scan the target cell plus its neighbours. Quadtrees and Uber's H3 hexagonal grid are alternatives. Redis offers GEOADD/GEOSEARCH. Trip matching needs strong consistency so that one driver is never assigned two riders.

A trie stores prefixes. Each node caches the top-k completions so lookups are fast. The trie is rebuilt offline from query logs (batch or periodic), not updated on every keystroke. It is then sharded by prefix and cached close to users. Clients debounce keystrokes, and the browser and CDN cache responses for popular prefixes.

concepts.term: Consistent hashing and quorum (cache, key-value store)
concepts.explanation: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes spread load evenly. A Dynamo-style key-value store replicates each key to N nodes. It uses read/write quorums R and W, sloppy quorum with hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, and gossip for membership. A distributed cache adds eviction policies (LRU/LFU), TTLs and protection against hot keys and stampedes.

A URL frontier holds URLs to crawl. It uses priority queues and per-host politeness queues, so no single site is overloaded and robots.txt is respected. Fetchers download pages and parsers extract links. Bloom filters or hash sets drop already-seen URLs, and content fingerprints (for example SimHash) detect duplicate pages. Raw pages go to object storage, and DNS results are cached because DNS lookups are a bottleneck.

keyFacts: 1 day ≈ 86,400 seconds, about 10^5. So 1 million requests/day is about 12 QPS. Plan peak at roughly 2–3x average.
Base62 with 7 characters gives 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion keys. That is enough for 100M new URLs/day for decades.
Use 301 (permanent redirect) to cut server load, because browsers cache it. Use 302 (temporary) when you need click analytics on every hit.
Consistent hashing remaps only about K/N keys when a node changes, where K is keys and N is nodes. Virtual nodes fix uneven load.
Quorum rule: R + W > N gives read-your-latest-write overlap. A common setting is N=3, W=2, R=2.
Rate limiter rejections return HTTP 429. Often add headers for limit, remaining requests and retry-after.
Amazon DynamoDB has a 400 KB maximum item size. Large blobs (pastes, videos, thumbnails) go to Amazon S3 with a pointer stored in the database.
Amazon S3 supports objects up to 5 TB. Use multipart upload for large files such as video uploads.
Read-heavy designs (URL shortener, feed, autocomplete) need a cache plus CDN. Write-heavy designs (chat, location updates, crawler) need partitioning plus queues or log-structured stores.
CAP choice per design: chat history, feeds and caches favour availability (AP). Payments, trip assignment and unique ID allocation need consistency (CP).

example.caption: Worked estimate and skeleton for a URL shortener (the 'estimates, API, data model' part of the checkpoint)
example.code:
REQUIREMENTS
  Functional: shorten URL, redirect, optional custom alias, expiry
  Non-functional: 100M new URLs/day, read:write = 100:1, p99 redirect < 50 ms, highly available

ESTIMATES
  Writes: 100M / 86,400 s  ≈ 1,160 /s   (peak ~3,000 /s)
  Reads : 1,160 x 100      ≈ 116,000 /s (peak ~300,000 /s)
  Storage: 100M x 365 x 5 yr = 182.5B rows x 500 B ≈ 91 TB
  Key space: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion  -> 7-char base62 key is enough
  Cache: 20% of daily reads hot -> 0.2 x 10B reads x 500 B ≈ 1 TB in Redis cluster

API
  POST /v1/urls      {longUrl, alias?, expiresAt?}  -> 201 {shortUrl}
  GET  /{key}        -> 302 Location: longUrl  (301 if no analytics)

DATA MODEL (DynamoDB / Cassandra, partition key = key)
  urls(key PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at)

DIAGRAM
  Client -> CDN -> Load balancer -> App servers -> Redis cache -> KV store
                                   \-> ID service (ranges of counters) -> base62

TRADE-OFFS
  1. Counter+base62 (no collisions, guessable) vs hash (unguessable, needs collision check)
  2. 301 (less load) vs 302 (full analytics)
  3. NoSQL KV (easy horizontal scale) vs SQL (unique constraints, harder sharding)

pitfalls: Drawing boxes before clarifying requirements and scale. Interviewers mark you down if you never ask about read/write ratio, users or latency targets.
Stopping at the happy path. Each design needs failure handling: retries, dead-letter queues, replication, and what happens when the cache or a shard dies.
Fan-out on write for every user in a news feed. Celebrity accounts with millions of followers break it, so state the hybrid approach.
Storing large blobs (videos, paste bodies, crawled pages) in the database instead of object storage with a CDN in front.
Using a single-node, in-memory counter for distributed rate limiting or ID generation. It is a single point of failure and gives wrong counts across servers.
Listing trade-offs without a decision. Say what you chose and why, for example 'AP for feeds because stale by a few seconds is acceptable'.

workflow.title: 45-minute whiteboard routine (use for each of the ten daily designs)

steps.label: Clarify requirements (5 min)
steps.detail: List functional features, non-functional targets (scale, latency, availability, consistency) and what is explicitly out of scope.

steps.label: Back-of-envelope estimates (5 min)
steps.detail: Compute average and peak QPS, storage over 5 years, bandwidth and cache size, rounding aggressively.

steps.label: Define the API (5 min)
steps.detail: Write 2–4 endpoints with methods, key parameters, response codes, and pagination or idempotency keys where needed.

steps.label: Design the data model (5 min)
steps.detail: Pick the store type, then define tables, partition keys and sort keys based on the main access patterns.

steps.label: Draw high-level diagram (10 min)
steps.detail: Show the client, CDN, load balancer, stateless services, cache, queue, databases and object storage, then trace one read and one write.

steps.label: Deep dive bottlenecks (10 min)
steps.detail: Zoom into the hardest part (for example hot keys, celebrity fan-out, geo index or transcoding) and cover scaling, sharding and failure handling.

steps.label: State three trade-offs (5 min)
steps.detail: Name each alternative you rejected, the cost of your choice, and the condition under which you would change it.

project.title: classic-designs-lab
project.summary: A runnable URL shortener with a counter-based base62 ID generator, a Redis token-bucket rate limiter, and a standalone consistent-hashing ring with an N/W/R quorum demo. The README is the 45-minute whiteboard template and the ten-day schedule. main.py shows ID generation and the API, ratelimit.py shows rate limiting, hashring.py shows the key-value store and cache partitioning, and the Docker files wire everything together.
project.run:
docker compose up --build -d
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/urls -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://example.com/docs","ttl_days":30}'
curl -si localhost:8000/<code-from-previous-response>
for i in $(seq 1 15); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST localhost:8000/api/v1/urls -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://example.com"}'; done
docker compose exec app python -m app.hashring
docker compose down

files.code:
# classic-designs-lab (Step 8: Classic designs, end to end)

Run it with the commands in the lesson. Then open each file in this order:
1. app/main.py: the URL shortener API and base62 ID generation
2. app/ratelimit.py: the token bucket rate limiter (an atomic Lua script in Redis)
3. app/hashring.py: consistent hashing, replicas and quorum (cache / KV store)

## Whiteboard template (45 min). The checkpoint needs all six parts.
| Min   | Part         | URL shortener answer (worked example) |
|-------|--------------|----------------------------------------|
| 0-5   | Requirements | Shorten, redirect, optional expiry. Non-functional: low-latency reads, highly available |
| 5-10  | Estimates    | 100M new URLs/month = ~40 writes/s. At 10:1 that is ~400 reads/s. 5 yr = 6B rows x 500 B = ~3 TB |
| 10-15 | API          | POST /api/v1/urls {url, ttl_days} -> 201 {code, short_url}; GET /{code} -> 302 |
| 15-20 | Data model   | url:{code} -> long URL (with TTL); clicks:{code} -> counter; url:counter -> next ID |
| 20-35 | Diagram      | See below. Then deep-dive into ID generation and the rate limiter |
| 35-45 | Trade-offs   | Name three, with the reason for each choice |

```
client -> LB -> app (stateless, N copies) -> Redis cache -> KV store (sharded by hashring)
                  |-- token bucket per client IP (Redis)
                  |-- ID: Redis INCR (or ID ranges per app node) -> base62
```

## Three trade-offs for this design
1. Counter + base62 vs hash of the URL. The counter never collides and gives short codes, but the codes are guessable. A hash needs collision checks. At scale, hand each app node a block of IDs so INCR is not a hot key.
2. 302 vs 301. A 302 sends every click to us, so analytics stay accurate. A 301 is cached by the browser, so there is less load but clicks are lost.
3. Token bucket vs sliding window. The token bucket allows short bursts and stores only 2 fields per client. A sliding-window log is exact but stores one entry per request.

## Ten-day plan: one design a day, timed at 45 minutes
| Day | Design | Key deep-dive |
|-----|--------|---------------|
| 1 | URL shortener + pastebin | ID generation, object storage for paste bodies |
| 2 | Rate limiter | Token bucket vs fixed and sliding window, Redis atomicity |
| 3 | News feed | Fan-out on write vs on read (celebrity problem) |
| 4 | Chat (WhatsApp) | WebSockets, message ordering, offline delivery |
| 5 | Notification system | Queues, retries, idempotency, user preferences |
| 6 | Video streaming (YouTube) | Transcoding pipeline, adaptive bitrate (HLS/DASH), CDN |
| 7 | Ride hailing (Uber) | Geohash / quadtree, location update rate |
| 8 | Search autocomplete | Trie with top-k per node, offline rebuild |
| 9 | Distributed cache + KV store | Consistent hashing, N/W/R quorum (run hashring.py) |
| 10 | Web crawler | URL frontier, politeness, dedup with Bloom filter |

# Two containers: a stateless app and Redis (counter, cache and rate-limit state)
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0   # read in app/main.py
      BASE_URL: http://localhost:8000   # prefix for short_url in responses
      RATE_CAPACITY: "10"              # bucket size = allowed burst
      RATE_REFILL: "1"                 # tokens added per second = steady rate
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy     # start only after Redis answers PING

# Small image for the FastAPI service
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /srv

# Install dependencies first so Docker caches this layer
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# The app package holds main.py, ratelimit.py and hashring.py
COPY app ./app

EXPOSE 8000

# The app is stateless, so you can scale it with more replicas behind a load balancer
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# Web framework and ASGI server
fastapi>=0.115,<1.0
uvicorn[standard]>=0.30
# The redis package includes redis.asyncio and Lua script support
redis>=5.0
# Validates HttpUrl in the request body
pydantic>=2.7
# Pinned with ranges so a fresh build picks up current patch releases
# Add load-testing tools (e.g. locust) here if you extend the lab
# Keep runtime deps minimal: fewer deps means a smaller attack surface
# hashring.py uses only the standard library (hashlib, bisect)
# ratelimit.py uses the Redis Lua script API from the redis package

"""URL shortener: counter-based IDs, base62 codes, 302 redirects, rate-limited writes."""
import os

import redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, HttpUrl

from app.ratelimit import TokenBucket

REDIS_URL = os.getenv("REDIS_URL", "redis://localhost:6379/0")
BASE_URL = os.getenv("BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8000")
ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
ID_OFFSET = 62**5  # first code is 6 chars; 7 chars cover 62^7 = ~3.5 trillion IDs

r = redis.from_url(REDIS_URL, decode_responses=True)
bucket = TokenBucket(
    r,
    capacity=int(os.getenv("RATE_CAPACITY", "10")),
    refill_per_sec=float(os.getenv("RATE_REFILL", "1")),
)
app = FastAPI(title="url-shortener")


class ShortenIn(BaseModel):
    url: HttpUrl
    ttl_days: int | None = None  # optional expiry (a requirement from the whiteboard)


def encode62(n: int) -> str:
    """Turn a unique integer into a short base62 string."""
    out = []
    while n:
        n, rem = divmod(n, 62)
        out.append(ALPHABET[rem])
    return "".join(reversed(out)) or "0"


@app.post("/api/v1/urls", status_code=201)
async def shorten(body: ShortenIn, request: Request):
    allowed, retry_after = await bucket.allow(f"rl:{request.client.host}")
    if not allowed:  # 429 + Retry-After is the standard rate-limit response
        raise HTTPException(429, "rate limit exceeded", headers={"Retry-After": str(retry_after)})
    n = await r.incr("url:counter")  # atomic, so no collisions; at scale hand out ID ranges
    code = encode62(n + ID_OFFSET)
    ttl = body.ttl_days * 86400 if body.ttl_days else None
    await r.set(f"url:{code}", str(body.url), ex=ttl)  # Redis expires the key itself
    return {"code": code, "short_url": f"{BASE_URL}/{code}"}


@app.get("/health")
async def health():
    return {"redis": await r.ping()}


@app.get("/{code}")
async def redirect(code: str):
    url = await r.get(f"url:{code}")  # read path: about 10x more traffic than writes
    if url is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, "unknown or expired code")
    await r.incr(f"clicks:{code}")  # analytics; in production, push this to a queue
    return RedirectResponse(url, status_code=302)  # 302 keeps clicks visible to us

"""Token bucket rate limiter, run atomically inside Redis with a Lua script.

Why Lua: read-modify-write in one step, so two app replicas cannot race.
Why Redis TIME: every replica uses one clock, so there is no client clock skew.
"""
import redis.asyncio as redis

TOKEN_BUCKET_LUA = """
local key      = KEYS[1]
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local t        = redis.call('TIME')
local now      = tonumber(t[1]) + tonumber(t[2]) / 1000000

local data   = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1]) or capacity   -- a new client starts full
local ts     = tonumber(data[2]) or now

-- refill for the time that has passed, capped at capacity
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)

local allowed, retry = 0, 0
if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens = tokens - 1
  allowed = 1
else
  retry = math.ceil((1 - tokens) / rate)        -- seconds until the next token
end

redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', tostring(now))
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate) * 2)  -- idle clients are cleaned up
return {allowed, retry}
"""


class TokenBucket:
    """capacity = burst size, refill_per_sec = sustained requests per second."""

    def __init__(self, r: redis.Redis, capacity: int, refill_per_sec: float):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.rate = refill_per_sec
        self.script = r.register_script(TOKEN_BUCKET_LUA)  # EVALSHA, cached on the server

    async def allow(self, key: str) -> tuple[bool, int]:
        allowed, retry = await self.script(keys=[key], args=[self.capacity, self.rate])
        return bool(int(allowed)), int(retry)

objective.question: A new API is expected to handle 50 million requests per day. You plan peak capacity at about 3x the average. Roughly what peak QPS should you design for?
options: About 1,500–1,800 QPS
About 50,000 QPS
About 15,000 QPS
About 150 QPS
objective.explanation: 50 million divided by about 10^5 seconds per day gives roughly 500–580 QPS on average, so 3x is about 1,500–1,800 QPS. 150 QPS is too low, and 15,000 or 50,000 QPS are off by an order of magnitude or more.

objective.question: A URL shortener must create 100 million new short codes per day and must not run out of codes for several decades. Using Base62 encoding, what is the shortest code length that meets this goal?
options: 6 characters
10 characters
7 characters
5 characters
objective.explanation: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion keys, which lasts about 35,000 days (roughly 95 years) at 100M/day. 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, which lasts only about 1.5 years, and 5 characters is far smaller. 10 characters works but is longer than needed.

objective.question: The marketing team of a URL shortener needs every click counted, including repeat clicks from the same browser. Which redirect response should the service return?
options: 302 Found (temporary redirect)
308 Permanent Redirect
404 Not Found with a link in the body
301 Moved Permanently
objective.explanation: A 302 is not cached by browsers by default, so every click reaches your servers and can be logged. 301 and 308 are permanent redirects that browsers cache, so repeat clicks skip your servers. A 404 breaks the redirect.

objective.question: A public API must enforce an average limit of 100 requests per minute per user. It should still allow short bursts, and the limiter must use little memory per user. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Sliding window log
Leaking bucket with a fixed outflow rate
Token bucket
Fixed window counter
objective.explanation: A token bucket stores only a token count and a timestamp per user. It allows bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing the refill rate on average. A fixed window allows up to 2x traffic at window edges. A sliding window log stores every timestamp, which uses a lot of memory. A leaking bucket smooths traffic and does not allow bursts.

objective.question: A search box must show the top 5 suggestions within about 100 ms as the user types each character. Query volume is very high. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Use a trie where each node stores the precomputed top-k completions, rebuild it offline from query logs, and serve it from memory or cache
Run a full-text search across all documents on every keystroke and rank the results live
Store each full query in a key-value store keyed by a hash of the complete query
Run SQL LIKE 'prefix%' on the raw query log table on every keystroke
objective.explanation: Storing top-k at each trie node makes a lookup a simple walk down the prefix with no ranking at request time. Rebuilding offline keeps the read path fast and cacheable. A LIKE scan on the log and live full-text ranking are too slow at scale, and hashing complete queries cannot answer prefix lookups.

objective.question: In a social news feed, most users have a few hundred followers, but some celebrities have 50 million. Posts must appear quickly, and home-feed reads must stay fast. Which approach is the standard choice?
options: Pure fan-out on read for every user
Send every post to every user's mailbox using a single global queue
A hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, and merge celebrity posts in at read time
Pure fan-out on write for every user, including celebrities
objective.explanation: Fan-out on write gives fast reads, but writing one celebrity post into 50 million feeds is very costly. A hybrid pre-computes feeds for normal authors and pulls celebrity posts in at read time. Pure fan-out on read makes every feed load slow, and a single global queue does not scale.

objective.question: You are designing a WhatsApp-style chat. Messages must reach online users in near real time, and offline users must get them later. What is the best delivery design?
options: Messages are sent by email (SMTP) and the app reads the inbox
Messages are kept only in chat server memory and dropped if the recipient is offline
Clients keep persistent WebSocket connections to chat servers; messages are stored durably, and offline users get them on reconnect plus a push notification
Clients poll a REST endpoint every second for new messages
objective.explanation: WebSockets give low-latency, two-way delivery over one long-lived connection. Durable storage with sync on reconnect and push notifications covers offline users. Short polling wastes resources and adds latency, SMTP is not suitable, and memory-only storage loses messages.

objective.question: A pastebin service stores paste metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Some users paste content up to 5 MB. How should you store the paste content?
options: Store the content in Amazon S3, and keep the S3 object key plus metadata in DynamoDB
Compress the paste and store it as a DynamoDB attribute in every case
Split each paste across many DynamoDB items in the same table
Store the content in the DynamoDB item, because DynamoDB has no item size limit
objective.explanation: DynamoDB items have a 400 KB maximum size, so large blobs belong in S3 with a pointer in the database. Splitting a paste across items adds complexity for no benefit. Compression does not guarantee that a 5 MB paste fits under 400 KB.

objective.question: Creators upload videos of up to 20 GB to a YouTube-like platform. Viewers on slow and fast networks must get smooth playback. Which pipeline is correct?
options: Store videos in DynamoDB items, and serve them directly from the database
Upload to S3, then serve only the original file through the CDN
Use S3 multipart upload; an upload event puts a job on a queue; workers transcode into several resolutions and bitrates, segmented for adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH); deliver through a CDN
Upload with a single PUT request to the web server, store the file on the server disk, and stream the original file
objective.explanation: Multipart upload handles large files reliably and allows retries per part. Queue-driven transcoding into multiple renditions enables adaptive bitrate streaming, and a CDN serves video close to viewers. A single PUT to a web server does not scale, DynamoDB cannot hold video, and serving only the original file fails on slow networks.

objective.question: A ride-hailing app indexes driver locations by geohash. A rider requests a car, and the system searches only the rider's own geohash cell. Drivers just across the cell boundary are never matched. What is the correct fix?
options: Search the rider's cell and its 8 neighbouring cells, then filter results by actual distance
Store all drivers in one list and compute the distance to every driver
Index drivers by latitude only, using a B-tree
Use a longer geohash so that cells are smaller
objective.explanation: Points that are close together can sit in different cells with different geohash prefixes, so you must also query the 8 neighbours and then filter by true distance. Longer geohashes make the edge problem worse. A latitude-only index and a full scan are both inefficient.

objective.question: A distributed cache has 10 nodes. You add an 11th node. Which statement about consistent hashing is correct?
options: Only about 1/11 of the keys move, and virtual nodes help spread the load evenly
Exactly half of the keys move to the new node
No keys move until the cluster restarts
Almost all keys move, just as with hash(key) mod N
objective.explanation: Consistent hashing remaps only about K/N keys when a node joins or leaves. Virtual nodes give each physical node many positions on the ring, which fixes uneven load. Modulo hashing is the approach that remaps most keys.

objective.question: A key-value store keeps N=3 replicas of each key. The team wants reads to overlap with the latest acknowledged write. Both reads and writes must still succeed if one replica is down. Which setting should they use?
objective.explanation: W=2, R=2 gives R+W=4 > 3, so read and write sets always overlap. Each operation still needs only 2 of 3 nodes, so one node can fail. W=3 blocks writes when any node is down, and W=1 with R=1 or R=2 gives R+W ≤ 3, so there is no guaranteed overlap.

objective.question: A URL shortener uses a Snowflake-style 64-bit ID generator with the bit layout shown. Ignoring clock limits, what is the maximum number of unique IDs one worker can generate per second?

code.code:
| 1 bit sign | 41 bits ms timestamp | 10 bits worker ID | 12 bits sequence |

id = (timestamp_ms - EPOCH) << 22 | (worker_id << 12) | sequence

objective.explanation: The 12-bit sequence gives 4,096 IDs per millisecond, and there are 1,000 ms in a second, so the limit is 4,096,000 per second per worker. 1,024 is the number of workers that 10 bits allow, not a per-second limit.

objective.question: A team implements a 100 requests-per-minute limit with the Redis logic below. Users report that some clients get far more than 100 requests through in a short time. What is the cause?
options: The EXPIRE call deletes the key too early, so the counter always starts at zero
Redis keys with a TTL are evicted first under memory pressure, so the counter is lost on every request
Fixed windows reset at the minute boundary, so a client can send 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00
INCR is not atomic, so concurrent requests from the same user lose updates
objective.explanation: This is a fixed window counter, and it allows up to twice the limit across a window boundary. INCR is atomic in Redis, and the TTL logic is correct. A sliding window counter or a token bucket removes the boundary burst.

objective.question: A web crawler uses a Bloom filter to track URLs it has already seen across billions of URLs. Which statement about this design is correct?
options: The filter gives exact answers, but it needs memory proportional to the total URL length
The filter supports deleting URLs, so recrawl scheduling can remove entries when pages change
The filter may wrongly say a seen URL is new, so some pages are crawled twice, but it never skips a page
The filter may wrongly say a new URL was seen, so a few pages are skipped, but it never says a seen URL is new
objective.explanation: Bloom filters have false positives but no false negatives. For a crawler, this means a small fraction of new URLs is wrongly skipped and no URL is fetched twice. A standard Bloom filter cannot delete entries, and its memory depends on the target error rate, not on URL length.

objective.question: A notification service reads jobs from Amazon SQS standard queues and calls a push provider. During a provider slowdown, workers time out and retry, and many users receive the same push notification two or three times. Which change fixes this most reliably?
options: Increase the SQS visibility timeout to 12 hours
Send each notification from two workers in parallel and keep the first response
Attach an idempotency key to each notification and have workers record sent keys in a fast store such as DynamoDB or Redis, skipping keys already sent
Switch to an SQS FIFO queue and remove all retries
objective.explanation: SQS standard queues deliver at least once, and retries after timeouts also cause duplicates, so the consumer must be idempotent. A dedup check on an idempotency key handles both cases. Removing retries loses notifications. A very long visibility timeout delays recovery and still does not stop duplicates from provider-side timeouts.

objective.question: A distributed cache uses consistent hashing with 4 physical nodes, each placed once on the ring. Monitoring shows one node holds about 45% of the keys while another holds about 10%. What is the standard fix?
options: Give each physical node many virtual nodes on the ring
Replicate every key to all 4 nodes
Increase the hash output from 32 bits to 128 bits
Switch to modulo hashing (hash(key) % 4) so keys spread evenly
objective.explanation: With only a few points on the ring, the gaps between nodes are uneven, so the load is uneven. Virtual nodes place each server at many points on the ring, which evens out the load and spreads keys more evenly when a node leaves. Modulo hashing remaps most keys on every resize. A larger hash range does not change how unevenly the few nodes are placed.

objective.question: A product page caches a very popular item in Amazon ElastiCache with a 5-minute TTL. Every time the key expires, database CPU spikes to 100% for a few seconds. Which approach best addresses this?
options: Use request coalescing: let one request take a short lock and rebuild the value while others serve the stale copy or wait, and add jitter to TTLs
Add more read replicas until the spike disappears
Lower the TTL to 30 seconds so each rebuild is smaller
Remove the TTL so the item is never refreshed
objective.explanation: This is a cache stampede: many requests miss at the same moment and all hit the database. A single rebuilder (lock, or a single-flight pattern) plus serving stale data and TTL jitter stops the stampede. A shorter TTL makes stampedes happen more often, and replicas only add cost without fixing the cause.

objective.question: A chat app stores messages in Amazon DynamoDB. The most common query is to load the latest 50 messages of a conversation in order, then page backward. Which key design fits best?
options: Partition key: sender_user_id; sort key: timestamp; Query both users and merge on the client
Partition key: date; sort key: conversation_id#timestamp
Partition key: conversation_id; sort key: a time-sortable message_id; Query with ScanIndexForward=false and Limit=50
Partition key: message_id; GSI on conversation_id; Scan with a filter
objective.explanation: Grouping messages by conversation_id and sorting by a time-ordered ID lets one Query return the newest 50 messages. LastEvaluatedKey then gives cheap backward paging. Scans are expensive and slow. Keying by date puts all of a day's traffic on one partition, which creates a hot partition.

subjective.question: Compare three ways to generate short codes for a URL shortener: hashing the long URL, a global counter encoded in Base62, and a distributed ID generator. Which would you choose and why?
subjective.answer: Hashing the long URL (for example MD5, then taking the first 7 characters) needs no coordination, but collisions happen. You must check the database and retry, and the same URL always maps to the same code, which may or may not be what you want. A global counter encoded in Base62 never collides and gives short codes. However, one counter is a single point of failure, and sequential codes are guessable. A distributed generator removes the bottleneck. You can give each server a pre-allocated range of IDs from a ticket service, or use a Snowflake-style ID made of timestamp, machine ID and sequence. Each server then allocates locally, and the ID is still unique. I would choose range allocation plus Base62. ID allocation must be consistent (CP), but a server only contacts the coordinator when its range runs out. If guessability matters, I would shuffle the bits or add a random suffix.
keyPoints: Hashing gives collisions, so you need check-and-retry logic
A counter in Base62 avoids collisions but is a single point of failure and is guessable
Range allocation or Snowflake-style IDs remove the bottleneck
Unique ID allocation needs consistency (CP)

subjective.question: Do a back-of-envelope estimate for a URL shortener with 100 million new URLs per day, a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, 5 years of retention, and about 500 bytes per record.
subjective.answer: Writes: 100M per day divided by about 10^5 seconds is about 1,000 to 1,200 QPS on average. At 2–3x for peak, that is about 3,000 QPS. Reads are 10x writes, so about 12,000 QPS on average and 30,000 or more at peak. Storage: 100M per day times 365 times 5 is about 180 billion records. At 500 bytes each, that is about 90 TB before replication, or about 270 TB with 3 replicas. Key space: 7 Base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes, which is plenty. These numbers drive the design. The system is read-heavy, so I put a cache such as Redis in front of the database and use a CDN or edge caching for popular links. A few hot URLs take most of the traffic, so caching the top 20% of daily reads covers most requests. 90 TB needs a partitioned key-value store, sharded by short code.
keyPoints: About 1,200 write QPS on average, about 3,000 at peak
About 12,000 read QPS on average because of the 10:1 ratio
About 90 TB raw over 5 years, multiplied by the replication factor
Read-heavy, so add a cache and CDN, and shard by short code

subjective.question: Design a distributed rate limiter for an API served by 50 stateless servers. Cover the algorithm, storage, failure handling and client response.
subjective.answer: I would use a token bucket per user or API key. It allows bursts and keeps only a token count and a timestamp. The state must be shared, because a user's requests hit any of the 50 servers. I keep it in a central in-memory store such as Redis.
