The check-and-decrement must be atomic, using a Lua script or atomic increment with expiry, to avoid race conditions. The limiter can run in the API gateway or as middleware. Rules (limits per endpoint and tier) live in config and are cached locally. When a request is over the limit, I return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with headers for the limit, the remaining requests and Retry-After. If Redis is unavailable, I choose between fail-open (allow traffic, which protects availability) and fail-closed (block traffic, which protects the backend). Most public APIs fail open. For very high scale, servers can keep local counters and sync them in batches, accepting small inaccuracy.
keyPoints: Token bucket per key; shared state in a central store such as Redis
Atomic operations (Lua or INCR with expiry) to avoid races
HTTP 429 with limit, remaining and Retry-After headers
Decide on fail-open vs fail-closed; local counters trade accuracy for latency

subjective.question: Explain fan-out on write vs fan-out on read for a news feed, and when you would use each.
subjective.answer: Fan-out on write (push) copies a new post ID into every follower's pre-computed feed, usually a list in a cache. Reads are then very fast, because the feed is ready. The cost is heavy write amplification: one post by a user with 50 million followers means 50 million writes. It also wastes work for inactive users. Fan-out on read (pull) stores posts only on the author's timeline. When a user opens the feed, the system fetches recent posts from everyone they follow and merges them. Writes are cheap, but reads are slow and expensive, and feeds are read far more often than posts are written. Most real systems use a hybrid. Normal users' posts are pushed, while celebrity posts are pulled and merged at read time. Inactive users may be skipped during push. The feed favours availability (AP). A post appearing a few seconds late is acceptable, so asynchronous queues handle the fan-out.
keyPoints: Push gives fast reads but high write amplification
Pull gives cheap writes but slow, costly reads
Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities
Feeds are AP, and async queues do the fan-out

subjective.question: Design the message flow for a WhatsApp-style one-to-one chat. Cover connections, storage, ordering and delivery receipts.
subjective.answer: Each client keeps a persistent WebSocket to a chat server. A presence and session service records which server each user is connected to. When A sends a message, A's server assigns a message ID that is ordered within the conversation, for example a per-chat sequence number or a time-based ID. It writes the message durably to a write-optimised store, partitioned by conversation ID, such as a wide-column or log-structured store. It then sends an acknowledgement back to A, which is the 'sent' tick. Next it looks up B's server and forwards the message through a queue or pub/sub. If B is online, B's client acknowledges, which gives the 'delivered' tick. If B is offline, the message waits in storage and a push notification goes out. B syncs from its last seen sequence number on reconnect. Clients deduplicate by message ID, because retries happen. Chat is write-heavy, so we partition and use queues. Chat history favours availability (AP), and ordering only needs to hold within a conversation, not globally.
keyPoints: Persistent WebSockets plus a session/presence service
Persist before acknowledging; partition by conversation ID
Per-conversation ordering with sequence IDs; clients dedupe on retry
Offline users: push notification plus sync from last sequence number

subjective.question: Design a notification system that sends push, SMS and email notifications for many internal services.
subjective.answer: Internal services call one notification API with a user ID, template, channel preferences and priority. The API validates the request, checks the user's preferences and opt-outs, applies rate limits so users are not spammed, and fills the template. It then publishes to a separate queue for each channel: push, SMS and email. Separate queues mean a slow SMS provider does not block push. Worker pools consume each queue and call third-party providers, such as the Apple and Google push services, an SMS gateway and an email service. Failures are retried with exponential backoff, and messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue. Each notification has an idempotency key so retries do not send duplicates. Delivery is at-least-once, so deduplication matters. A notification log stores status for tracking and analytics. Device tokens and contact details live in a user store. Trade-offs include at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery, and high-priority queues for OTPs vs batching for marketing messages.
keyPoints: Single API that checks preferences, opt-outs and rate limits
A separate queue and worker pool per channel
Retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue and idempotency keys
Priority separation: OTPs vs bulk marketing

subjective.question: Walk through the video upload and playback pipeline of a YouTube-like service on AWS.
subjective.answer: The client asks the API for upload permission and gets pre-signed URLs. It then uploads directly to Amazon S3 using multipart upload, which suits large files: parts upload in parallel and failed parts can be retried. S3 objects can be up to 5 TB. When the upload completes, an event places a job on a queue. Transcoding workers split the video and encode several resolutions and bitrates, for example 240p to 4K. They package the output into short segments with manifests for HLS or DASH, and generate thumbnails. Outputs are stored in S3. Video metadata such as title, owner, status and S3 keys goes into a database. The player downloads the manifest and fetches segments through a CDN such as Amazon CloudFront. Adaptive bitrate switching picks a quality that matches the viewer's bandwidth. Trade-offs include pre-transcoding all renditions vs transcoding unpopular videos on demand, how much to cache at the edge vs storage cost, and moving rarely watched videos to cheaper storage classes.
keyPoints: Pre-signed URLs and S3 multipart upload; the API servers never carry the bytes
Queue-driven transcoding into multiple renditions and segments
HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate delivered via CDN
Metadata in a DB; blobs in S3; storage tiering for the long tail

subjective.question: How would you store and query driver locations in a ride-hailing system, and how do you avoid assigning one driver to two riders?
subjective.answer: Drivers send their location every few seconds, which is a write-heavy stream. I would not write each update to a relational database. Instead, a location service keeps the current position in memory, for example in Redis geospatial sets or an in-memory index, partitioned by city or region. The index uses geohash or a quadtree. To find nearby drivers, I query the rider's cell and its neighbouring cells, then filter and rank by real distance or ETA. Location history goes to a log or stream for analytics. Assignment is different. It needs consistency (CP). When the matching service offers a trip to a driver, it must atomically change the driver's status from available to reserved. It uses a conditional write, compare-and-set, or a short lease on the driver record. If the driver declines or the lease times out, the status goes back to available. This prevents double booking even when two matchers pick the same driver at once.
keyPoints: Location updates are write-heavy: in-memory, partitioned by region
Geohash or quadtree; query neighbouring cells, then filter by distance or ETA
Trip assignment is CP: atomic conditional update or lease on driver status
Location history streamed to a log for analytics

subjective.question: Design search autocomplete that returns the top 5 suggestions per prefix with low latency.
subjective.answer: I would split the system into a read path and a build path. The build path collects search query logs. A batch or streaming job aggregates the logs, for example daily or hourly, into query frequencies. It can also weight recent queries more heavily and filter out offensive terms. From this it builds a trie, and at each node it precomputes and stores the top-k completions for that prefix. The trie is serialised, sharded by prefix range, and loaded into in-memory servers. A prefix-to-suggestions map in a cache also works. The read path is then just a lookup with no ranking at request time. Responses are cacheable at the CDN and in the browser, because the same prefixes repeat. Clients reduce load by debouncing keystrokes and only sending requests after 1–2 characters. Trade-offs: freshness vs cost (rebuilding often vs rarely), memory use of storing top-k at every node, and sharding by prefix, where popular letters need finer splits to avoid hot shards.
keyPoints: Offline aggregation of query logs into frequencies
Trie with precomputed top-k at each node, held in memory
Cache at the CDN and browser; client debounce
Trade-offs: freshness, memory, hot prefix shards

subjective.question: Design a distributed key-value store. Explain partitioning, replication, quorum and conflict handling.
subjective.answer: Partitioning uses consistent hashing. Keys and nodes sit on a hash ring, and each key belongs to the next node clockwise. When a node joins or leaves, only about K/N keys move. Virtual nodes give each server many positions on the ring, which balances load and lets bigger machines take more. Replication copies each key to the next N distinct nodes, for example N=3, ideally across availability zones. Quorum: a write succeeds after W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. With R + W > N, such as N=3, W=2, R=2, read and write sets overlap, so a read sees the latest write while one node can be down. Lower W or R gives lower latency and higher availability, but reads may be stale. Conflicts from concurrent writes are resolved with last-write-wins timestamps (simple, but can lose data) or with vector clocks that keep conflicting versions for the client to merge. Repair uses read repair, hinted handoff and background anti-entropy with Merkle trees.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; about K/N keys move
Replication factor N across failure domains
R + W > N for overlap; N=3, W=2, R=2 is common
Conflicts: LWW vs vector clocks; read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle trees

subjective.question: Design a web crawler that fetches a billion pages a month politely and without duplicates.
subjective.answer: A billion pages a month is about 400 pages per second on average, and more at peak. That makes this a write-heavy, queue-driven system. It starts from seed URLs placed in a URL frontier. The frontier has priority queues (based on importance and how often a page changes) and per-host queues. Each host is handled by one worker at a time, with a delay between requests, so we stay polite. Workers check robots.txt (cached per host), resolve DNS through a local cache, and fetch pages. Content goes to blob storage such as S3, with metadata in a database. A content fingerprint, such as a hash, detects duplicate pages. The parser extracts links and normalises them. A URL-seen check, often a Bloom filter backed by a store, drops URLs already crawled. Then new links go back to the frontier. Workers are partitioned by host hash. Trade-offs: a Bloom filter saves memory but has false positives, which means a few pages are skipped. Other trade-offs are crawl freshness vs breadth, and defending against spider traps with depth limits.
keyPoints: About 400 pages/second; queue-driven and partitioned by host
URL frontier with priority and per-host politeness queues
robots.txt, DNS caching, depth limits against traps
Dedup: Bloom filter for URLs, content hash for pages

subjective.question: How do you structure a 45-minute system design interview, and how do you decide between consistency and availability for different designs?
subjective.answer: I spend about 5 minutes on requirements: functional, non-functional and scale. I agree on scope before drawing anything. I spend about 5 minutes on estimates: QPS (1 day is about 10^5 seconds, and peak is 2–3x average), storage and read/write ratio. Next comes about 5 minutes on the API and the data model. Then about 15 minutes on the high-level diagram, and about 10 minutes on a deep dive into the hardest part. I keep the last minutes for three explicit trade-offs and for failure cases. For CAP, I decide per feature, not per system. Feeds, chat history, caches and view counts favour availability (AP), because slightly stale data is fine. Payments, trip assignment, inventory and unique ID allocation need consistency (CP), because a double charge or double booking is unacceptable. I also state the read/write profile. Read-heavy designs get caches and a CDN. Write-heavy designs get partitioning, queues and log-structured stores.
keyPoints: Requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, deep dive, trade-offs
Use 10^5 seconds per day and 2–3x for peak in estimates
Choose CAP per feature: AP for feeds and caches, CP for payments and IDs
Read-heavy: cache plus CDN; write-heavy: partitioning plus queues

subjective.question: Explain what this Redis Lua script does, why it is written as a Lua script rather than separate commands, and how you would call it from 50 API servers.

code.code:
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 't') or ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ts') or ARGV[3])
local cap, rate, now = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - last) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120)
return allowed

subjective.answer: This is a token bucket. For each user key, it reads the current tokens and the last refill time. It adds tokens for the elapsed time at the refill rate, capped at the bucket capacity. If at least one token is left, it takes one and allows the request. It then saves the new state and sets a TTL so idle users do not use memory. It is a Lua script because Redis runs a script atomically. If two servers ran separate HGET and HSET commands, both could read 1 token and both could allow a request, which is a race. Each API server calls EVALSHA with the user's key, the capacity, the rate and the current time. Passing the time from the app risks clock skew between servers, so I would read time inside the script with redis.call('TIME'). If Redis is down, I fail open for most APIs and fail closed for sensitive ones such as login. A rejected request returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
keyPoints: Identifies the token bucket: refill by elapsed time, capacity cap, take one token per request
Atomic Lua execution prevents the read-modify-write race across servers
The TTL bounds memory for idle keys
Clock skew risk; use Redis TIME
Fail-open vs fail-closed choice, and a 429 response with Retry-After

subjective.question: In a distributed cache, one key (a celebrity profile) receives 500,000 reads per second and overloads the single node that owns it. How do you handle hot keys?
subjective.answer: First, I confirm the problem with per-key metrics, because consistent hashing sends one key to one node however many nodes we add. For read-heavy hot keys, I have three main tools. First, a small in-process L1 cache on each app server with a short TTL of a few seconds. This absorbs most reads and accepts slightly stale data. Second, key replication: store copies as profile:123#0 to profile:123#N spread across nodes, and have clients read a random suffix. Writes must update all copies, or the copies must expire quickly. Third, read replicas for the shard that owns the key. A CDN can also cache public profile data at the edge. For write-hot keys, such as a like counter, I split the counter into sub-counters and sum them on read, or batch increments. The trade-off is freshness and write cost against read capacity. I also detect hot keys automatically so I can apply these steps dynamically.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing alone cannot spread a single key
Local L1 cache with a short TTL, accepting slight staleness
Key replication with random suffixes; writes must update or expire the copies
Split counters for write-hot keys
Monitoring and automatic hot-key detection

subjective.question: Your Snowflake-style ID service suddenly produces duplicate IDs on one host after an NTP correction. Explain the cause and how you would make the generator safe.
subjective.answer: A Snowflake ID combines timestamp, worker ID and sequence. If NTP moves the clock backward, the host reuses milliseconds it has already issued. The same worker ID and sequence then produce IDs that already exist. A duplicate worker ID, for example two containers given the same ID, causes the same symptom, so I check that too. Fixes: the generator stores the last timestamp it used. If the current time is earlier, it either waits until the clock catches up, for small drifts, or refuses to issue IDs and raises an alert, for large drifts. Some designs keep using the last timestamp and borrow from the sequence bits. Configure NTP to slew the clock gradually rather than step it. Assign worker IDs from a coordinator such as ZooKeeper or a DynamoDB conditional write, with leases, so no two live processes share an ID. Finally, a unique constraint on the short-code table is a last line of defence.
keyPoints: Clock moving backward reuses timestamps, causing duplicates
Track the last timestamp; wait or fail when the clock regresses
NTP slewing instead of stepping
Unique worker ID assignment with leases
A database unique constraint as a safety net

subjective.question: Design online presence and 'last seen' for a WhatsApp-scale chat app with hundreds of millions of connected users. What trade-offs do you make?
subjective.answer: Each client holds a WebSocket to a gateway server. A heartbeat every 20 to 30 seconds refreshes a presence key in a sharded store such as Redis, for example presence:user = gateway_id, with a TTL of about two heartbeats. If heartbeats stop, the key expires and the user is offline. 'Last seen' is written when the key expires or the user disconnects. Pushing every status change to every contact causes huge fan-out. So I send updates only to contacts who have that chat open, or who subscribe while viewing it, and batch or debounce flapping on mobile networks. The trade-offs: presence is eventually consistent and can be wrong for up to the TTL window. A longer heartbeat interval saves battery and server load but makes status less fresh. Presence data is soft state, so losing a Redis shard is acceptable; it rebuilds from heartbeats. Privacy settings must be checked before showing last seen.
keyPoints: Heartbeats with TTL keys in a sharded in-memory store
Fan-out limited to active viewers or subscribers, with debouncing
Eventual consistency bounded by the TTL
Battery and load vs freshness trade-off
Presence is rebuildable soft state; privacy checks

subjective.question: A pastebin on AWS supports pastes that expire after 10 minutes, 1 day or never. Metadata is in DynamoDB and content is in S3. How do you implement expiry correctly and cheaply?
subjective.answer: I store an expires_at epoch attribute on each DynamoDB item and enable DynamoDB TTL on it. TTL deletes items for free, but deletion can be delayed, typically by up to a few days. So the read path must also check expires_at and return 404 if the time has passed. That check is what enforces correctness. For S3 content, I enable DynamoDB Streams and use a Lambda that deletes the S3 object when TTL removes the item. As a backup, I write objects under prefixes or tags by expiry class and add S3 Lifecycle rules, for example expire objects tagged ttl=1d after one day. Lifecycle rules work in whole days, so 10-minute pastes rely on the read check plus the stream cleanup. If a CDN caches pastes, its Cache-Control max-age must not exceed the remaining lifetime. 'Never' pastes get no TTL and can move to a cheaper storage class.
keyPoints: DynamoDB TTL is free but delayed; the read path must check expires_at
Streams plus Lambda to delete S3 objects
S3 Lifecycle rules as a backup, with day granularity
CDN max-age bounded by the remaining lifetime
Cost: cheaper storage classes for permanent pastes

subjective.question: Your web crawler's frontier keeps growing, and most new URLs come from a single site with URLs like /calendar?date=2031-01-01, /calendar?date=2031-01-02 and so on. Diagnose the problem and describe the fixes.
subjective.answer: This is a spider trap: a site that generates endless unique URLs, here a calendar, so the crawler never finishes the site and the frontier fills with low-value pages. Fixes, in layers: Normalise URLs by lowercasing the host, sorting query parameters and removing session IDs and tracking parameters. This collapses obvious duplicates. Set per-host and per-domain budgets, such as a maximum number of pages and a maximum URL depth. Limit URL length and the number of distinct values of one query parameter for the same path. Detect content duplicates with checksums or SimHash: if many URLs return near-identical content, lower that pattern's priority. Use the priority queue so low-value hosts do not starve others, and respect robots.txt, which often disallows such paths. Add manual blocklists and alerts when one host's share of the frontier spikes. The trade-off is that strict limits may miss some real pages, which is acceptable for most crawls.
keyPoints: Identifies the spider trap
URL normalisation
Per-host page and depth budgets, URL length and parameter limits
Content fingerprinting (checksum or SimHash) to detect near-duplicates
Prioritisation, robots.txt and monitoring host share

subjective.question: Your news feed uses fan-out on write into per-user Redis feed lists. How do you handle a user deleting a post, or a user unfollowing someone, without rewriting millions of feeds?
subjective.answer: I store only post IDs in feed lists, never post bodies. Post content lives in a post store and cache, and is hydrated at read time. For a delete, I mark the post as deleted in the post store and invalidate its cache entry. During hydration, deleted or hidden posts are filtered out, so they disappear from every feed at once without touching follower lists. An async background job can then remove the ID from feeds lazily, or the ID simply ages out because feeds are capped at a few hundred entries. For an unfollow, I filter at read time against the current follow graph, or run a low-priority async job that removes that author's IDs from the one affected feed, which is cheap. The same read-time filter handles blocks and privacy changes. The trade-off is a little extra read-time work and some dead IDs in the lists, in exchange for instant correctness and no write storms.
keyPoints: Feeds store post IDs; content is hydrated at read time
Soft delete plus filtering during hydration
Lazy cleanup, or let capped feeds age entries out
Unfollow handled by a read-time filter or a small async job
Trades read-time work for avoiding write storms

steps.overview: This final step turns everything you learned into two outcomes: a repeatable 4-step interview framework (clarify, estimate, high-level design, deep dive) and a mapping from generic patterns to the AWS services that SAA-C03 tests. You will also learn the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, which shape how scenario questions are written and how interviewers judge trade-offs.
objectives: Run a 45-minute system design interview using the clarify, estimate, high-level design and deep dive framework inside the time box.
Explain trade-offs out loud by naming the options, the deciding requirement and the cost of the choice.
Map load balancing, scaling, caching, relational storage, NoSQL storage and queueing patterns to ELB, Auto Scaling, ElastiCache, RDS, DynamoDB and SQS.
Apply the six Well-Architected pillars to eliminate wrong answers in SAA-C03 scenario questions.
Score above 80% on a full-length SAA-C03 practice exam and review every wrong answer by domain.

concepts.explanation: Spend about 5 minutes asking about users, core features, read/write ratio, latency targets, consistency needs and availability goals. Write down functional requirements (what it does) and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, durability). Agree on what is out of scope so you do not design features nobody asked for.

Convert daily users into requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth. Round aggressively: 1 day is about 100,000 seconds, and peak is often 2–3x average. The numbers decide whether you need sharding, caching or a queue, so say that link out loud.

Draw the main boxes: client, CDN, load balancer, stateless app tier, cache, database, queue and workers. Walk one read path and one write path end to end. Keep it simple first; an interviewer wants a working design before an optimised one.

Pick the one or two hardest parts, such as the data model, hot keys, fan-out or failure handling, and go deep. Discuss bottlenecks, single points of failure, consistency and monitoring. Let the interviewer steer you if they show interest in a component.

Use a simple pattern: 'Option A gives X, option B gives Y; because our requirement is Z, I choose A, and the cost is W.' Typical pairs are SQL vs NoSQL, strong vs eventual consistency, push vs pull fan-out and cache-aside vs write-through. Saying the cost of your choice shows seniority more than the choice itself.

Load balancer maps to Elastic Load Balancing (ALB for HTTP/HTTPS at layer 7, NLB for TCP/UDP at layer 4 with static IPs). Horizontal scaling maps to EC2 Auto Scaling groups across multiple AZs. Cache maps to ElastiCache (Redis OSS or Valkey for rich data types and replication, Memcached for simple multi-threaded caching), relational data to RDS or Aurora, key-value at massive scale to DynamoDB, and decoupling to SQS.

Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ for automatic failover; it is for availability, not read scaling. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be promoted manually. Exam rule: 'high availability' points to Multi-AZ, while 'read-heavy workload' points to read replicas or a cache.

Standard queues give at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering and very high throughput. FIFO queues give strict ordering and exactly-once processing, with lower throughput limits. Use SQS to absorb spikes and decouple producers from consumers, and scale the workers on queue depth.

It has six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. SAA-C03 questions often hide one pillar as the deciding factor, for example 'most cost-effective' or 'least operational overhead'. In interviews, use the pillars as a final checklist for your design.

keyFacts: SAA-C03: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored), 130 minutes, pass mark 720 on a 100–1000 scale, USD 150.
SAA-C03 domain weights: Design Secure Architectures 30%, Design Resilient Architectures 26%, Design High-Performing Architectures 24%, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%.
Well-Architected has six pillars; Sustainability was added in 2021 as the sixth.
A 45-minute interview time box: about 5 min clarify, 5 min estimate, 15 min high-level design, 15–20 min deep dive and wrap-up.
Estimation shortcuts: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s (use 100,000); 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 requests/second average.
SQS visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds (max 12 hours); message retention defaults to 4 days (max 14 days).
DynamoDB maximum item size is 400 KB; for large objects, store them in S3 and keep a pointer in DynamoDB.
ALB = layer 7 with path- and host-based routing; NLB = layer 4, ultra-low latency, static/Elastic IP per AZ.
Keywords in a question decide the answer: 'least operational overhead' points to managed or serverless services, and 'decouple' points to SQS/SNS.

example.caption: Worked estimate and AWS mapping for a URL shortener (spoken in Step 2 and Step 3)
example.code:
Clarify: 100M new URLs/month, read:write = 100:1, p99 redirect < 50 ms, 5-year retention

Estimate:
  Writes: 100M / (30 x 100,000 s) ~= 35 writes/s (peak ~100/s)
  Reads:  35 x 100 ~= 3,500 reads/s (peak ~10,000/s)
  Storage: 100M x 12 months x 5 yrs = 6B rows x ~500 B ~= 3 TB
  Decision: read-heavy, simple key lookup -> cache + key-value store

High-level design (AWS):
  Route 53 -> CloudFront -> ALB -> EC2 Auto Scaling group (multi-AZ, stateless)
  Read path: app -> ElastiCache (cache-aside, TTL 24h) -> DynamoDB on miss
  Write path: app -> DynamoDB (partition key = short_code)
  Analytics: app -> SQS -> worker fleet -> S3 (click logs)

Trade-off said out loud:
  'DynamoDB over RDS because access is a single-key lookup at 10k reads/s
   and 3 TB grows steadily; I give up ad-hoc SQL joins, which we do not need.'

Well-Architected check:
  Reliability: multi-AZ ASG, DynamoDB replicated across AZs
  Cost: on-demand DynamoDB first, then provisioned capacity once traffic is known
  Security: HTTPS on ALB, IAM roles for EC2, no secrets in code

pitfalls: Jumping to the diagram before clarifying requirements; interviewers mark this down even if the design is good.
Doing estimates and then never using them; every number should drive a decision such as cache, shard or queue.
Choosing RDS Multi-AZ to scale reads; the standby does not serve reads, so use read replicas or ElastiCache.
Ignoring qualifier words like 'most cost-effective', 'least operational overhead' or 'minimal code change'; on the exam, several options often work, but only one matches the qualifier.
Choosing SQS FIFO by default; pick it only when strict ordering or exactly-once processing is required, because Standard scales further.
Spending the whole deep dive on one component and running out of time; watch the clock and summarise at the end.

steps.detail: List functional and non-functional requirements and confirm scale, latency and consistency with the interviewer.

steps.label: Estimate traffic and storage
steps.detail: Calculate QPS, peak load, storage and bandwidth, then state which design choices the numbers force.

steps.label: Define APIs and data model
steps.detail: Write the key endpoints and the main entities with their access patterns.

steps.detail: Connect client, CDN, ELB, Auto Scaling app tier, cache, database and queue, and walk the read and write paths.

steps.detail: For each major choice, name the alternative, the deciding requirement and the cost you accept.

steps.detail: Check the design against the six pillars and mention monitoring, security and cost improvements.

files.code:
# shortlink-mock-design (Step 9: Interview framework)

Practise one system design question end to end: "Design a URL shortener".

## 1. Mock interview (do this twice, with a friend)
- `python3 interview/mock_interview.py` runs a 45-minute time box:
  clarify 5, estimate 5, high-level design 15, deep dive 15, wrap-up 5.
- Your friend reads the prompts aloud. You talk through every trade-off.
- Checkpoint: finish every phase inside its time. The script reports any overrun.

## 2. Estimation
- `python3 interview/estimate.py` prints QPS, storage and cache size.
- Round the numbers and say them out loud. Interviewers want the method, not exact digits.

## 3. Pattern -> AWS service (SAA-C03)
| Pattern | AWS service | File |
|---|---|---|
| Load balancing | Application Load Balancer (ELB) | infra/compute.tf |
| Horizontal scaling | EC2 Auto Scaling (target tracking) | infra/compute.tf |
| Cache-aside | ElastiCache (Redis OSS) | infra/data.tf, app/app.py |
| Key-value store | DynamoDB on-demand | infra/data.tf |
| Relational HA | RDS Multi-AZ (standby, for failover) | infra/data.tf |
| Read scaling | RDS read replica (async) | infra/data.tf |
| Async decoupling | SQS Standard + DLQ | infra/data.tf |
| Strict ordering | SQS FIFO | infra/data.tf |

Exam traps: a Multi-AZ standby instance does not serve reads. A read replica uses async replication,
so reads can be stale. SQS Standard gives at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering.
FIFO gives ordering and exactly-once processing but has lower throughput.

## 4. Well-Architected review (six pillars)
- Operational excellence: everything is in Terraform.
- Security: least-privilege IAM role; security groups only allow ALB -> app -> data.
- Reliability: ASG across AZs, Multi-AZ RDS, Redis failover, SQS DLQ.
- Performance efficiency: cache-aside in front of DynamoDB.
- Cost optimisation: DynamoDB on-demand, Graviton (t4g) data nodes.
- Sustainability: scale in with target tracking; no idle capacity.

## 5. Practice exam
Take one full-length SAA-C03 practice exam in 130 minutes (for example, the official
practice material in AWS Skill Builder). Target above 80%.

Cost warning: `terraform apply` creates billable resources. Run `terraform destroy` when you finish.
RDS is created only to demonstrate Multi-AZ vs read replica; the app does not use it.

"""Timed 4-step mock interview. Partner reads prompts; you answer aloud."""
import time

# (phase, minutes, prompts to cover)
PHASES = [
    ("1. Clarify requirements", 5, [
        "Functional: shorten URL, redirect, custom alias? expiry?",
        "Non-functional: latency target, availability, read:write ratio",
        "Out of scope: say it explicitly (e.g. user accounts)"]),
    ("2. Back-of-envelope estimate", 5, [
        "Run estimate.py numbers: write QPS, read QPS, storage, cache"]),
    ("3. High-level design", 15, [
        "Draw: client -> ALB -> ASG app -> ElastiCache -> DynamoDB",
        "Click events -> SQS -> worker (async)",
        "API: POST /shorten, GET /{code}"]),
    ("4. Deep dive", 15, [
        "Key generation: random base62 + conditional write vs counter",
        "Cache: cache-aside, TTL, hot keys",
        "Failure: AZ loss, Redis failover, poison messages -> DLQ"]),
    ("Wrap-up", 5, [
        "Bottlenecks, what you would do at 10x, Well-Architected pillars"]),
]

# Template for saying every trade-off out loud
TRADE_OFF = "I choose {A} over {B} because {reason}; the cost is {downside}."


def run():
    overruns = []
    print("Trade-off sentence:", TRADE_OFF, "\n")
    for name, minutes, prompts in PHASES:
        print(f"=== {name} ({minutes} min) ===")
        for p in prompts:
            print("  -", p)
        start = time.monotonic()
        input("Press Enter when this phase is done... ")
        used = (time.monotonic() - start) / 60
        print(f"  used {used:.1f} of {minutes} min\n")
        if used > minutes:
            overruns.append((name, used - minutes))
    if overruns:  # checkpoint: finish inside the time box
        for name, extra in overruns:
            print(f"OVER TIME: {name} by {extra:.1f} min")
    else:
        print("PASS: all phases inside the time box")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

"""Back-of-envelope numbers for the URL shortener (Step 2)."""

SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400  # round to ~100k in interviews

new_urls_per_month = 100_000_000  # assumption agreed in Step 1
read_write_ratio = 100            # reads per write
bytes_per_record = 500            # code + long URL + metadata
years_kept = 5
peak_factor = 3                   # peak vs average traffic

writes_per_day = new_urls_per_month / 30
write_qps = writes_per_day / SECONDS_PER_DAY
read_qps = write_qps * read_write_ratio

total_records = new_urls_per_month * 12 * years_kept
storage_tb = total_records * bytes_per_record / 1e12

# 80/20 rule: cache 20% of one day's reads
cache_gb = 0.2 * read_qps * SECONDS_PER_DAY * bytes_per_record / 1e9

print(f"Write QPS avg/peak : {write_qps:,.0f} / {write_qps * peak_factor:,.0f}")
print(f"Read  QPS avg/peak : {read_qps:,.0f} / {read_qps * peak_factor:,.0f}")
print(f"Records in {years_kept} yrs  : {total_records:,.0f}")
print(f"Storage            : {storage_tb:,.1f} TB")
print(f"Cache (upper bound): {cache_gb:,.0f} GB")
print("Note: many reads repeat the same hot URLs, so real cache need is lower.")

# 7 base62 chars give 62**7 = ~3.5 trillion codes: enough for 6 billion records
print(f"Base62 length 7 capacity: {62**7:,}")

"""URL shortener service: cache-aside on ElastiCache, DynamoDB store, SQS events."""
import json
import os
import secrets
import string

import boto3
import redis
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
from flask import Flask, abort, jsonify, redirect, request

REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-south-1")
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name=REGION).Table(os.environ["TABLE_NAME"])
sqs = boto3.client("sqs", region_name=REGION)
QUEUE_URL = os.environ["QUEUE_URL"]
cache = redis.Redis(host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"], port=6379, decode_responses=True)
ALPHABET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits  # base62
app = Flask(__name__)


@app.get("/health")  # ALB target group health check
def health():
    return "ok"


@app.post("/shorten")
def shorten():
    url = request.get_json(force=True)["url"]
    for _ in range(3):  # retry on rare collision
        code = "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(7))
        try:
            # Conditional write: no coordination service needed for unique keys
            table.put_item(Item={"code": code, "url": url},
                           ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(code)")
            return jsonify(code=code), 201
        except ClientError as e:
            if e.response["Error"]["Code"] != "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
                raise
    abort(503)


@app.get("/<code>")
def resolve(code):
    url = cache.get(code)  # 1. try cache
    if url is None:
        item = table.get_item(Key={"code": code}).get("Item")  # 2. miss -> DB
        if not item:
            abort(404)
        url = item["url"]
        cache.set(code, url, ex=3600)  # 3. fill cache with TTL
    try:
        # Async analytics: SQS Standard (at-least-once), so the consumer must be idempotent
        sqs.send_message(QueueUrl=QUEUE_URL, MessageBody=json.dumps({"code": code}))
    except ClientError:
        pass  # trade-off: lose a click event rather than fail the redirect
    # 302 so every click reaches us (analytics); 301 would let browsers cache it
    return redirect(url, code=302)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8080")))

objective.question: In a 45-minute system design interview, which time split best follows the 4-step framework?
options: About 15 min clarify, 15 min estimate, 10 min high-level design, 5 min deep dive
About 2 min clarify, 0 min estimate, 40 min deep dive on the database
About 20 min high-level design, 20 min estimate, 5 min clarify at the end
About 5 min clarify, 5 min estimate, 15 min high-level design, 15–20 min deep dive and wrap-up
objective.explanation: The recommended split keeps clarifying and estimating short and gives most of the time to design and deep dive. The other splits either skip steps, spend too long on numbers, or clarify too late to shape the design.

objective.question: A service expects 10 million requests per day. Using the interview shortcut of 1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds, what is the approximate average request rate?
options: About 100 requests per second
About 10,000 requests per second
About 1,000 requests per second
About 10 requests per second
objective.explanation: 10,000,000 ÷ 100,000 ≈ 100 requests per second. The exact figure is about 116, which is consistent with 1 million per day ≈ 12 per second. The other options are off by a factor of 10 or more.

objective.question: A company runs one web application. Requests to /api/* must go to one group of EC2 instances and requests to /images/* to another. Which load balancer should a solutions architect choose?
options: Application Load Balancer with path-based routing rules
Gateway Load Balancer in front of both groups
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Network Load Balancer with two listeners
objective.explanation: ALB works at layer 7 and supports path- and host-based routing to different target groups. NLB works at layer 4 and cannot read URL paths, Gateway Load Balancer is for third-party network appliances, and sticky sessions do not route by path.

objective.question: A gaming company needs a load balancer for a TCP/UDP game server fleet. It needs ultra-low latency, millions of requests per second, and fixed IP addresses that partners can allow-list. What should it use?
options: Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP in each Availability Zone
Amazon CloudFront with an S3 origin
Application Load Balancer behind Amazon Route 53 weighted records
Application Load Balancer with host-based routing
objective.explanation: NLB operates at layer 4, handles TCP/UDP with very low latency, and supports a static or Elastic IP per AZ for allow-listing. ALB is HTTP/HTTPS only and does not give static IPs per AZ, and CloudFront with S3 does not serve a game server fleet.

objective.question: An e-commerce site uses Amazon RDS for MySQL. Nightly reporting queries slow down the production database and hurt checkout performance. What is the MOST suitable fix?
options: Increase the backup retention period
Move the reporting queries into an SQS queue
Create a read replica and point the reporting tool at it
Enable Multi-AZ and send reports to the standby instance
objective.explanation: A read replica offloads read-heavy work, such as reporting, from the primary. In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby cannot serve reads. Backup retention has no effect on query load, and SQS does not run SQL queries.

objective.question: A company needs its Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database to survive an Availability Zone failure with automatic failover and no data loss for committed transactions. Which option meets this requirement?
options: Daily automated snapshots copied to another Region
An ElastiCache cluster in front of the database
RDS Multi-AZ deployment with a synchronous standby in another AZ
A cross-Region read replica with manual promotion
objective.explanation: Multi-AZ replicates synchronously to a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically, so committed data is not lost. Read replicas replicate asynchronously and need manual promotion. Snapshots can lose data written since the last snapshot, and a cache does not give database high availability.

objective.question: A banking app sends account transactions through a queue. For each account, transactions must be processed in the exact order they were sent, and duplicates must not be introduced. Which service configuration fits?
options: SQS FIFO queue using the account ID as the message group ID
SQS Standard queue with a dead-letter queue
SNS standard topic with multiple subscribers
SQS Standard queue with long polling
objective.explanation: FIFO queues preserve order within a message group and support exactly-once processing through deduplication. Using the account ID as the group ID keeps each account in order while different accounts are processed in parallel. Standard queues and standard SNS topics give best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery, and a DLQ does not change ordering.

objective.question: Workers poll an SQS Standard queue. Each message takes about 90 seconds to process. The team sees many messages processed twice, although no worker crashed. The queue uses default settings. What should the architect change?
options: Increase the visibility timeout to longer than the processing time
Switch to short polling
Reduce the number of worker instances
Increase the message retention period to 14 days
objective.explanation: The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds, so the message becomes visible again while it is still being processed and another worker picks it up. Setting the timeout above the processing time fixes this. Retention only controls how long unprocessed messages are kept, and polling mode or worker count does not address the root cause.

objective.question: A mobile app stores user profiles in Amazon DynamoDB. Each profile now needs a high-resolution photo of about 3 MB. What is the recommended design?
options: Split the photo across several DynamoDB items and join them in the app
Store the photo in Amazon S3 and save the object key in the DynamoDB item
Move the whole table to Amazon RDS to allow larger rows
Store the photo as a binary attribute in the same DynamoDB item
objective.explanation: The maximum DynamoDB item size is 400 KB, so large objects belong in S3 with a pointer kept in DynamoDB. Splitting items adds complexity and cost, and moving to RDS is a large change that is not needed.

objective.question: A product catalogue on Amazon RDS gets the same read queries thousands of times per minute. Database CPU is high and page latency is rising. The data changes only a few times a day. Which solution gives the BEST read performance improvement?
options: Enable RDS Multi-AZ
Put an SQS queue between the web tier and RDS
Increase the EBS volume size of the web servers
Add Amazon ElastiCache in front of RDS using a cache-aside pattern
objective.explanation: Repeated reads of slowly changing data are a classic case for an in-memory cache like ElastiCache, which cuts database load and latency. Multi-AZ is for availability, not read scaling. SQS is for asynchronous writes and work, not synchronous reads, and web server disk size is unrelated.

objective.question: Which pillar was added to the AWS Well-Architected Framework in 2021, bringing the total to six?
options: Cost Optimization
Performance Efficiency
Sustainability
Operational Excellence
objective.explanation: Sustainability was added in 2021 as the sixth pillar. Operational Excellence, Cost Optimization and Performance Efficiency were already pillars, along with Security and Reliability.

objective.question: A video platform's upload API sends transcoding jobs directly to EC2 workers. Traffic spikes cause workers to be overwhelmed and jobs are lost. The company wants to decouple the components and scale workers automatically with the LEAST operational overhead. What should the architect do?
options: Add a larger EC2 instance type for the workers and increase EBS IOPS
Store jobs in an RDS table and have workers poll it every second
Place an NLB in front of the workers with cross-zone load balancing
Put the jobs in an SQS queue and scale an EC2 Auto Scaling group of workers based on queue depth per instance
objective.explanation: 'Decouple' points to SQS, which buffers spikes so jobs are not lost, and scaling on backlog per instance matches worker count to demand. A bigger instance still overloads during spikes, polling a database table adds load and custom code, and an NLB only spreads load without buffering it.

objective.question: A solutions architect attaches this scaling policy to an EC2 Auto Scaling group. What does the policy do?
options: It adds exactly one instance each time any single instance goes above 50% CPU
It launches 50% more instances on a fixed schedule during business hours
It terminates any instance whose CPU stays below 50% for five minutes
It adds or removes instances automatically to keep the group's average CPU utilisation close to 50%
objective.explanation: This is a target tracking policy. Auto Scaling creates the CloudWatch alarms itself and adjusts capacity to hold the average metric near the target value. It does not react to single instances. It is not a scheduled or step policy, and it does not terminate instances based on their own CPU.

objective.question: An SQS queue has the following redrive policy. What happens to a message that consumers keep failing to process?
options: SQS returns the message to the producer after five retries
The message is copied to orders-dlq and kept there for five days
After the message has been received five times without being deleted, SQS moves it to the orders-dlq queue
SQS deletes the message after five failed processing attempts
objective.explanation: maxReceiveCount counts how many times a message is received but not deleted. When the receive count goes past this value, SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue so it stops blocking the main queue. SQS never deletes failed messages on its own and never returns them to the producer. The DLQ's retention period is a separate setting.

objective.question: Worker EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group process jobs from an SQS queue. Queue depth swings from near zero to 50,000 messages within minutes. Scaling on CPU reacts too late, and jobs wait too long. The team knows how long one job takes and the maximum acceptable wait time. Which scaling approach does AWS recommend?
options: Target tracking on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, with a fixed target of 1,000 messages
Step scaling on the NetworkIn metric of the worker instances
Target tracking on a custom backlog-per-instance metric (visible messages ÷ running instances), with the target set to acceptable latency ÷ time per message
Scheduled scaling that doubles capacity every hour
objective.explanation: AWS recommends a backlog-per-instance metric because it ties capacity directly to the work waiting for each worker and to your latency goal. Raw queue depth on its own does not change as instances are added, so it is a poor target-tracking metric. Scheduled scaling and network metrics do not follow an unpredictable backlog.

objective.question: A gaming company needs a real-time leaderboard that ranks millions of players by score with sub-millisecond reads. The cache must replicate across Availability Zones with automatic failover, and data should survive a node restart. Which service fits BEST?
options: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of an RDS MySQL table
An Amazon RDS read replica with an ORDER BY score query
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis OSS (or Valkey) with Multi-AZ replication, using sorted sets
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes
objective.explanation: Redis-compatible ElastiCache supports sorted sets, which suit ranking. It also supports replicas with Multi-AZ automatic failover and optional persistence. Memcached has no replication, no persistence and no rich data types. DAX works only with DynamoDB. An RDS ORDER BY query over millions of rows will not give sub-millisecond reads.

objective.question: An IoT platform writes sensor readings to a DynamoDB table whose partition key is the current date (for example, 2026-03-14). Writes are throttled during the day, even though total consumed capacity is well below the table's provisioned capacity. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add a global secondary index on the date attribute
Increase the table's provisioned write capacity tenfold
Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as device ID with a timestamp sort key, or add a random suffix to spread writes (write sharding)
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode and keep the same key
objective.explanation: All writes for a day land on one partition key, so one partition hits its per-partition throughput limit even when table-level capacity is free. A high-cardinality key or write sharding spreads the load across partitions. Changing capacity mode or raising capacity does not remove the per-partition limit. A GSI on date would create the same hot key.

objective.question: Users of a web app behind an Application Load Balancer are randomly logged out, usually when the Auto Scaling group scales in. Sticky sessions are enabled, and session data is held in each instance's memory. What should the architect do?
options: Increase the ALB stickiness cookie duration to seven days
Disable scale-in on the Auto Scaling group
Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer
Store session state in Amazon ElastiCache or Amazon DynamoDB so the web tier becomes stateless
objective.explanation: Sessions are lost when the instance that holds them is terminated. Moving state to a shared store means any instance can serve any user, and scaling stays safe. A longer cookie does not help once the instance is gone. Disabling scale-in wastes money, and an NLB does not solve the session-state problem.

objective.question: A developer changes a consumer to run the command below instead of making receive calls with no wait time. What is the main effect?

code.code:
aws sqs receive-message \
  --queue-url https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/111122223333/jobs \
  --wait-time-seconds 20 \
  --max-number-of-messages 10

options: SQS delays delivery of new messages by 20 seconds
The call uses long polling: it waits up to 20 seconds for messages to arrive and returns up to 10 at once, which cuts empty responses and request cost
The queue is converted to a FIFO queue with batches of 10
Received messages stay hidden from other consumers for 20 seconds
objective.explanation: --wait-time-seconds turns on long polling, up to its maximum of 20 seconds. Fewer empty receives means lower cost and less CPU spent on polling. Message hiding is controlled by --visibility-timeout, delivery delay is a delay-queue setting, and a queue cannot be converted to FIFO.

subjective.question: Walk me through how you would use the 4-step framework to design a URL shortener in a 45-minute interview.
subjective.answer: First, I clarify for about five minutes. I confirm the core features, which are shortening a URL and redirecting. I ask about custom aliases, expiry, analytics, and scale, for example 100 million new URLs a month with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. Second, I estimate. About 100 million writes a month is roughly 40 writes per second, so reads are about 4,000 per second. At about 500 bytes per record, that is about 50 GB a month. Third, I draw the high-level design: clients, a load balancer, stateless API servers, a key generation approach such as base62 of a unique ID, a key-value store, and a cache for hot redirects. Fourth, I deep dive where the risk is. Here that means ID generation without collisions, cache hit rates, and a 301 vs 302 redirect, which trades caching against analytics. I finish by stating bottlenecks and what I would change at 10x scale.
keyPoints: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements before drawing anything
Estimate QPS, read/write ratio and storage with round numbers
High-level design: LB, stateless app tier, data store, cache
Deep dive on the riskiest part, such as key generation and caching
Keep to the time box and wrap up with bottlenecks and scaling

subjective.question: You are asked to design a chat application. What questions would you ask in the clarify step, and why do they matter?
subjective.answer: I would split my questions into functional and non-functional ones. Functional: Is it one-to-one only, or are there group chats too, and how large can groups get? Do we need online status, read receipts, media sharing and message history? Should it work across devices? Non-functional: How many daily active users are there, and how many messages does each send? What latency is acceptable for delivery? Must messages never be lost, and must they arrive in order? Are there data residency or encryption rules? These answers change the design. Large groups push me toward fan-out strategies. Strict ordering points to per-conversation sequencing. Long history drives the storage choice. Real-time delivery suggests WebSockets. I would also agree on what is out of scope so I don't waste time later. I write the agreed requirements on the board so both of us can refer back to them.
keyPoints: Separate functional from non-functional requirements
Ask about scale: DAU, messages per user, group size
Ask about latency, durability, ordering and security needs
Agree what is out of scope
Explain how each answer changes the design

subjective.question: Do a back-of-envelope estimate for a photo-sharing app with 10 million daily active users. Each user uploads 0.2 photos a day, each photo is about 2 MB, and each user views 50 photos a day.
subjective.answer: Uploads: 10 million × 0.2 = 2 million photos a day. Using 1 day ≈ 100,000 seconds, that is about 20 uploads per second on average. If I assume peak is about three times the average, that is about 60 per second. Storage: 2 million × 2 MB = 4 TB a day, or about 1.5 PB a year before replication and thumbnails. Reads: 10 million × 50 = 500 million views a day, which is about 5,000 reads per second on average and around 15,000 at peak. Conclusions: the system is heavily read-dominated, at about 250:1. Photos belong in object storage such as S3 behind a CDN, with metadata in a scalable database. The write path is modest, so I would spend my design effort on caching, the CDN, and storage cost tiers. I say every assumption out loud so the interviewer can correct it.
keyPoints: Use round numbers: 1 day ≈ 100,000 s
Calculate average and peak QPS separately for reads and writes
Calculate daily and yearly storage, and mention replication
Draw conclusions: read-heavy, so use CDN, object storage and cache
State assumptions aloud

subjective.question: How do you talk through trade-offs out loud? Give an example with choosing between a relational database and DynamoDB.
subjective.answer: I name the options, the criteria, my choice, and what I give up. For example: 'For orders I could use RDS or DynamoDB. The criteria are query flexibility, consistency, scale and operational effort. RDS gives joins, ad-hoc queries and strong transactional guarantees, but it scales writes mainly by moving to bigger instances or sharding. DynamoDB scales almost without limit with predictable latency and very little operations work, but I must design around known access patterns, and complex queries are harder. Our access patterns are simple key lookups at high volume, so I choose DynamoDB. The cost is less flexible reporting, so I would export data to an analytics store.' I also say what would change my mind, for example 'if finance needs complex joins, I would pick RDS.' This shows judgement rather than memorised answers, and it invites the interviewer to steer.
keyPoints: State the options and the decision criteria
Give pros and cons of each against the requirements
Make a clear choice and name what you give up
Say what condition would change the decision
Link the choice back to the clarified requirements

subjective.question: Explain the difference between Amazon RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas. When would you use each, and can you use both together?
subjective.answer: Multi-AZ is for high availability. RDS keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone. If the primary or its AZ fails, RDS fails over automatically and the DNS endpoint points to the new primary. In the classic Multi-AZ instance deployment, the standby cannot serve reads, so it does not improve read performance. Read replicas are for read scaling. They use asynchronous replication, so they can lag slightly behind. They serve read traffic such as reporting, and they can be placed in other Regions. A replica can be promoted manually for disaster recovery, but that is not automatic failover. In the exam, 'high availability' or 'automatic failover' points to Multi-AZ, and 'read-heavy' or 'offload reporting' points to read replicas. Yes, they are often combined: Multi-AZ protects the primary, and replicas absorb reads.
keyPoints: Multi-AZ: synchronous standby with automatic failover, for availability
Classic Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads
Read replicas: asynchronous, for scaling reads, can be cross-Region
Replica promotion is manual, so possible lag and data loss
The two are commonly used together

subjective.question: Compare SQS Standard and SQS FIFO queues. How do you pick one in a design?
subjective.answer: Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, with nearly unlimited throughput. This means a message may occasionally arrive twice or out of order, so consumers must be idempotent. FIFO queues guarantee first-in-first-out order within a message group and support exactly-once processing through deduplication. They have lower throughput limits than Standard. I pick Standard for most decoupling work where order doesn't matter, such as sending emails, resizing images, or processing logs, because it scales the most. I pick FIFO when order or no-duplicates is a business rule, such as bank transactions or inventory updates. Even then, I use the message group ID wisely, for example one group per account, so different groups still process in parallel. Both support dead-letter queues, a visibility timeout that defaults to 30 seconds, and retention of 4 days by default, configurable up to 14 days.
keyPoints: Standard: at-least-once, best-effort order, highest throughput
FIFO: strict order per message group, exactly-once processing, lower throughput
Consumers of Standard queues should be idempotent
Use message group IDs for parallelism in FIFO
Shared features: DLQ, visibility timeout, retention settings

subjective.question: Map a classic scalable three-tier web application to AWS services, and explain the role of each service.
subjective.answer: At the edge, Route 53 handles DNS and CloudFront caches static content. Static assets live in S3. An Application Load Balancer spreads HTTP traffic across EC2 instances in at least two Availability Zones. The instances sit in an Auto Scaling group that adds or removes capacity based on metrics such as CPU or request count. The app tier is stateless. Sessions go to ElastiCache or DynamoDB, so any instance can serve any user. ElastiCache also caches hot database reads. For relational data, I use RDS with Multi-AZ for availability and read replicas for read-heavy work. For high-scale key-value data, I use DynamoDB. Slow or spiky work, such as sending emails or generating reports, goes through SQS to worker instances, which decouples the tiers. Each service maps to a pattern: load balancing, horizontal scaling, caching, replication, and asynchronous messaging.
keyPoints: ALB and Auto Scaling across multiple AZs for a stateless web tier
ElastiCache for caching and session storage
RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas, or DynamoDB, for data
SQS to decouple slow or spiky work
Each service corresponds to a general system design pattern

subjective.question: Name the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework and give one practical design practice for each.
subjective.answer: Operational Excellence: automate deployments with infrastructure as code and learn from incidents through runbooks and post-mortems. Security: apply least-privilege IAM, encrypt data at rest and in transit, and enable traceability with logging. Reliability: deploy across multiple Availability Zones, use automatic recovery such as Auto Scaling and RDS Multi-AZ, and test recovery procedures. Performance Efficiency: choose the right resource types, use caching and CDNs, and use managed or serverless services so you can experiment easily. Cost Optimization: right-size instances, use Savings Plans or Spot where they fit, and switch off unused resources. Sustainability: maximise utilisation, choose efficient managed services, and reduce unnecessary data movement and storage. Sustainability was added in 2021 as the sixth pillar. In an interview, I use the pillars as a checklist during wrap-up to show I have thought beyond functionality.
keyPoints: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability
Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability
Sustainability added in 2021
One concrete practice per pillar
Use the pillars as a design review checklist

subjective.question: In the deep dive step, how do you decide what to go deep on? Give an example of handling a hot key or cache stampede.
subjective.answer: I go deep on the part most likely to fail or limit scale, based on my estimates, or on whatever the interviewer signals interest in. Typical candidates are the data store under peak write load, hot keys, consistency, and failure handling. For example, in a news site, a viral article can cause a cache stampede. When its cache entry expires, thousands of requests hit the database at once. Fixes include request coalescing, where only one request rebuilds the entry while the others wait or get the stale value. Others are adding random jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire together, refreshing hot keys early, and serving stale data briefly. For a hot partition key in DynamoDB, I would spread writes by adding a suffix to the key, or cache reads in front of it. I explain the trade-off each time: more complexity and slightly stale data in exchange for protecting the database.
keyPoints: Pick the riskiest bottleneck, guided by estimates and interviewer cues
Explain the failure mode clearly first
Offer concrete mitigations: coalescing, TTL jitter, early refresh, key sharding
State the trade-off, such as staleness or complexity
Tie the fix back to the requirements

subjective.question: Describe your strategy for the SAA-C03 exam: its format, domain weights, and how to read scenario questions.
subjective.answer: SAA-C03 has 65 questions, of which 50 are scored and 15 are unscored, in 130 minutes. The pass mark is 720 on a 100–1000 scale, and the fee is USD 150. The domains are Design Secure Architectures at 30%, Design Resilient Architectures at 26%, Design High-Performing Architectures at 24%, and Design Cost-Optimized Architectures at 20%. Security therefore deserves the most revision. That is about two minutes per question, so I flag long ones and return to them later. There is no penalty for guessing, so I answer everything. For scenarios, I find the deciding keyword first. 'Least operational overhead' points to managed or serverless services. 'Decouple' points to SQS or SNS. 'Highly available' points to Multi-AZ. 'Read-heavy' points to read replicas or caching. 'Most cost-effective' rules out over-built options. Then I eliminate answers that break a stated requirement. Before booking, I aim to score above 80% on full-length practice exams.
keyPoints: 65 questions (50 scored), 130 minutes, 720/1000 to pass, USD 150
Domain weights 30/26/24/20, with Security the heaviest
Find the deciding keyword in each scenario
Eliminate options that break a requirement; answer every question
Target above 80% on practice exams before booking

subjective.question: Design a reliable order-processing pipeline on AWS using SQS. Cover failures, duplicates and scaling.
subjective.answer: The API tier on an ALB with Auto Scaling validates the order, saves it with a 'pending' status, and sends a message to SQS. This decouples checkout from slow downstream steps such as payment and inventory. Workers in an Auto Scaling group, or Lambda functions, poll with long polling. Workers scale on queue backlog per instance. I set the visibility timeout longer than the worst-case processing time so that a message is not picked up twice while still in progress. A worker deletes the message only after it succeeds. If processing keeps failing, a redrive policy moves the message to a dead-letter queue after a set number of receives, where I alarm on it and inspect it. With a Standard queue, delivery is at-least-once, so I make workers idempotent, using an order ID with a conditional write in DynamoDB. If per-customer order matters, I use FIFO with the customer ID as the message group ID.
keyPoints: SQS decouples the API from slow downstream work
Visibility timeout set above processing time; delete only after success
Dead-letter queue with redrive policy and alarms
Idempotent consumers for at-least-once delivery, or FIFO when order matters
Scale workers on queue backlog

subjective.question: Late in the interview, the interviewer says: 'Traffic just grew 10x. What breaks in your design?' How do you answer?
subjective.answer: I stay calm and go through the design layer by layer, using numbers. First, the stateless app tier: Auto Scaling and the load balancer handle 10x by adding instances, but I would check account limits and warm-up time. Next, the cache: a larger working set means I may need more ElastiCache nodes or cluster mode to shard data. The database usually breaks first. Reads can move to more read replicas and the cache. Writes at 10x may exceed a single primary, so I would consider sharding, moving hot tables to DynamoDB, or buffering writes through SQS. I would also check hot keys, connection limits, and costs, because 10x traffic may mean 10x spend unless I use Savings Plans or caching. I finish by ranking the fixes by urgency. This shows I understand bottlenecks rather than just saying 'add more servers'.
keyPoints: Re-estimate with 10x numbers
Check each layer: app tier, cache, database, queues
Identify the database write path as the usual first bottleneck
Propose specific fixes: sharding, replicas, DynamoDB, SQS buffering
Mention limits and cost, then rank fixes by priority

subjective.question: This cache-aside code runs in front of RDS for a product catalogue. Users report that prices stay wrong for days after an update. Explain why, and how you would fix it.
subjective.answer: This is lazy loading (cache-aside), and it has two bugs. First, redis.set has no TTL, so a cached entry never expires. Second, update_price writes to the database but never touches the cache. After an update, readers keep getting the old cached row until it is evicted for memory reasons, which can take days. To fix it, delete the key after the database write succeeds, so the next read reloads fresh data. Deleting is safer than updating the cache in place because it avoids race conditions. Also set a TTL, for example with redis.set(key, value, ex=3600), as a safety net in case an invalidation is ever missed. For hot keys, add jitter to the TTL so many keys do not expire together, and consider a short lock or request coalescing to avoid a stampede on a miss. If staleness must be near zero, use write-through, accepting extra write latency and cache space for rarely read items.
keyPoints: No TTL means entries never expire
Writes do not invalidate the cache, so data stays stale
Delete the key after the DB commit; add a TTL as a safety net
TTL jitter and request coalescing prevent a stampede
Write-through is an option, with its own cost trade-off

subjective.question: After a new deployment, the instances behind your ALB keep getting marked unhealthy. The Auto Scaling group terminates and replaces them in a loop. How do you troubleshoot this?
subjective.answer: First, I check the target group's health check settings: the path, port, protocol and success codes. A common cause is a new release that moved or protected the health endpoint, so it now returns 404 or 401 instead of 200. Next, I compare how long the app takes to start with the health check grace period. If the app needs 3 minutes to warm up but the grace period is 60 seconds, Auto Scaling kills instances before they are ready. I would raise the grace period, or use lifecycle hooks. Then I check the security groups: the instance security group must allow traffic from the ALB's security group on the health check port. I also read the instance logs, using SSM Session Manager or CloudWatch Logs, for crashes or missing configuration and secrets. To stop the churn while I investigate, I can suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy process, or roll back with an instance refresh to the previous launch template version.
keyPoints: Check the health check path, port and success codes
Health check grace period compared with app start-up time
Security group must allow ALB-to-instance traffic on the health port
Check app logs for crashes and missing configuration
Suspend ReplaceUnhealthy or roll back the launch template

subjective.question: A start-up runs its app on two EC2 instances in a single Availability Zone, using a single-AZ RDS instance with automated backups turned off. Admins SSH in to deploy by hand, and the instances are oversized at 10% CPU. Review it against the Well-Architected pillars.
subjective.answer: Reliability is the biggest risk. One AZ and a single-AZ database mean an AZ outage takes everything down. With no backups, a bad delete is permanent. I would spread an Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an ALB, enable RDS Multi-AZ, and turn on automated backups with point-in-time recovery. Operational excellence: manual SSH deployments are error-prone. Use infrastructure as code, such as CloudFormation or CDK, and a CI/CD pipeline that ships small, reversible changes. Security: SSH access widens the attack surface. Use SSM Session Manager, least-privilege IAM roles and encryption. Cost optimisation: right-size the instances and consider Savings Plans or Graviton. Performance efficiency: add caching and scale horizontally instead of buying big instances. Sustainability: right-sizing and managed services cut wasted resources. I would fix reliability and backups first, because data loss cannot be undone.
keyPoints: Single AZ and no backups is the top reliability risk
Multi-AZ ALB, Auto Scaling and RDS Multi-AZ, plus PITR backups
IaC and CI/CD instead of manual SSH (operational excellence)
Session Manager and least privilege for security
Right-sizing for cost and sustainability; prioritise by impact

subjective.question: Design a DynamoDB table for an orders service with these access patterns: get one order by ID, list a customer's orders newest first, and list all orders in PENDING status for an ops dashboard. What keys and indexes would you use?
subjective.answer: I start from the access patterns, not the entities. For the base table, I use partition key PK = CUSTOMER#<customerId> and sort key SK = ORDER#<ISO timestamp>#<orderId>. A Query on PK with ScanIndexForward=false lists a customer's orders newest first. For lookup by order ID, I add a GSI keyed on orderId, or write a small item keyed ORDER#<orderId>. The PENDING dashboard is the trap. A GSI with status as its partition key would have very low cardinality: almost all writes would hit a few keys such as PENDING and SHIPPED, creating a hot partition. Better is a sparse GSI. Set an attribute such as pendingShard = PENDING#<0-9> only while the order is pending, and remove it when the status changes. The index then holds only pending orders, spread over 10 shards, and the dashboard queries the shards in parallel. The trade-off is that DynamoDB gives predictable scale, but ad-hoc queries need new indexes, unlike SQL.
keyPoints: Design keys from the access patterns
Customer partition key with a timestamp sort key for newest-first queries
GSI or separate item for lookup by order ID
Low-cardinality status key creates a hot partition
Sparse, sharded GSI for pending orders; trade-off with SQL flexibility

subjective.question: You will also sit the Google Cloud Professional Cloud Architect and Azure AZ-305 exams. Map the classic scalable pattern (load balancer, autoscaled compute, cache, relational DB, NoSQL, queue) to the equivalent services on GCP and Azure.
subjective.answer: The patterns stay the same; only the product names change. Load balancer: AWS ELB (ALB/NLB) maps to Google Cloud Load Balancing (Application or Network Load Balancer) and to Azure Application Gateway for layer 7 or Azure Load Balancer for layer 4, with Front Door for global HTTP. Autoscaled compute: EC2 Auto Scaling maps to Managed Instance Groups on GCP and Virtual Machine Scale Sets on Azure. Cache: ElastiCache maps to Memorystore and Azure Cache for Redis. Relational database: RDS maps to Cloud SQL (or AlloyDB/Spanner for bigger needs) and Azure SQL Database or Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL. NoSQL: DynamoDB maps roughly to Firestore or Bigtable, and to Azure Cosmos DB. Queue: SQS maps to Pub/Sub and to Azure Service Bus or Storage Queues. In an interview, name the pattern first and the product second. This shows you understand the design, not just one vendor.
keyPoints: ELB ↔ Cloud Load Balancing ↔ Application Gateway/Load Balancer
Auto Scaling ↔ Managed Instance Groups ↔ VM Scale Sets
ElastiCache ↔ Memorystore ↔ Azure Cache for Redis
RDS ↔ Cloud SQL ↔ Azure SQL; DynamoDB ↔ Firestore/Bigtable ↔ Cosmos DB
SQS ↔ Pub/Sub ↔ Service Bus; lead with the pattern

subjective.question: Design a rate limiter for a public API that allows 100 requests per minute per API key, running across many stateless API servers. Walk through it with the framework.
subjective.answer: Clarify: Is the limit per key or per IP? Should it be a hard or a soft limit? Is it global or per region? What should a client see when limited? I would return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. Estimate: at 1 million keys and 50,000 requests per second, each check must add under a millisecond, so it cannot hit a database. High level: the API gateway or middleware calls a shared counter store, ElastiCache for Redis, because local counters on each server cannot see the global total. On AWS, API Gateway usage plans can handle simple per-key throttling without custom code. Deep dive on the algorithm: a fixed window is simple but allows bursts at window edges. A sliding window or token bucket is smoother. I would use a token bucket in a Redis Lua script so the check and the decrement are atomic. Trade-offs: if Redis is down, do we fail open (stay available) or fail closed (stay protected)? For most APIs I would fail open and alert.
keyPoints: Clarify scope, limit type and the 429 response
Shared Redis counter, because servers are stateless
Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket
Atomic check-and-decrement with a Lua script
Fail-open vs fail-closed trade-off; API Gateway throttling as an option

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'Why not just buy a bigger server instead of all these load balancers and caches?' How do you answer, and where does each approach fit?
subjective.answer: I agree that vertical scaling is a valid first step, and I say so. A bigger instance is simple: there are no code changes, no distributed-systems problems, and strong consistency comes for free. For an early product with a few thousand users, it is often the right answer. But it has three limits. There is a hardware ceiling. It is still a single point of failure, so one instance or AZ failure means a full outage. And resizing usually needs downtime, while you pay for peak capacity all day. Horizontal scaling with stateless servers behind an ELB in an Auto Scaling group across AZs removes the single point of failure and follows demand. The cost is complexity: external session state, cache invalidation and eventual consistency. My usual answer is a mix. Scale the database vertically for as long as possible, because databases are hard to shard, and scale the stateless web tier horizontally from day one, because it is cheap. Then I tie the choice back to the availability and growth numbers we agreed in the clarify step.
keyPoints: Acknowledge that vertical scaling is simple and valid early on
Limits: hardware ceiling, single point of failure, downtime, paying for peak
Horizontal: high availability and elasticity, at the cost of complexity
Common mix: stateless tier horizontal, database vertical as long as possible
Link the decision to the requirements set in the clarify step
